r1-avg-margin.evidence:
Source: Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao, Kakade, "Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks", ICLR 2024 Spotlight, arXiv:2311.07568v2. I fetched the HTML and the abs page and grepped them.

What they prove:
- Sec 3.2 "Multi-Class Classification" defines the class-weighted margin for any weighting tau(x,y) over the wrong labels: g'(theta,x,y) = f(theta,x)[y] - sum_{y' != y} tau(x,y)[y'] f(theta,x)[y'].
- Same section, verbatim: "Note that g'(theta,x,y) >= g(theta,x,y) as g' replaces the max by a weighted sum."
- q* is uniform on the data (Sec 3.3, step 1).
- App. F.1 (proof of Thm 7) defines, for a single neuron, eta_{u,v,w}(delta) := E_{a,b}[(u(a)+v(b))^2 w(a+b-delta)]. It maximises eta(0) - E_{delta != 0} eta(delta) (Eq. 4) with uniform tau(a,b)[c'] = 1/(p-1).

Why our lemma is a specialisation: lem:avg is exactly Morwani's inequality with q uniform on D_p and tau set to the point mass on y(x)-delta, summed over neurons (eta_theta = sum_i eta_{omega_i} by linearity).

The only difference: we use a point-mass tau at each offset instead of a uniform tau. That gives one inequality per delta, which the later coverage min over delta needs. The step is trivial and adds nothing as a result.

The paper's current wording already credits Morwani appropriately. The bib entry is correct: title, authors and ICLR 2024 confirmed.

App. F.1 defines the single-neuron eta_{u,v,w}(delta), of which our eta_theta is the network-level sum. Already cited; only the section pointers need tightening.

r2-spectrum.evidence:
This is a standard Fourier computation, and the single-neuron version is already in print. I read both PDFs with pdftotext.

(1) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568), App. F.1 Eq. (5):
- They define eta~_{u,v,w}(delta) := E_{a,b}[u(a)v(b)w(a+b-delta)].
- They derive eta~(delta) = p^{-3} sum_j uhat(j) vhat(j) what(-j) rho^{j delta}, noting "(only terms where j+l = k+l = 0 survive)".
- Eq. (6) and what follows give the class-weighted margin 2/((p-1)p^2) sum_{j != 0} uhat vhat what(-j). This becomes 4/((p-1)p^2) sum |uhat||vhat||what| cos(theta_u+theta_v-theta_w), which is our cosine/phase form.
- The Theorem 7 proof outline repeats the identity.

(2) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025 (arXiv 2402.09469), Def. D.5 and Lemma D.7 proof:
- For k inputs, eta~(delta) = E[w(a1+...+ak-delta) prod u_i(a_i)] = p^{-(k+1)} sum_j what(-j) rho^{j delta} prod_i uhat_i(j). This is exactly our product-neuron beta_ij for general n.
- Lemma F.1 and Thm G.1 use the network-level diagonal mode: the max-margin f has fhat(j1,j2,j3,j4) > 0 when j1=j2=j3=-j4 != 0.

(3) Nanda et al., ICLR 2023 (2301.05217) and Gromov 2023 (2301.02679): the learned or analytic circuits compute cos(w(a+b-c)). I confirmed this from the abstract pages only. Neither states the averaging lemma.

(4) In general harmonic analysis, averaging over the coset c = sum a_t - delta keeps only the Fourier coefficients on the annihilator (Poisson summation on finite abelian groups). This is textbook material; I did not fetch a specific source.

What is new: stating the identity for an arbitrary network table (off-diagonal part = interference; the same identity applies to ReLU), and pairing j with -j to get Re(beta_j) cov_j(delta). Both are trivial extensions.

Search: I fetched the Morwani PDF, the Li et al. PDF, and the Nanda and Gromov arXiv abstract pages. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r2-spectrum/CHECK.md.

Supports the n-operand product-neuron form of beta_ij. Lemma D.7 (proof) gives eta~(delta) = p^{-(k+1)} sum_j what(-j) rho^{j delta} prod_i uhat_i(j). Lemma F.1 and Thm G.1 single out the network-level diagonal mode fhat(j,...,j,-j).

r3-phase-lemma.evidence:
Morwani et al. ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568v2 HTML, fetched):
- Sec 3.2 / Lemma 5 gives the class-weighted margin.
- The Sec 4 proof outline uses uniform class weighting tau = 1/(p-1), which gives E[psi'] = 2/((p-1)p^2) sum_{j!=0} u^(j)v^(j)w^(-j).
- The phase condition theta_u* + theta_v* = theta_w* is part of Theorem 7, which is in Section 4. So the paper's "Section 4" pointer is correct, and this settles the open point in LIT_cite.md.
- Our lemma puts all the weight on a single offset delta. Averaged uniformly over delta, it reduces to Morwani's quantity (p/(p-1)) sum Re beta_j, so it strictly refines their bound.

The 1-cos separation for idealized phase-aligned cosine logits is known:
- Nanda et al. 2023: logits are proportional to sum alpha_k cos(w_k(a+b-c)).
- McCracken et al. arXiv 2505.18266 Thm 4.7: h(k) = sum_l cos(2 pi f_l (k-i-j)/n), with a bound on h(i+j)-h(k). This is an idealized model, not a bound for arbitrary networks.
- Kam, Bessafi, Cadet arXiv 2609.17926 (15 Sep 2026, NeurReps review), App. A.3.2 Eq. 15: Delta_S(beta) = min_s sum_k beta_k(1-cos(omega_k s)). It is introduced as a definition or heuristic ("the logit separation ... at offset s is ..."; loss <= log(1+(p-1)e^{-Delta})). The general shape of the programme is known. The specific programme is not: a cosine-coverage max-min over Z_p under a concave l_{1/s} budget with 1/s = b/nu, used to bound the margin of every network and to count its features. No paper found states it.

Reviewers are likely to recognise three reformulations:

(1) **Max-margin under an l_q quasi-norm on Fourier coefficients (q < 1), with the exponent set by homogeneity.**
- Source: Gunasekar, Lee, Soudry, Srebro, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv 1806.00468). I read Theorem 2a in the PDF.
- For depth-L linear convolutional nets, the GD limit direction is "a scaling of a first order stationary point of min_beta ||beta_hat||_{2/L} s.t. forall n, y_n<beta,x_n> >= 1". Here beta_hat is the vector of DFT coefficients.
- Theorem 2 covers L=2 and gives ||beta_hat||_1. The paper notes that p=2/L<1 is non-convex.
- The template is the same as ours: homogeneity gives an l_{2/depth} bridge penalty in frequency space, and that gives frequency sparsity.
- Differences: generic data, linear convnets only, no coverage or modular structure, no bound over all networks, no K* or log p count.
- Related: Jagadeesan, Razenshteyn, Gunasekar, COLT 2022 (arXiv 2102.12238). In multichannel linear convnets, the l2 weight norm induces a nuclear norm or an l_{2,1} norm on the Fourier coefficients.

(2) **Laplacian spectral gap of a weighted circulant graph.**
- sum_j y_j(1-cos(2 pi j delta/p)) is the delta-th Laplacian eigenvalue of the weighted Cayley graph Cay(Z_p, {±j}). So Gamma_s is the largest algebraic connectivity reachable under an l_{1/s} weight budget.
- The s=1 endpoint is the convex edge-weight problem in Boyd, "Convex Optimization of Graph Laplacian Eigenvalues", Proc. ICM 2006, 3:1311-1319 (confirmed on Boyd's page).
- The s->infinity endpoint is the cardinality problem in Ghosh & Boyd, "Growing Well-connected Graphs", 45th IEEE CDC 2006. From the PDF: "maximize lambda_2(L(E_base u E)) subject to |E|=k, E subset E_cand", solved with an SDP relaxation.
- Alon-Roichman (already cited) covers random O(log p) generators.
- I found no version with an interpolating l_q budget with q<1, and no result for circulants of the form K* = Theta(log p).

(3) **The same coverage objective in modular-addition ML work.**
- Kam, Bessafi, Cadet, arXiv 2609.17926 (15 Sep 2026). I fetched the HTML of App. A.3.2.
- Eq. 15: Delta_S(beta) = min_{s!=0} sum_k beta_k(1-cos(omega_k s)), with ||beta||_2 = B.
- Prop. 5: the uniform allocation is optimal at full frequency content.
- This is our objective with a convex l2 budget in place of l_{1/s}, which is why their optimum is dense. Treat it as concurrent work.
- Morwani et al. 2024 is the s=1 endpoint.

**Adjacent problems, no overlap:**
- The Chowla cosine problem asks for the minimum of an unweighted cosine sum, which is a different extremum.
- Ge-Jiang-Ye 2011 is generic theory for l_p minimisation with p<1.
- LPBoost covers l1 margins only.
- Thinned-array sidelobe design is an unweighted analogue. I did not fetch a source for it, so it has no bib entry.

(2) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025, PMLR 258:523-531 (arXiv 2402.09469). PDF read in full.

r7-universal-bound.evidence:
The b = nu endpoint is known. Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568; I fetched the HTML) prove all their theorems only at L_{2,nu}. Their Thm 7 gives the max L_{2,3} margin as sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) for the quadratic net with width >= 4(p-1). Plain L2 appears only empirically: Fig 4b says L2 ReLU neurons are "nearly 1-sparse ... but not quite". Li, Liang, Shi, Song and Zhou, AISTATS 2025, PMLR 258:523-531 (proceedings page fetched) state only a maximum L_{2,k+1} margin, with m >= 2^{2k-2}(p-1). Our cor:dense reproduces Morwani Thm 7, and the paper already says so.

The b < nu case, including b = 2 weight decay, was not found anywhere. Papers I checked:
- Mohamadi et al., ICML 2024 (2407.12332, HTML): the norm is l_inf. Prop 3.8 only shows that zero-loss solutions exist with ||theta||_inf <= floor(h/8p)^{-1/3}; Thm 4.5 is a generalisation bound for Omega(p) margin. There is no upper bound on the max margin over all widths.
- Tian, NeurIPS 2025 (2410.01779): Thm 5 says "lower-order solutions are preferred if trained with L2 regularization", argued by path-connectivity. There is no margin bound.
- Jacobs and Montufar 2026 (2605.19458): mirror flow. No modular addition and no L_{2,b} bound.
- Kam, Bessafi and Cadet 2026 (2609.17926, HTML App. A.3.2): Eq 15 is max over ||beta||_2 = B of min_s sum_k beta_k(1-cos(omega_k s)), and Prop 5 finds a uniform allocation optimal. The l2 budget on the amplitudes is posited for the quadratic net only; it is not derived from homogeneity, and they make no claim for all networks or widths. This is the closest analogue of the coverage programme, but not of the universal bound.
- Memana 2026 (2608.04451) and Nguyen 2026 (2606.17399) are irrelevant.

The pricing step (amplitude A costs A^{b/nu}, then subadditivity) is a known ingredient:
- Hoff (arXiv 1611.00040): "a subclass of L_q penalties with q<=1 can be expressed as sums of L_2 penalties".
- Dai, Karzand and Srebro, NeurIPS 2021: the representation cost of l2 regularisation on the parameters.
- Fan, Ding, Yang, Zhang and Udell, TMLR 2023 (2012.03436): regularisers built from the Euclidean norms of CP components are "monotonic transformations of tensor Schatten-p quasi-norm". A product neuron is a rank-one CP term, so our pricing is the diagonal (Fourier) case of this.

What is new: an upper bound on the max L_{2,b} margin for b < nu that holds for every width and every kind of neuron (mixed frequencies, interference, inactive). I found no margin upper bound for modular addition under any norm other than L_{2,nu}.

The maximum L2,3-margin of such a network on the dataset D_p is gamma* = sqrt(2/27)·1/(p^{1/2}(p-1))." The neuron is (u_a+v_b)^2 w. Every neuron uses a single frequency, and "For every frequency zeta ... at least one neuron in the network uses this frequency."

r9-interference-free-def.evidence:
I read the full texts, pulling the PDFs and grepping them for cancel/interference/phase/a-b terms.

(1) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568), App. F.2. The max-margin witness uses 8 neurons per frequency: pairs of neurons with phases (0,0,0) and (0,pi,pi), and so on, so that the sum is exactly sum_zeta cos_zeta(a+b-c). They write: "for each input (a,b), f takes the same value on all incorrect labels c', satisfying C.1." Their network is therefore interference-free, but they never isolate that property. Condition C.1 is stronger than ours. Their sparse-parity construction (Thm 8, App. G) uses 2^{k-1} sign-pattern neurons, and "every term other than Pi x_{S_i} cancels out in the sum". This is the Boolean analogue.

(2) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025 (arXiv 2402.09469), App. E. They build an explicit k-input network with 2^k * 2^{k-1} neurons per frequency, using sign-pattern polarisation. It computes exactly sum cos(sum a_i - c) and satisfies Condition 3.8. So an interference-free construction exists for every k, at 2^{2k-1} neurons per frequency against our nu. It is a construction only; there is no class and no cost lemma.

(3) Gromov, arXiv 2301.02679. Eq. 11 lists the sign-flipped waves cos(n-m-q) etc. Eq. 12 is the phase constraint phi1+phi2=phi3, which gives "constructive interference". The paper says "we need to ensure that all other waves ... interfere destructively", and Eq. 15 is the "destructive interference condition", satisfied only approximately by random phases. This is the closest conceptual precedent and even uses the same word.

(4) Doshi, He, Das, Gromov, "Grokking Modular Polynomials" (ICLR 2024 BGPT workshop, arXiv 2406.03495). The multi-operand version of Gromov: "all other terms will vanish due to random phase approximation".

(5) He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849. Def. 4.1(iii) is an exact phase-moment cancellation: sum_{m in N_k} exp(i*iota*phi_m)=0 for iota in {2,4}. It kills the "residual noise" terms of Eq. 4.1. In Prop. 4.2 spurious peaks at 2x and 2y survive, so their condition is not interference-free in our sense. It is nonetheless a close cousin of our Eq. (JF).

r12-cost-of-feature.evidence:
Reframing (the paper does not say this): on one frequency block, (JF) asks for an exact real rank-1 (separated) decomposition of cos(theta_1+...+theta_n-theta_0), which is the tensor Re(z_1...z_n conj z_0) in (R^2)^{⊗nu}. Over C this tensor has rank 2. The count part of the lemma (at least nu neurons) is therefore a real-rank lower bound, and the nu-block is a known trig identity.

(1) Beylkin & Mohlenkamp, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 26(6):2133-2159, 2005. I read the PDF and confirmed the metadata on Crossref.
- §2.1.1 "Sine of a sum", Lemma 2.4 (eq. 2.9): sin(sum x_j) = sum_j sin(x_j) prod_{k≠j} sin(x_k+alpha_k-alpha_j)/sin(alpha_k-alpha_j). That is d real separable terms, against 2^{d-1} from the angle-addition formulas.
- Def. 2.2 defines an l2 coefficient condition number, kappa = (sum s_l^2)^{1/2}/||F||.
- §3 observes that "choosing alpha_j equally spaced in the identity leads to kappa ≈ 7". This is a numerical remark with no proof and uses an l2 cost, not l_r.

(2) Mohlenkamp & Monzón, Math. Intelligencer 27(2):65-69, 2005. I read the preprint PDF and confirmed the metadata on Crossref.
- Thm 2 is the n-variable identity.
- On minimality they write: "to find a minimal rank representation ... is still an open problem. We believe that our Theorems 2 and 5 are an example of such minimal representations." So the lower bound is NOT proved there.

(3) Comon & Ottaviani, Linear Multilinear Algebra 60(6):657-667, 2012 (arXiv 0909.4865; abstract fetched, Crossref-confirmed).
- The abstract states "a real binary form of degree d with d real roots has rank d". This gives real Waring rank d for Re((x+iy)^d), which is the symmetric (power-neuron) analogue of the count. It carries no weights.
- Related: Blekherman arXiv 1205.3257 (typical ranks), and Huang-Tang-Ye-Zhu arXiv 2601.03560 (harmonic binary forms have Waring rank equal to their degree).

(4) The transfer from Thorin-Bernstein functions to x^r is known (Rajan-Tepedelenlioglu 2015; Schilling-Song-Vondracek). See the sibling item r13. The ML phase-cancellation precedents (He et al. Def 4.1(iii), Gromov, Morwani App F.2, Li App E) are covered in items r9 and r10.

What I did not find:
- A proof that the non-symmetric real tensor rank of Re(z_1...z_d) equals d. Mohlenkamp and Monzón leave it as a belief. Our Prop esym gives it, since e_nu(x) ≥ 1.
- Any weighted l_r (r<1) lower bound on the coefficients of such decompositions, or an equality characterisation (equal weights, orthogonal chain vectors, rotated roots of unity).

Searches run:
- sine-of-sum separation rank lower bound
- real rank of Re(z_1...z_d) and of 2x...x2 tensors
- real rank of binary forms with all real roots
- Reznick sums of powers with equally spaced angles
- polyphase / roots-of-unity cancellation with l_p weights
- det(I+tA) with Bernstein-function majorization

One caveat: I did not read Hackbusch's tensor book or Wang-Seigal 2023 in full. Check them before claiming the rank-d lower bound as new.

r13-cost-sublemmas.evidence: The transfer from the generating inequality to power sums and other penalties is a known general principle. Rajan & Tepedelenlioglu (IEEE TIT 61(4):1619-1628, 2015; arXiv 1302.5383) define the "ergodic capacity order" (Def. 1): X <=_c Y iff E log(1+rho X) <= E log(1+rho Y) for all rho >= 0. Their Property S1 states "X <=_c Y <=> E[g(X)] <= E[g(Y)] for all g in TBF", where TBF is the Thorin-Bernstein class g(x) = a + bx + int log(1+x/s) mu(ds) (their eq. 6). The proof of Property M1 (App. A, eqs. 28-31) matches ours step for step: take rho -> 0 for the linear term, then integrate log(1+t rho x) against a positive measure. Applied to the empirical measure of x (zero padding is allowed because a=0), it gives Remark "other penalties" verbatim, and Lemma cost at 0<r<1 is the case g = x^r. The class psi = cx + int log(1+xt) mu(dt) is exactly the Thorin-Bernstein functions vanishing at 0, which is Schilling-Song-Vondracek, Bernstein Functions, de Gruyter Studies in Math 37, Ch. 8 (1st-ed. TOC fetched; Ch. 8 starts p. 73). Lemma bernstein (the integral formula for x^r) is a standard Beta-integral representation. Going from e_k >= binom(nu,k) to prod(1+x t) >= (1+t)^nu is trivial because all coefficients are nonnegative. Searches of majorization work (power majorization, Cuttler-Greene-Skandera, trumping) found nothing closer. We found no prior statement of the chain lemma (the sign constraints JF force H = sum beta_l m_l m_l^* to be upper triangular with constant diagonal) or of its consequence e_k(|nu beta|) >= binom(nu,k) with the orthogonal equality case, obtained via Sylvester, minor expansion and Hadamard. That part is ours; its tools are textbook. Queries run: Thorin-Bernstein representation (Schilling Song Vondracek); elementary symmetric e_k domination implies fractional power sums via log(1+tx). Metadata was confirmed through Crossref. Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r13-cost-sublemmas/CHECK.md

Ch. 8 (Thorin-Bernstein functions) gives the representation a + bx + int log(1+x/s) mu(ds). This names the class psi in Remark 'other penalties' and is the standard reference for the integral representation of x^r in Lemma bernstein.

r20-cyclic-theorem.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r20-cyclic-theorem/CHECK.md.

**The theorem itself: not found anywhere.** No paper gives the max-margin value for b<nu. No paper reduces the margin to a budget programme or derives a frequency count from one. No paper proves that exactly nu neurons per frequency is necessary at a norm optimum. No paper prices sparsity by the gap nu-b.

**The construction that attains it (prop:block): known.** It appears in Marchetti, Kunin, Myers, Acosta, Miolane, "Sequential Group Composition: A Window into the Mechanics of Deep Learning", arXiv 2602.03655. The arXiv comment field reads "Accepted at ICML 2026". The construction is App. B, Lemma B.8 Case 1:
- N >= (k+1) n_rho^{k+1} sigma-pi-sigma (product) neurons solve the per-irrep cost minimisation.
- Inputs are multiplied by e^{pi i j/(k+1)} and the output by e^{-pi i j k/(k+1)}/(k+1), for j=1..k+1. For real irreps they take real parts.
- Cross terms are then scaled by (1/(k+1)) sum_j e^{-2 pi i j (k-|A|)/(k+1)} (their eq. 71). This vanishes "since A is a proper subset of {1..k}, 0<k-|A|<=k, and thus k-|A| != 0 (mod k+1)".

For cyclic groups (n_rho=1) this is exactly our nu-block: nu=k+1 neurons, input phases pi l/nu, output phase n alpha_l. They use it only as a sufficient construction for square-loss minimisation under AGF dynamics. They make no claim that it is norm-optimal or necessary, and give no count. Their Lemma B.6 and Remark B.7 (Waring decomposition, 2^{k-1} powers needed, citing Carlini et al. 2011) explain why power neurons need exponential width (Li et al. need m >= 2^{2k-2}(p-1)) while product neurons need only nu.

**Other related work:**
- **Tian, NeurIPS 2025** (arXiv 2410.01779 v4, PDF read). Quadratic nets, L2 loss, weight decay.
  - Corollary 2: global solutions in which "each frequency [is] affiliated with 6 hidden nodes (order-6)", built from 3rd/4th roots of unity (Table 1).
  - Corollaries 4 and 5: order-4 and mixed order-4/6 solutions.
  - Theorem 5 ("Occam's Razer"): "lower-order solutions are preferred if trained with L2 regularization".
  - All frequencies are used. There is no margin and no norm optimum.
- **Gromov 2023** (arXiv 2301.02679, PDF read):
  - Uses all frequencies, with random phases under the constraint phi1+phi2=phi3 (Eq. 12).
  - Cancellation is only approximate at large N (Eq. 15).
  - Nothing is claimed about norm or margin optimality.
- **Morwani et al. ICLR 2024** (fetched): Thm 7 is the b=nu=3 dense endpoint.
- **Li et al. AISTATS 2025** (fetched): Thm 4.1 is the L_{2,k+1} endpoint for power neurons; every frequency is used.

r21-nu-block.evidence:
The trigonometric identity behind the nu-block is classical. Mohlenkamp and Monzón, "Trigonometric identities and sums of separable functions", Math. Intelligencer 27(2):65-69 (2005), DOI 10.1007/BF02985795 (metadata confirmed via Crossref; preprint read at ohiouniversityfaculty.com/mohlenka/research/sine.pdf). Their Thm 2 gives sin(sum_{j=1}^n x_j) = sum_j sin(x_j) prod_{k!=j} sin(x_k+alpha_k-alpha_j)/sin(alpha_k-alpha_j) for any distinct alpha, together with a shifted version with free a_j (sum a_j = 0). They state that sin of a sum "is exactly separated with separation rank n", compared with 2^{n-1} terms from the standard trig expansion. Their Fig. 1 (right) uses equally spaced alpha = 0, pi/3, 2pi/3. Minimality is only conjectured ("We believe..."). I checked numerically that the choice alpha_k = pi k/nu, a_k = -alpha_k, together with prod_{k=1}^{nu-1} sin(pi k/nu) = nu/2^{nu-1}, gives exactly our identity sum_{l=0}^{nu-1} (-1)^l prod_{k=1}^{nu} cos(x_k + pi l/nu) = nu 2^{1-nu} cos(sum x_k). This matches for nu = 2..7, and our block is that identity with x_nu = -theta_c.

None of the ML constructions uses a nu-neuron roots-of-unity block:
- Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, App. F.2 (PDF read): 8 neurons per frequency. They expand cos(a+b-c) into 4 trig terms and implement each with a neuron pair, with phases (0,0,0)/(0,pi,pi), (pi/2,-pi/2,0)/(pi/2,pi/2,pi) and so on. They credit Gromov's scheme.
- Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025, Lemma E.1 Part 3 and Lemma E.2/E.3: 2^{2k-1} neurons per frequency pair, built by sign-vector polarisation of 2^k trig terms. No roots-of-unity phases.
- Gromov 2023 (arXiv 2301.02679), Eqs. 6-16: random uniform phases with phi1+phi2=phi3. Spurious terms cancel only approximately (the random phase approximation). Doshi, He, Das, Gromov 2024 (arXiv 2406.03495), Eq. 2 is the same random-phase scheme for S-term sums.
- He, Wang, Chen, Yang (arXiv 2602.16849), Def 4.1(iii): phase-moment cancellation for iota in {2,4} within each frequency group (roots of unity satisfy it). Their setting is quadratic sum-activation nets, where noise peaks at 2x and 2y survive (Prop 4.2). There is no minimal block and no norm optimality.

The roots-of-unity filter itself is the textbook series-multisection identity.

What remains ours: the product-network norm accounting (nu lambda^2 p/2), the amplitude weighting lambda_j^nu = 2^n y*_j/nu, and the result that one block per support frequency attains Gamma_s. Cost-optimality of nu neurons is the separate lem:cost; the minimal-rank question is only conjectured in Mohlenkamp and Monzón.

(i) Minimisers of sum v^{1/s} over P_p are vertices, and every minimiser is a vertex.

r23-bottleneck.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r23-bottleneck/CHECK.md.

The proof in appendix.tex (app:shape) has three steps:
(a) a maximizer is Gamma_s times a vertex of P_p, because a concave, monotone phi is minimised over a line-free polyhedron;
(b) at a vertex the active constraints have full rank, so K coverage rows are independent on the support;
(c) y_S is the unique solution of the square system.

Steps (a) and (b) are textbook: concave minimisation at extreme points (Rockafellar, Convex Analysis, Sec. 32) and the vertex characterisation of LP basic feasible solutions.

Closest prior art is Shapley and Snow, "Basic Solutions of Discrete Games" (Contributions to the Theory of Games Vol. I, AM-24, Princeton UP, pp. 27-36). Crossref lists it as 1951, DOI 10.1515/9781400881727-004; it is often cited as 1950. At s=1 the programme is the matrix game with payoff cov(j,delta), and Shapley-Snow characterise extreme optimal strategies through a square sub-game G'. Restated as Thm 2.3.1 in Attia and Oliu-Barton, arXiv 1810.08798: "A couple (x,y) is a basic solution of G iff there exists a square sub-game G' satisfying ... G' y' = val(G) 1". Prop 2.3.4(iii) there gives Ker(G' - vU') = <y'>, which is uniqueness. Our proposition is the s>1 analogue: the concave budget keeps the optimum at a vertex of the same polyhedron.

Chebyshev equioscillation is only an analogy. Alternation needs the Haar condition, and the Kolmogorov / Rivlin-Shapiro characterisation gives at most n+1 extremal points (survey: Goldsztejn, arXiv 2310.01851). Our coverage system is not Haar, the problem is a budgeted max-min, and our count is a lower bound from vertex rank.

On the ML side, Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, Lemma 6, says "all points in the support of q* are on the margin for any maximum margin solution". That is the dense analogue of tight wrong labels.

I found no paper stating that there are at least K tight wrong-answer offsets for K features in modular addition, or that the amplitude ratios are fixed by an equalising system. Search queries covered Shapley-Snow basic solutions, concave minimisation at vertices, Chebyshev/Haar characterisation, the max-min cosine-sum LP, and modular addition max-margin with tight wrong labels and vertices.

r25-log-scaling.evidence:
Dictionary: 1-cos(2 pi j delta/p) summed with weights y_j is half the Laplacian eigenvalue at character delta of the weighted Cayley graph Cay(Z_p, {+-j}, y_j). So Gamma_s(p) is half the largest spectral gap under an l_{1/s} budget on the generator weights. With equal shares on K frequencies, the coverage equals K^{1-s} times the normalised gap of a 2K-regular abelian Cayley graph.

Sources (all PDFs fetched and read):
(1) Alon and Roichman, Random Cayley graphs and expanders, RSA 5(2):271-284, 1994.
- Thm 1: c(delta) log n random generators give an expander.
- Thm 2: (1+eps) log2 n random elements suffice for any abelian group; for Z_n, eps log2 n suffice.
- Prop 3 (Sec 3.1): "If A is an Abelian group of order n, and X(A,S) is a delta-expander, then |S| >= c log2 n."
- Abstract: "For Abelian groups this is essentially tight."
- Prop 7' uses a closed-walk (trace) count.
(2) Friedman, Murty and Tillich, Spectral estimates for Abelian Cayley graphs, JCTB 96(1):111-121, 2006.
- Abstract: "for fixed d, a d-regular Cayley graph on an Abelian group of order n has second eigenvalue bounded below by d - O(d n^{-4/d}) ... for a large odd prime n, the O(dn^{-4/d}) cannot be improved."
- With d=2K this is a normalised gap of at most C p^{-2/K}. That is the unweighted analogue of our Cor few / eq. (Kbound), which gives the weaker exponent p^{-1/(2 a_s K)} but holds for arbitrary weights.
- They mention a "large trace" approach, which is what our Bessel positive-Fourier inequality is.
(3) Cioaba, CRAS 342 (2006) 635-638: closed-walk lower bounds for abelian Cayley graphs. This is the combinatorial twin of our "resonances only add non-negative terms".
(4) McCracken et al., arXiv 2505.18266, Sec 4.3. Thm 4.7 and Cor 4.8: "Learning O(log n) distinct frequencies gives a logit margin Omega(log n)". The margin is unnormalised and only sufficiency is shown; they write "we don't know why it occurs"; no necessity bound; no expander citations.

Consequence: the equal-share restriction of thm:scaling (Theta((log p)^{1-s}), K = Theta(log p)) is essentially a corollary of AR Thm 2 plus FMT. Not found anywhere:
- the weighted two-sided bound under the concave l_{1/s} budget with explicit constants, for arbitrary weights;
- the maximiser support Theta(log p) and the share floor;
- the network statement gamma*_b = Theta(p^{-nu/2}(log p)^{1-nu/b}) over all product networks, and Cor few.

Checked and only related:
- Chowla cosine problem (Bourgain/Ruzsa/Sanders; Bedert arXiv 2509.05260; arXiv 2509.03490, 2609.05338). It concerns the negative tail of the cosine sum; ours is the near-period/Dirichlet tail.
- Small-bias sets (two-sided bias).
- Weighted Cayley sparsification (arXiv 2508.08078).

The paper already cites alon1994random, but only for the random lower bound; that bib entry is correct (Princeton record: RSA 5(2) 271-284, doi 10.1002/rsa.3240050203). The mccracken2025 bib entry is wrong: the correct first author is Gavin McCracken. Queries run: FMT second eigenvalue abelian; Alon-Roichman abelian log generators; weighted Cayley spectral gap log n; small-bias Z_p; Chowla cosine. r26-few-features.evidence:
Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r26-few-features/CHECK.md.

Reduction. The coverage is F_y(delta) = sum_j y_j (1 - cos(2 pi j delta/p)). With equal weights on a set S, min over delta != 0 of F is K minus half the largest non-trivial eigenvalue of Cay(Z_p, S u -S); the eigenvalues of that graph are character sums (Alon-Roichman Sec. 3). So the equal-share form of cor:few is the statement that an abelian Cayley graph with o(log p) generators has a vanishing normalised one-sided spectral gap.

(1) Alon & Roichman, "Random Cayley graphs and expanders", RSA 5(2) 1994. I fetched the PDF at web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf.
- Prop 3: "For every fixed delta>0 there is a constant c=c(delta)>0 such that the following holds; If A is an Abelian group of order n, and X(A,S) is a delta-expander, then |S| >= c log2 n." The proof is a diameter/volume count.
- The abstract says of the log bound: "For Abelian groups this is essentially tight".
- The paper already cites this work, but only for the random lower bound (appendix l.196).

(2) Friedman, Murty & Tillich, "Spectral estimates for Abelian Cayley graphs", JCTB 96(1):111-121, 2006, DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2005.06.012.
- Main result: for fixed d, a d-regular Cayley graph on an abelian group of order n has second eigenvalue >= d - O(d n^{-4/d}), with an absolute constant.
- How confirmed: the ScienceDirect listing is pii S0095895605000948, and the DOI resolves to that pii. The article page itself gave a 403. I fetched Cioaba, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 342 (2006) 635-638, which cites it as ref [6] with this bibliographic data and quotes "second largest eigenvalue of a k-regular Abelian Cayley graph with n vertices is at least k - O(k n^{-4/k})".
- With d = 2K and equal shares y = K^{-s}, this gives m <= C K^{1-s} e^{-2x}. So m / Gamma_s <= C x^{s-1} e^{-2x} -> 0, which is exactly cor:few for equal shares, with a better exponent.
- The one-line reason is folklore Dirichlet simultaneous approximation: some delta != 0 has ||j delta/p|| <= p^{-1/K} for all j in S.

(3) Two-sided epsilon-biased-set lower bounds, e.g. Alon, "Perturbed identity matrices have high rank", CPC 18 (2009). I only saw this in search results and did not fetch the paper. It is less relevant: two-sided and mainly Z_2^n.

What appears new:
- The weighted version under the concave l_{1/s} budget (sum y^{1/s} <= 1, support <= K), compared against Gamma_s ~ (ln p)^{1-s} and hence against gamma* over all networks, interference included.
- The naive Dirichlet bound gives only m <= 2 pi^2 e^{-2x} ||y||_1 <= 2 pi^2 e^{-2x}. That vanishes relative to (ln p)^{1-s} only for K = O(log p / log log p).
- The paper's positive-Fourier / Bessel-I_0 averaging (eq:posfourier, eq:psisum) extends this to all K = o(log p).
- I found no weighted or quasi-norm-budget analogue in the expander, Bohr-set or ML literature. Queries run: FMT title; "Cayley graphs of abelian groups not expanders need log n generators Klawe lower bound"; a weighted cosine-sum / simultaneous-Dirichlet query (no relevant hits); Alon epsilon-biased lower bound.
- The Bessel moment-generating trick is standard in flavour, but I found no exact source.

Verdict: the unweighted / equal-share specialisation is classical (Alon-Roichman Prop 3 qualitatively; Friedman-Murty-Tillich quantitatively). The weighted l_{1/s} result for every K = o(log p), and its application to network margins, are novel as far as found.

What is known (all fetched this session):

(1) Derksen, FoCM 16:779-811 (2016), arXiv 1308.3860.
- Thm 1.9: the schoolbook decomposition sum e_ij(x)e_jk(x)e_ki of M_{p,q,r} is a diagonal SVD, with all pqr singular values equal to 1.
- Cor 1.10: ||M_{p,q,r}||_* = pqr.
- He remarks that Strassen's decomposition has length 2sqrt2+12 > 8: "minimization of the rank, and minimization of the nuclear norm do not always coincide".
- Thm 1.11: the group-algebra tensor T_G has singular values sqrt(n/d_i), each with multiplicity d_i^3. So ||T_G||_* = sqrt|G| sum d_i^{2.5}, which is exactly the d^{2.5} in Morwani Thm 9.
- Consequences: our K1 at r=1 (kappa=1) is Derksen Cor 1.10, and our "Strassen costs 10 > schoolbook 8" is the quasi-norm analogue of his remark.

(2) Christandl & Zuiddam, Comput. Complexity 28:27-56 (2019), arXiv 1606.04085.
- Eqs. 7-8: the max-cut flattening gives n^{f(G)} <= R(T_n(G)). "For bipartite graphs, each inequality in (8) is an equality."
- Even cycles are bipartite, so the rank of tr(A1...Ak) is d^k for even k. Our rank corollary (tr(ABCD) has rank d^4) is known, and the proof of K2 uses the same cut argument.

(3) Fan, Ding, Yang, Zhang, Udell, TMLR 01/2023, arXiv 2012.03436.
- Def 3 defines the tensor Schatten-p quasi-norm.
- Thm 1: ||X||_{S_{q/d}}^{q/d} = inf (1/d) sum_i sum_j ||x_i^(j)||^q.
- Our price N_r(T) is exactly ||T||_{S_r}^r with r = q/nu.

(4) Cheng et al., arXiv 2506.22134, Thm 1: the variational S_p quasi-norm upper-bounds ||T_(D)||_{S_p}^p for every unfolding. This is our flattening bound, Lemma F applied to a flattening. Hu, LAA 478:188-199 (2015), proves the p=1 case; that entry was confirmed through the Crossref API only.

(5) Shutman-Louidor-Tessler, arXiv 2509.06931. Prop 5.2: the single-irrep projection has rank <= m_d, 3m_{d/2} or 8m_{d/2}, where m_d is the tensor rank of dxd matrix multiplication. (6) Marchetti-Kunin-Myers-Acosta-Miolane, ICML 2026, arXiv 2602.03655. Lemma B.8: (k+1) n_rho^{k+1} sigma-pi-sigma (product) neurons suffice for one irrep. The construction is the schoolbook, with s_w = E_{a0a1} and S = E_{a_h a_{h+1}}, i.e. d^nu terms. It is an existence construction only.

The step in approach.tex l.64-67 is sum_j A_j^r <= sum_{i,j}|beta_ij|^r for r = b/nu <= 1. It uses subadditivity of t^r, which is the p-subadditivity (a+b)^p <= a^p + b^p that defines a p-norm for 0<p<=1. This is textbook material on quasi-Banach spaces; the canonical reference is Kalton-Peck-Roberts, An F-space Sampler, LMS LNS 89 (bibliographic data confirmed via abebooks; the book text was not read).

The ML version of the same argument is in Ongie & Parhi, arXiv 2606.14954. I fetched the PDF and grepped it:
- Def 3.5 defines a p-seminorm by Q(f+g)^p <= Q(f)^p + Q(g)^p.
- Prop 3.6: if K is absolutely p-homogeneous and subadditive, then K^{1/p} is a p-seminorm.
- Prop 3.13: parameter-level q-subadditivity makes the representation cost subadditive.
- Sec. 8, after eq. 8.30: "the subadditivity follows by concatenating neurons".
- Thm 9.3: for depth L>=2, R_L is a (2/L)-seminorm.

This is the statement "a merged feature costs no more than its split pieces" for weight-decay costs.

Gunasekar-Lee-Soudry-Srebro, arXiv 1806.00468, abstract fetched: depth-L linear conv nets go to "the l_{2/L} bridge penalty in the frequency domain". That is the closest precedent for a product parametrisation giving an l_{2/L} quasi-norm on Fourier coefficients.

Our contribution is not the inequality. It is using it so the universal bound holds with no hypothesis on neuron structure (mixing, interference, inactive neurons).

t3-determinant-gram.evidence:
Every step of the technique in app:cost is standard. The inequality it proves, sum_l|beta_l|^r >= nu^{1-r}|beta|^r for 0<r<=1, also has a two-line classical proof.

(a) Sylvester's determinant identity, the principal-minor expansion of det(I+tX), and Hadamard's inequality for Gram/PSD matrices are textbook results in Horn & Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed. I confirmed the book on cambridge.org. I did not verify section numbers.

(b) The integral x^r = (r sin(pi r)/pi) ∫ log(1+xt) t^{-1-r} dt is the Stieltjes/complete-Bernstein representation of x^r. The operator-monotone chapter of Bhatia gives x^r = (sin r pi/pi) ∫ x/(x+lambda) lambda^{r-1} dlambda, and integrating by parts gives the log form. I did not verify Bhatia's section or equation numbers. I could not fetch the de Gruyter page for the Schilling-Song-Vondracek monograph.

(c) The step from the generating function to power sums (prod(1+x_l t) >= (1+t)^nu for all t implies sum x^r >= nu) has no named majorization-literature precedent that I found. It is not ordinary weak majorization, but it is elementary.

(d) Main finding: the lemma follows from two classical theorems.
- Weyl's majorant theorem: Weyl, PNAS 35:408-411, 1949, fetched via PMC; also Bhatia Thm II.3.6 per secondary sources. It says sum phi(|lambda_i|) <= sum phi(sigma_i) when phi(e^s) is convex. H is upper triangular with unit diagonal, so all its eigenvalues are 1, and with phi = x^r this gives nu <= sum sigma_i(H)^r.
- The Rotfel'd/Thompson inequality: R.C. Thompson, Pacific J. Math 66(1):285-290, 1976. I fetched the PDF. Its eq. (1) reads: "f(γ1)+...+f(γn) <= f(α1)+...+f(αn)+f(β1)+...+f(βn) when f is an increasing concave function of a nonnegative real variable, with f(0)=0", where α, β, γ are the singular values of A, B, A+B. Apply it to the rank-one summands d_l u_l u_l^* with f = x^r. This gives sum sigma_i(H)^r <= sum_l |d_l|^r.
- Together these give sum|d_l|^r >= nu, which is the lemma.

The paper's own route is still valuable because it gives the equality case cleanly. Searches run: Thompson 1976 title; Rotfel'd concave singular values; Weyl majorant Bhatia II.3.6; Weyl 1949 PNAS; Bernstein integral representation of x^r; Schilling-Song-Vondracek. (3) Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, App. F.2.

t6-exp-sum-zeros.evidence:
The claim, in the appendix (app:shape (ii), sections/appendix.tex around line 156): a real exponential sum sum_k c_k e^{lambda_k u} with N distinct exponents, not all c_k zero, has at most N-1 real zeros. The paper proves it by Rolle induction.

This is classical. It is the generalized Descartes rule of signs (Laguerre): substitute t = e^u, and the number of zeros is at most the number of sign changes in (c_k), which is at most N-1. Equivalently, the functions e^{lambda_k u} form a Chebyshev (Descartes) system.

t7-active-constraints.evidence:
The proof step at appendix.tex:166 (proof of Prop. bottleneck) is a textbook LP fact. A point of a polyhedron in R^n is a vertex (extreme point) exactly when it is a basic feasible solution, meaning n of its active constraints are linearly independent. Source: Bertsimas & Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Linear Optimization (1997), Def. 2.9 (p. 50) and Theorem 2.3 (vertex = extreme point = BFS).

How this was confirmed:
- Wikipedia "Basic solution (linear programming)" was fetched. It gives the definition ("of all the constraints that are active at that vector, at least n of them must be linearly independent") and cites B&T 1997, Athena Scientific, p. 50, ISBN 978-1-886529-19-9.
- arXiv 2302.12364 was fetched and its text extracted. It states "basic feasible solutions are precisely extreme points (vertices) of the feasible set (Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, 1997, Theorem 2.3)". Its bib entry is "Athena Scientific, 1st edition, 1997. ISBN 1886529191".

Our argument is the standard basis-matrix argument (B&T Sec 2.3):
- The active bounds v_j=0 for j outside S are unit vectors supported outside S.
- So the active coverage rows, restricted to S, must have rank K, and the resulting K×K system is invertible.
The step is correct and nothing in the technique is new.

Chebyshev alternation analogue: the programme is a discrete max-min problem. A basic optimal solution of the LP form of discrete Chebyshev approximation is pinned by a reference set of n+1 active points, which becomes alternation under the Haar condition. We get K tight offsets rather than K+1 because the normalisation constraint is absorbed into the scaling. I did not fetch a canonical approximation-theory source (e.g. Cheney 1966), so it is unconfirmed and has no bib entry.

What is ours is the interpretation of the tight offsets as simultaneous hardest wrong answers in the constructed network.

The technique is standard. The paper already attributes it correctly ("cyclic case of the random Cayley graph argument of Alon-Roichman", appendix.tex l.196). The arithmetic is correct. Hoeffding with range 2 gives exp(-L t^2/2), and the needed deviation is t = 1/2 + 1/(p-1) >= 1/2, so the bound is <= e^{-L/8} <= 1/p. The union bound over p-1 offsets gives (p-1)/p < 1.

(1) Alon & Roichman, RSA 5(2):271-284, 1994. Metadata confirmed via Crossref 10.1002/rsa.3240050203; I read the PDF at https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf.

- Sec 3.1, Thm 2 (Abelian groups): a multiset S of (1+eps) log2 n random elements, chosen with repetitions, gives |mu1*| <= 1-delta almost surely.
- The proof bounds each nontrivial character separately (Pr(chi(sigma+sigma^-1) >= 1.8) <= 1/2) and then takes a union bound over characters.
- The eigenvalues of X(Z_p, ±J) are 2 sum_l cos(2 pi J_l delta/p). Our lemma is exactly this for Z_p, with a one-sided threshold of 1/2, explicit constant 8, and a Hoeffding step. The random-multiset model is also the same.

(2) Small-bias sets (explicit constructions over Z_2^n; they supply the eps-biased-set vocabulary):

t9-positive-fourier.evidence:
Main finding: the mechanism behind eq:posfourier is a known closed-walk (trace) comparison for abelian Cayley graphs; what is new here is the weighted, budget-normalised version and its log p consequence. Full notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t9-positive-fourier/CHECK.md.

How to read the inequality: take unit weights on K frequencies. Then F_y(delta) = K - lambda_chi/2, where lambda_chi is the eigenvalue of Cay(Z_p, {+-j}) at character delta.
- The left side is e^{-tK} times the exponential generating function of closed walks, i.e. the continuous-time return probability on that Cayley graph.
- The right side, prod e^{-t} I_0(t), is the same return probability on the free cover Z^K.
- "Resonances only add non-negative terms" means that extra relations mod p only add closed walks.

(1) Cioaba, "Closed walks and eigenvalues of Abelian Cayley graphs", C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Ser. I 342 (2006) 635-638 (PDF fetched from numdam).
- Sec. 2 puts closed r-walks in bijection with r-tuples whose product is 1.
- It counts only the "trivial" 2r-tuples, where each x_i is paired with x_i^{-1} and each involution appears an even number of times. This gives Phi_{2r}(X) >= n W_{2r}(X) (eq. 2, Lemma 2.1).
- This is the moment/combinatorial form of our inequality: the trivial pairings are our constant-term product, and summing over r with t^{2r}/(2r)! gives prod I_0.
- Cioaba uses it to prove Thm 1.2, a Serre-type result: C|G| eigenvalues are >= k - eps.

(2) Friedman, Murty, Tillich, "Spectral estimates for Abelian Cayley graphs", JCTB 96 (2006) 111-121 (author PDF fetched from Tillich's page).
- Abstract: a d-regular Abelian Cayley graph on n vertices has lambda_2 >= d - O(d n^{-4/d}), and this is tight for prime n.
- Sec. 2 proves it by sphere packing/pigeonhole (Thm 2, Cor 3).
- Sec. 3 uses a covering argument: a Dirichlet eigenfunction on the universal cover Z^r is pushed forward to G.
- Sec. 1 names the "large trace" approach [Ci05] as another route.
- They call "Abelian Cayley graphs cannot be good expanders" a folklore result, credited to Alon-Roichman [AR94, Sec. 3].
- Our upper bound on m(y) is the weighted, l_{1/s}-budget analogue of this spectral-gap bound: m(y) is the normalised weighted gap.

(3) Alon-Roichman, "Random Cayley graphs and expanders" (author PDF fetched). Sec. 3 says the log n generator count is "essentially tight" for abelian groups (Prop. 2, stated for Z_2^m only). The paper already cites this for its lower-bound half.

What we have not found anywhere:
- the weighted version with a concave l_{1/s} budget;
- the scalar bound psi(z) <= a_s ln(1+z^r);
- the conclusions m(y) <= C (ln p)^{1-s} and eq:Kbound, and K* = Theta(log p).
The published results are for fixed degree with unit weights.

Checked and not overlapping:
- The Chowla cosine problem (Bourgain 1986, Ruzsa 2004, Sanders, Bedert arXiv 2509.05260) is about how negative min_x sum cos(a x) must be. Our bound controls the other side: some delta != 0 makes sum y_j cos close to sum y_j, i.e. simultaneous approximation / Bohr-set non-emptiness. The direction and method differ.
- Wang-Ye, arXiv 2503.06908 (positive definite functions on finite abelian groups; I read only the abstract) is adjacent, not overlapping.
- The Bessel generating function e^{z cos theta} = sum I_n(z) e^{in theta} is textbook; I did not fetch a source for it.

t10-bessel-bound.evidence: Paper (appendix.tex lines 198-214) uses three things. (1) The integral representation I_0(z) = (1/pi) int_0^pi e^{z cos th} dth, which is DLMF 10.32.1 (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.32, section 10.32(i)). (2) The Fourier coefficients of e^{z cos th} are I_k(z) >= 0. This is the Jacobi-Anger expansion DLMF 10.35.2, "e^{z cos th} = I_0(z) + 2 sum_{k>=1} I_k(z) cos(k th)" (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.35), and non-negativity follows from the power series in 10.25.2. (3) An elementary Laplace-type lower bound, I_0(z) >= e^{z-1/2}/(pi sqrt z) for z >= 1. You get it by cutting the integral off at th <= z^{-1/2} and using cos th >= 1 - th^2/2. I checked the derivation and it is correct. Numerically, I_0/bound = 2.41 at z=1 and tends to about 2.07 as z grows, so the constant is weaker than the leading asymptotic e^z/sqrt(2 pi z) from DLMF 10.40.1 (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.40). That does not matter here, because only psi(z) <= (1/2) ln z + O(1) is needed. The bound would fail for small z (e.g. z=0.01), but the paper applies it only for z >= 1 and handles z <= 1 through I_0 >= 1, so the argument is valid for all z >= 0. Sharper inequalities (Baricz; Soni-type monotonicity) exist in the literature and turned up in a WebSearch, but I did not fetch them in full, so I do not cite them. This is a standard textbook fact. Nothing novel is claimed, and none is needed. Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t10-bessel-bound/CHECK.md. Searches: DLMF 10.32/10.35/10.40 pages; "inequality modified Bessel I_0(x) > e^x/sqrt(2 pi x) lower bound Baricz".

t12-dense-uniqueness.evidence:
Source read: Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao, Kakade, "Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks", arXiv 2311.07568v2. The arXiv abs page says "Accepted as Spotlight at ICLR 2024". I fetched the full HTML and extracted the math from its alttext.

(1) Our averaging step (average the coverage over delta != 0 to get Gamma_1 <= p/(p-1)) is their uniform class-weighting certificate. Sec 4 proof outline: "We will use the uniform class weighting: tau(x,y)[y'] = 1/(p-1) for all c' != a+b". This is combined with Lemma 5 (class-weighted margin) and Lemma 6 (the max-min certificate). The second part of Lemma 6 says: "all points in the support of q* are on the margin for any maximum margin solution."

(2) Our equality/uniqueness step is App. F.3, "Proof that all frequencies are used". Lemma 6 makes the margin equal across classes, so they write f(a,b,c) = F(a,b) + lambda * 1_{a+b=c}. The 3-D DFT of the indicator term is "lambda p^2 if j=k=-l". They conclude: "Hence, when j=k=-l != 0, we must have f^(j,k,l) > 0 ... there is at least one neuron for each frequency."

Our proof uses the same argument: constant margin/coverage, Fourier inversion of an indicator, every frequency nonzero. Their Theorem 7 claims only (1) single-frequency neurons and (2) every frequency used by at least one neuron. It does not state equal amplitudes, although their decomposition already gives the same value lambda p^2 at every diagonal frequency.

What is new in ours:
- uniqueness of the whole flat amplitude vector y_j = 2/(p-1) in the reduced programme Gamma_1;
- this holds for any network at b = nu, via Thm universal;
- a one-variable inversion in place of a 3-D DFT.

The averaging-then-constant-correlation pattern also resembles Welch/simplex bounds (folklore). I found no citation that fits better than Morwani. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t12-dense-uniqueness/CHECK.md.

- The paper's description of Morwani's proof structure is accurate.

c1-morwani-dense-baseline.evidence:
Sources I fetched: the arXiv 2311.07568 abstract page, which confirms the title, the five authors and "Accepted as Spotlight at ICLR 2024"; the full LaTeX source (e-print); and the arXiv HTML v2 page, which I used for theorem numbers. The refs.bib entry is correct.

What Morwani et al. actually state:
- **Neuron (Sec 2):** the neuron is (u_a+v_b)^2 w. This is a quadratic neuron, so nu=3.
- **Thm 1:** restates Wei et al. 2019 Thm 4.1 about global minimisers: gamma_lambda -> gamma* as lambda -> 0.
- **Thm 7 (modular addition):** "with m >= 4(p-1) neurons. The maximum L_{2,3}-margin ... is gamma* = sqrt(2/27)·1/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). Any network achieving this margin satisfies: (1) for each neuron ... there exists a scaling constant lambda and a frequency zeta" so that u, v, w are cosines at zeta with theta_u+theta_v=theta_w; "(2) For every frequency zeta in {1..(p-1)/2}, at least one neuron in the network uses this frequency."
- **Thm 8 (sparse parity):** uses x^k neurons with L_{2,k+1} and m >= 2^{k-1}, and gives gamma* = k! sqrt(2(k+1)^{-(k+1)}). Every neuron's support is exactly S. This is not an "all features" result.
- **Thm 9 (groups):** quadratic neurons, L_{2,3}, groups with REAL irreps. It needs m >= 2·sum d^3 and the character condition sum_{n>=2} d^{1.5} chi_{R_n}(C) < 0 for every non-trivial conjugacy class. Then gamma* = 2/(3 sqrt(3|G|) sum d^{2.5}). Each neuron is spanned by one non-trivial irrep, and every non-trivial irrep is used.
- **Informal theorem (intro):** "For m >= 4(p-1), any global minimizer ... For every neuron, there exists a frequency such that the input and output weight vectors only use that frequency. There exists at least one neuron of each frequency."
- **Sec 3, "Combining neurons":** works only at b=nu. This supports our intro paragraph 3.
- **Discussion:** "Our proof holds for the case of x^2 activations (x^k activations, in the k-sparse parity case) and L_{2,nu} norm, where nu is the homogeneity constant."

How the paper's claims compare:
- **Intro paragraph 1:** "every max L_{2,3}-margin net uses Fourier features, one frequency per neuron, every frequency" is supported by Thm 7. The theorem needs width m >= 4(p-1).
- **Our b=nu bound recovers their margin:** 2B_p p/(p-1) = 4(6p)^{-3/2} p/(p-1) = sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). I checked this numerically (4/6^1.5 = 0.27217 = sqrt(2/27)). Supported for Thm 7.
- **Overreach in the abstract / paper.tex paragraph 1:** "in networks where L_{2,nu} matches homogeneity nu, all features would be used for modular addition or group composition" goes beyond what Morwani proves. Their proof is for nu=3 only. The general-nu modular-addition result is Li et al. AISTATS 2025 Thm 4.1. Their group result also carries the conditions above (real irreps, character sum, width).
- **"Networks approach max margin"** is Morwani Thm 1 / Wei Thm 4.1. It holds for global minimisers, not for trained networks. This is minor.

Searches: none were needed. I read the primary source directly. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/c1-morwani-dense-baseline/CHECK.md.

c2-morwani-wei-principle.evidence:
Checked Wei, Lee, Liu, Ma, "Regularization Matters: Generalization and Optimization of Neural Nets v.s. their Induced Kernel", NeurIPS 2019. I fetched the arXiv 1810.05369 PDF and confirmed the NeurIPS proceedings page.

**Wei et al., Section 4 setting.** f is a-positive-homogeneous and continuous in Theta. The norm can be any general norm. The objective is binary logistic loss + lambda||Theta||^r with r>0 fixed (eq. 4.1).

**Wei et al., Theorem 4.1 (verbatim).** "Assume the training data is separable by a network f(.;Theta*) in F with an optimal normalized margin gamma*>0. Then, the normalized margin of the global optimum of the weakly-regularized objective (equation 4.1) converges to gamma* as the regularization goes to zero ... gamma_lambda -> gamma* as lambda -> 0."

**Wei et al., multi-class version.** Theorem 4.1 is binary only. The multi-class cross-entropy statement is Theorem C.1 in App. C, with margin f_y - max_{j!=y} f_j: "Assume gamma*>0 in the multi-class setting with cross entropy loss. Then as lambda -> 0, gamma_lambda -> gamma*."

**Hypotheses hold in our setting.** L_{2,b} with 2<=b<=nu is a true norm. Here r=b. The polynomial neurons are continuous and nu-homogeneous, and the width is fixed. The result covers global minimizers only, and approach.tex already says so.

**Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568, PDF fetched).** Section 2 restates "Theorem 1 (Wei et al. (2019a), Theorem 4.1). For any norm, a fixed r>0 and any homogeneous function f with homogeneity constant nu>0, if gamma*>0, then lim gamma_lambda = gamma*." It continues: "This provides the motivation behind studying maximum margin classifiers as a proxy for understanding the global minimizers of L_lambda." Its abstract says "the principle of margin maximization alone can be used to fully specify the features learned by the network." So the "one principle" framing in our sentence is correctly attributed.

**Minor points.**
- The precise multi-class result is Thm C.1, not Thm 4.1. Morwani cites 4.1 too, so this is not an error.
- "Networks approach" informally means that global minimizers of the regularized loss approach gamma* in normalized margin.

**Bib entries.** Both refs.bib entries match the fetched pages.

c7-morwani-definitions.evidence:
Fetched the arXiv 2311.07568 PDF from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.07568 and extracted it with pdftotext. Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao, Kakade, ICLR 2024.

1. **The L_{2,ν} norm.** Sec. 2 defines ||θ||_{a,b} = (Σ_i ||ω_i||_a^b)^{1/b}, and homogeneity as φ(λω,x) = λ^ν φ(ω,x). Sec. 3.2 says "we will primarily focus on maximum margin with respect to L2,ν norm in this work". This matches "b=ν is Morwani's norm".

2. **The quadratic neuron.** Sec. 2 gives φ({u,v,w},a,b) = (u_a + v_b)^2 w, with one-hot inputs, no biases and w ∈ R^{|G|}. This is our power neuron at n=2 (ν=3).

3. **The margins.** Sec. 3 defines:
   - g(θ,x,y) = f(θ,x)[y] − max_{y'≠y} f(θ,x)[y'];
   - h(θ) = min_{(x,y)∈D} g;
   - γ* = max_{θ∈Θ} h(θ) with Θ = {||θ|| ≤ 1};
   - the normalized margin as h(θ/||θ||).

   Our h(θ)/||θ||^ν is equal to theirs by ν-homogeneity. Their Theorem 1 restates Wei Thm 4.1 ("any norm, fixed r>0"), which covers our λ||θ||^b.

5. **η_{u,v,w}(δ) := E_{a,b}[(u(a)+v(b))^2 w(a+b−δ)]** is defined only in Appendix F.1, not in the main text.

6. **The phase condition** θ_u* + θ_v* = θ_w* is in Thm 7 part 1 (Sec. 4) and App. F.1 Eq. (7).

7. **The maximum margin.** Thm 7: "with m ≥ 4(p−1) neurons. The maximum L2,3-margin ... γ* = sqrt(2/27)·1/(p^{1/2}(p−1))". Parts 1 and 2 give "single frequency per neuron" and "every frequency used".

c9-feature-definition.evidence:
Both papers treat Fourier frequencies as the learned units, but neither defines a feature as a frequency with nonzero logit amplitude. "As in" is therefore too strong.

**Nanda et al., ICLR 2023** (arXiv 2301.05217; PDF fetched, header says "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023").
- Sec. 4.1: "W_E is sparse in the Fourier basis -- it only has significant nonnegligible norm at 6 frequencies. Of these frequencies, only 5 appear to be used significantly in later parts of the model (k in {14,35,41,42,52}). We dub these the key frequencies of the model."
- Fig. 3 caption: "W_L is well-approximated by the 5 key frequencies". Sec. 4.4 uses ablations (restricted and excluded loss).
- The paper never calls frequencies "features". The only occurrence of the word is "some feature of the loss landscape".
- Its criterion is empirical and thresholded, and it excludes a frequency that has nonzero embedding norm. So it is not "exactly nonzero means feature". It does match the idea of an amplitude measured at the logit level (in W_L).

c11-morwani-single-neuron.evidence:
I read Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 Spotlight, arXiv 2311.07568 v2, in full from the arXiv PDF and checked the venue on the abs page.

Sec 3.1, Lemma 3 (binary; proof in App E.1) and Sec 3.2, Lemma 5 (multi-class, class-weighted; App E.2) each have a 'Single neuron optimization' bullet. It says that for a fixed distribution q, any theta in argmax_{||theta||_{a,b}<=1} E_q[g(theta)] 'has directional support only on' Omega*_q = argmax_{||omega||_a<=1} E_q[psi(omega)]. The justification is that 'the expected margin of the network decomposes into the sum of expected margin of individual neurons', so E_q g = sum_i ||omega_i||^nu E_q psi(omega_i/||omega_i||) <= gamma max_{||w||_b<=1} ||w||_nu^nu. Combining neurons needs b = nu, and the Remark in App E.1 says other b values do not give the flexibility needed to satisfy Eq. 1. These lemmas serve the certificate-pair method (Lemma 2 / Lemma 6). Thm 7 applies it by maximising sum_j u^(j) v^(j) w^(-j) over one unit neuron.

What is shared: a network sum is reduced by homogeneity to a single unit-norm neuron problem.

What differs:
- Morwani's per-neuron objective is a linear expected margin under a dual q, used for a primal-dual certificate at b = nu.
- The paper's C_b = max_{||omega||<=1} sum_j |beta_j(omega)|^{b/nu} is a concave l_{b/nu} budget. It feeds a subadditivity upper bound for all 2 <= b <= nu and uses no dual distribution.

So 'as in Morwani' fits the decomposition idea but not their lemma as stated. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/c11-morwani-single-neuron/CHECK.md.

The citation is at sections/appendix.tex line 196, closing the lower-bound proof in app:scaling. That proof draws L = ceil(8 ln p) frequencies at random and uses Hoeffding plus a union bound over offsets to show that the average of cos(2 pi J delta/p) is at most 1/2 for every delta != 0.

- Sec 3.2 gives the group-lasso l_{2/k} version.
- This is exactly our statement for b=2. Ours is the one-line generalisation to an L_{2,b} cost, which gives A^{b/nu}.

Sources I fetched and read this session:

(1) Alon & Roichman, RSA 5(2):271-284, 1994. Metadata from Crossref; text from the author PDF web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf.
- Abstract: "For Abelian groups this is essentially tight."
- Sec. 3, Proposition 3, verbatim: "For every fixed delta>0 there is a constant c=c(delta)>0 such that the following holds; If A is an Abelian group of order n, and X(A,S) is a delta-expander, then |S| >= c log_2 n."

- This entry is already in the bib (alon1994random), but the paper cites it only for the random lower bound. It is not cited for the Omega(log) necessity.

(2) Friedman, Murty & Tillich, JCTB 96(1):111-121, 2006. Metadata from Crossref; text from the author PDF at rocq.inria.fr.
- Abstract, verbatim: "a d-regular Cayley graph on an Abelian group of order n has second eigenvalue bounded below by d - O(dn^{-4/d}) ... for a large odd prime, n, the O(dn^{-4/d}) cannot be improved."
- Sec. 2, Thm 2 is the sphere-packing proof. Sec. 4, Thm 7 covers random Cayley graphs on Z/nZ with n prime.
- This is the quantitative unweighted form of our upper bound.

(3) Alon, "Perturbed identity matrices have high rank", CPC 18(1-2):3-15, 2009. Metadata from the Cambridge page; text from the author PDF identity1.pdf.
- Thm 7.1: an eps-biased family of n ±1 variables needs a sample space of size Omega(n/(eps^2 log(1/eps))).

That analogue is the two-sided Theta((log p)^{1-s}), the Theta(log p) support with a share floor, and the o(log p) vanishing fraction. r6-single-neuron-budget.corrected_verdict: KNOWN for the product and power neurons at every 2<=b<=nu. The per-frequency AM-GM/Parseval budget is Hoff 2017 Lemma 2 in Fourier form, via Gunasekar et al. 2018 Lemma 7. That covers b=2, including the observation that a neuron can carry several frequencies at no extra cost. At b=nu it is Morwani App. F.1 for n=2 and Li et al. Lemmas D.7-D.8 for all n. For 2<b<nu it follows in one line from monotonicity of l_q quasi-norms. The power-neuron bound is an equality: C_b^{nu/b} = n! B_p exactly. The ReLU bound C_2 <= p^{-n}/2 is FALSE for n>=2. The correct bound from the same argument is C_2 <= 1/(2p), independent of n. It is novel in application but elementary.

I re-fetched and re-read both of the checker's confirmed citations, and both are accurate.
- Morwani et al. 2311.07568 (ICLR 2024 spotlight per the arXiv comments): App. F.1, "Proofs for cyclic groups (Theorem 7)", eqs. (6)-(9), pp. 25-26. The steps are Plancherel, then "inequality of quadratic and geometric means", then Cauchy-Schwarz with ||z||_2 <= ||z||_1 <= p/2, giving sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). Lemma 18 is on p. 36. The checker's "eqs (6)-(9)" is right; call the location "App. F.1" rather than "the appendix".
- Li et al.: PMLR 258:523-531 (AISTATS 2025), confirmed on proceedings.mlr.press/v258/li25b.html. Lemma D.7 (eq. 15, coefficient k!) and Lemma D.8 (value 2(k!)/((2k+2)^{(k+1)/2}(p-1)p^{(k-1)/2})) are as the checker describes. The refs.bib entry for li2025nsum lacks series, volume and pages, and the key is still cited nowhere in the sections (only a TODO at intro.tex:22).

Where the checker's verdict fails:

(1) Missed prior art (math lens), Gunasekar, Lee, Soudry, Srebro, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv 1806.00468).
- Lemma 3: for full-width circular convolutions, beta^ = diag(w^_1)...diag(w^_{L-1}) w^_L.
- Lemma 7: min_{w:Pconv(w)=beta} ||w||_2^2 = L ||beta^||_{2/L}^{2/L}. The proof in App. D, eq. (85), is per-coordinate AM-GM.
- Our product neuron's coefficient beta_j = 2p^{-nu} prod_t u^_t(j) conj(w^(j)) is the same Hadamard product of nu DFTs. So our C_2 statement, with equality for balanced neurons carrying any number of frequencies, is Gunasekar Lemma 7 with L=nu, up to normalisation and the pairing of j with -j.
- The checker called the "several frequencies at no extra cost" observation new. It is not.

chk.evidence:
Morwani et al. ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568v2 HTML, fetched):
- Sec 3.2 / Lemma 5 gives the class-weighted margin.
- The Sec 4 proof outline uses uniform class weighting tau = 1/(p-1), which gives E[psi'] = 2/((p-1)p^2) sum_{j!=0} u^(j)v^(j)w^(-j).

Not found anywhere: a rigorous upper bound on the min-margin of an arbitrary network (with interference and misaligned phases) by the amplitude-weighted coverage at each offset. The lemma is elementary, though, and should be presented as an adaptation.

chk.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r4-programme/CHECK.md.

The general shape of the programme is known. The specific programme is not: a cosine-coverage max-min over Z_p under a concave l_{1/s} budget with 1/s = b/nu, used to bound the margin of every network and to count its features. No paper found states it.

Reviewers are likely to recognise three reformulations:

(1) **Max-margin under an l_q quasi-norm on Fourier coefficients (q < 1), with the exponent set by homogeneity.**
- Source: Gunasekar, Lee, Soudry, Srebro, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv 1806.00468). I read Theorem 2a in the PDF.
- For depth-L linear convolutional nets, the GD limit direction is "a scaling of a first order stationary point of min_beta ||beta_hat||_{2/L} s.t. forall n, y_n<beta,x_n> >= 1". Here beta_hat is the vector of DFT coefficients.
- Theorem 2 covers L=2 and gives ||beta_hat||_1. The paper notes that p=2/L<1 is non-convex.
- The template is the same as ours: homogeneity gives an l_{2/depth} bridge penalty in frequency space, and that gives frequency sparsity.
- Differences: generic data, linear convnets only, no coverage or modular structure, no bound over all networks, no K* or log p count.
- Related: Jagadeesan, Razenshteyn, Gunasekar, COLT 2022 (arXiv 2102.12238). In multichannel linear convnets, the l2 weight norm induces a nuclear norm or an l_{2,1} norm on the Fourier coefficients.

(2) **Laplacian spectral gap of a weighted circulant graph.**
- sum_j y_j(1-cos(2 pi j delta/p)) is the delta-th Laplacian eigenvalue of the weighted Cayley graph Cay(Z_p, {±j}). So Gamma_s is the largest algebraic connectivity reachable under an l_{1/s} weight budget.
- The s=1 endpoint is the convex edge-weight problem in Boyd, "Convex Optimization of Graph Laplacian Eigenvalues", Proc. ICM 2006, 3:1311-1319 (confirmed on Boyd's page).
- The s->infinity endpoint is the cardinality problem in Ghosh & Boyd, "Growing Well-connected Graphs", 45th IEEE CDC 2006. From the PDF: "maximize lambda_2(L(E_base u E)) subject to |E|=k, E subset E_cand", solved with an SDP relaxation.
- Alon-Roichman (already cited) covers random O(log p) generators.
- I found no version with an interpolating l_q budget with q<1, and no result for circulants of the form K* = Theta(log p).

(3) **The same coverage objective in modular-addition ML work.**
- Kam, Bessafi, Cadet, arXiv 2609.17926 (15 Sep 2026). I fetched the HTML of App. A.3.2.
- Eq. 15: Delta_S(beta) = min_{s!=0} sum_k beta_k(1-cos(omega_k s)), with ||beta||_2 = B.
- Prop. 5: the uniform allocation is optimal at full frequency content.
- This is our objective with a convex l2 budget in place of l_{1/s}, which is why their optimum is dense. Treat it as concurrent work.
- Morwani et al. 2024 is the s=1 endpoint.

**Adjacent problems, no overlap:**
- The Chowla cosine problem asks for the minimum of an unweighted cosine sum, which is a different extremum.
- Ge-Jiang-Ye 2011 is generic theory for l_p minimisation with p<1.
- LPBoost covers l1 margins only.
- Thinned-array sidelobe design is an unweighted analogue. I did not fetch a source for it, so it has no bib entry.

**Searches run:**
- "maximizing algebraic connectivity edge weights convex optimization Ghosh Boyd"
- "maximize minimum nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue circulant graph weights sparse concave cost"
- "max-min cosine sum nonnegative coefficients l_p quasi-norm p<1 sparse optimal support"
- "linear programming boosting margin maximization l_q quasi-norm q<1"
- "frequency selection nonnegative weights maximize worst-case 1-cos offset cyclic group sparse log p": nothing relevant
- "maximum margin l_p quasi-norm p<1 support size bound"
- "weighted Cayley graph cyclic group maximize spectral gap budget on weights sparse generating set": nothing relevant

recommended_citations.why: Cite at eq:programme. Its Thm 2a shows homogeneity producing a max-margin problem under an l_{2/L} bridge quasi-norm on Fourier coefficients, the same template that gives our l_{1/s} budget with 1/s = b/nu. Reviewers will expect this precedent for 'depth or homogeneity gives frequency sparsity'.

Concurrent work with the same coverage max-min objective (App. A.3.2, Eq. 15) under a convex ||beta||_2=B budget. Their Prop. 5 finds the uniform (dense) allocation optimal, which contrasts with our concave budget.

Gamma_s is the largest spectral gap of a weighted circulant graph. At s=1 (l1 budget) this is Boyd's convex edge-weight problem for algebraic connectivity. Supports the sentence placing Cor. dense as its circulant case.

The s->infinity (cardinality) endpoint: choose k edges to maximise lambda_2 (their Eq. 2), which is combinatorial, with an SDP relaxation. Our l_{1/s} budget interpolates between this and the s=1 convex problem. The first page (6605) was read from the PDF; the last page, 6610, is inferred and not confirmed, so check it before submission.

Optional. Shows that the l2 weight norm induces nuclear or l_{2,1} group-sparse norms on Fourier coefficients: an explicit representation cost pushing toward frequency sparsity, like our AM-GM pricing.

chk.recommended_change: Add after eq:programme (approach.tex, after the AM-GM sentence): "Equivalently, Gamma_s is the l_{1/s}-quasi-norm maximum margin of a nonnegative separator of the coverage vectors kappa(delta). The same reduction, from homogeneity to an l_{2/L} bridge penalty on Fourier coefficients, appears for depth-L linear convolutional networks \citep{gunasekar2018implicit}. It is also the largest Laplacian spectral gap of a weighted circulant graph on Z_p under an l_{1/s} weight budget, which interpolates between the convex l_1 edge-weight problem at s=1 \citep{boyd2006convex} and the cardinality-constrained problem as s->infinity \citep{ghosh2006growing}. Concurrently, \citet{kam2026symmetry} study the same coverage objective under a convex l_2 amplitude budget and find the uniform (dense) allocation optimal; the concave budget that homogeneity forces is what makes ours sparse." Do not claim the programme's form is new. Claim that it is derived from L_{2,b} homogeneity and bounds every network, and claim its solution (K* = Theta(log p), shapes, offsets).

item.what_to_check: Core result; search for L_{2,b} (b != nu, esp. weight decay b=2) max-margin analyses of modular addition: Morwani, Li et al. 2025, Tian 2024 algebraic objects, Jacobs-Montufar, AdamW/l_inf margin papers

chk.evidence:
The b = nu endpoint is known. Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568; I fetched the HTML) prove all their theorems only at L_{2,nu}. Their Thm 7 gives the max L_{2,3} margin as sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) for the quadratic net with width >= 4(p-1). Plain L2 appears only empirically: Fig 4b says L2 ReLU neurons are "nearly 1-sparse ... but not quite". Li, Liang, Shi, Song and Zhou, AISTATS 2025, PMLR 258:523-531 (proceedings page fetched) state only a maximum L_{2,k+1} margin, with m >= 2^{2k-2}(p-1). Our cor:dense reproduces Morwani Thm 7, and the paper already says so.

The b < nu case, including b = 2 weight decay, was not found anywhere. Papers I checked:
- Mohamadi et al., ICML 2024 (2407.12332, HTML): the norm is l_inf. Prop 3.8 only shows that zero-loss solutions exist with ||theta||_inf <= floor(h/8p)^{-1/3}; Thm 4.5 is a generalisation bound for Omega(p) margin. There is no upper bound on the max margin over all widths.
- Tian, NeurIPS 2025 (2410.01779): Thm 5 says "lower-order solutions are preferred if trained with L2 regularization", argued by path-connectivity. There is no margin bound.
- Jacobs and Montufar 2026 (2605.19458): mirror flow. No modular addition and no L_{2,b} bound.
- Kam, Bessafi and Cadet 2026 (2609.17926, HTML App. A.3.2): Eq 15 is max over ||beta||_2 = B of min_s sum_k beta_k(1-cos(omega_k s)), and Prop 5 finds a uniform allocation optimal. The l2 budget on the amplitudes is posited for the quadratic net only; it is not derived from homogeneity, and they make no claim for all networks or widths. This is the closest analogue of the coverage programme, but not of the universal bound.
- Memana 2026 (2608.04451) and Nguyen 2026 (2606.17399) are irrelevant.

The pricing step (amplitude A costs A^{b/nu}, then subadditivity) is a known ingredient:
- Hoff (arXiv 1611.00040): "a subclass of L_q penalties with q<=1 can be expressed as sums of L_2 penalties".
- Dai, Karzand and Srebro, NeurIPS 2021: the representation cost of l2 regularisation on the parameters.
- Fan, Ding, Yang, Zhang and Udell, TMLR 2023 (2012.03436): regularisers built from the Euclidean norms of CP components are "monotonic transformations of tensor Schatten-p quasi-norm". A product neuron is a rank-one CP term, so our pricing is the diagonal (Fourier) case of this.

item.statement: Gamma_1(p)=p/(p-1) with unique flat maximizer y_j=2/(p-1); recovers Morwani's max L_{2,3} margin sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) exactly
item.what_to_check: Verify the constant against Morwani's quadratic theorem; check Li et al. 2025 general-nu dense endpoint overlap

chk.evidence:
The constant matches exactly, and the result is known. I read the full PDF text of arXiv 2311.07568v2 and 2402.09469v4 with pdftotext.

(1) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 spotlight, Theorem 7 (Sec. 4): "Consider one-hidden layer networks f(theta,a,b) of the form given in section 2 with m >= 4(p-1) neurons. The maximum L2,3-margin of such a network on the dataset D_p is gamma* = sqrt(2/27)·1/(p^{1/2}(p-1))." The neuron is (u_a+v_b)^2 w. Every neuron uses a single frequency, and "For every frequency zeta ... at least one neuron in the network uses this frequency."

(2) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025 (PMLR 258:523-531), Theorem 4.1 (informal version of Thm G.2): neurons (sum_i u_i(a_i))^k w, L_{2,k+1}, m >= 2^{2k-1}(p-1)/2, gamma* = 2(k!)/((2k+2)^{(k+1)/2}(p-1)p^{(k-1)/2}), and every frequency is used. Our b=nu bound n!·B_p·Gamma_1(p), with B_p=2(2p nu)^{-nu/2} and nu=n+1, simplifies algebraically to Li's gamma*. I checked it numerically for n=2,3,4 and p=7,113: the ratio is 1 to 1e-15. At n=2 it equals sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). The general-nu dense endpoint is therefore Li et al.'s result.

(3) The flat maximizer is implicit in Morwani. In App. F.3 ("Proof that all frequencies are used"), Lemma 6 splits any max-margin f into F(a,b) plus lambda·1[a+b=c]. So f-hat(j,j,-j) = lambda·p^2 at every nonzero j, which is the same amplitude on every frequency. Their F.2 construction and Li's Lemma 4.3 are also flat.

(4) Our averaging step (1/(p-1))·sum over delta≠0 is the coverage-space version of Morwani's and Li's uniform class weighting tau[c'] = 1/(p-1).

What is new: only the explicit uniqueness proof of the flat maximizer within the programme Gamma_1, which is elementary Fourier inversion, and the framing of this endpoint as the s=1 case of a family that is sparse for s>1.

Internal wording issue: app:models justifies C_3=2B_p by citing Cor. dense, and app:dense then uses C_3=2B_p. This is not a real circularity: C_3 <= 2B_p is proved, and Morwani Thm 7 supplies attainment. The text should say so.

Searches: an adversarial harmonic-analysis search for the l1 max-min cosine problem found nothing; it is a trivial averaging bound. A second search for margin plus equal-amplitude results on modular addition turned up only Morwani, McCracken, Kam (l2 budget, Prop 5 uniform), He et al., and Huang-Li 2511.23443 (sine activations, related only). Venues were confirmed at iclr.cc/virtual/2024/poster/18073 and proceedings.mlr.press/v258/li25b.html. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r8-dense-corollary/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.why: Theorem 7 gives the exact max L_{2,3} margin sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) that Cor. dense recovers. App. F.3 (via Lemma 6) implies that every max-margin net has the same diagonal Fourier amplitude at every frequency, which is the flat maximizer. It also supplies the attainment that makes C_3 = 2B_p.

Theorem 4.1 gives gamma* = 2(k!)/((2k+2)^{(k+1)/2}(p-1)p^{(k-1)/2}) for power-k neurons under L_{2,k+1}, with every frequency used. It equals our n! B_p Gamma_1(p) exactly for every n (checked algebraically, and numerically for n=2,3,4), so the general-nu dense endpoint is theirs.

Equal amplitude on every frequency is also implicit in \citet[App. F.3]{morwani2024feature}. What we add is that this dense endpoint is the s=1 case of a programme that is sparse for every s>1." Their networks attain it, so C_\nu^{1}=n!B_p there." This removes the apparent circularity with app:dense.

item.statement: A network is interference-free if beta_{j,T}=0 for all j in F and nonempty T subset [n] (sign-flipped modes at a used frequency cancel in the logit table)
item.what_to_check: Check related notions in Morwani/Gromov/Nanda (cos(a-b) terms) and any 'clean' circuit definitions

chk.evidence:
I read the full texts, pulling the PDFs and grepping them for cancel/interference/phase/a-b terms.

(1) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568), App. F.2. The max-margin witness uses 8 neurons per frequency: pairs of neurons with phases (0,0,0) and (0,pi,pi), and so on, so that the sum is exactly sum_zeta cos_zeta(a+b-c). They write: "for each input (a,b), f takes the same value on all incorrect labels c', satisfying C.1." Their network is therefore interference-free, but they never isolate that property. Condition C.1 is stronger than ours. Their sparse-parity construction (Thm 8, App. G) uses 2^{k-1} sign-pattern neurons, and "every term other than Pi x_{S_i} cancels out in the sum". This is the Boolean analogue.

(2) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025 (arXiv 2402.09469), App. E. They build an explicit k-input network with 2^k * 2^{k-1} neurons per frequency, using sign-pattern polarisation. It computes exactly sum cos(sum a_i - c) and satisfies Condition 3.8. So an interference-free construction exists for every k, at 2^{2k-1} neurons per frequency against our nu. It is a construction only; there is no class and no cost lemma.

(3) Gromov, arXiv 2301.02679. Eq. 11 lists the sign-flipped waves cos(n-m-q) etc. Eq. 12 is the phase constraint phi1+phi2=phi3, which gives "constructive interference". The paper says "we need to ensure that all other waves ... interfere destructively", and Eq. 15 is the "destructive interference condition", satisfied only approximately by random phases. This is the closest conceptual precedent and even uses the same word.

(4) Doshi, He, Das, Gromov, "Grokking Modular Polynomials" (ICLR 2024 BGPT workshop, arXiv 2406.03495). The multi-operand version of Gromov: "all other terms will vanish due to random phase approximation".

(5) He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849. Def. 4.1(iii) is an exact phase-moment cancellation: sum_{m in N_k} exp(i*iota*phi_m)=0 for iota in {2,4}. It kills the "residual noise" terms of Eq. 4.1. In Prop. 4.2 spurious peaks at 2x and 2y survive, so their condition is not interference-free in our sense. It is nonetheless a close cousin of our Eq. (JF).

(6) Zhong, Liu, Tegmark, Andreas, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2306.17844). Clock logits are cos(w(a+b-c)). Pizza logits are |cos(w(a-b)/2)| cos(w(a+b-c)). The a-b factor is label-independent same-frequency interference, so informally Clock is interference-free and Pizza is not.

Conclusion: exact or approximate cancellation of the sign-flipped copies across neurons is a known construction device. Not found in any of these papers: interference-freeness as a named class over which the margin is maximised, the sign rule, the finite system (JF), and the nu-neuron cost.
