item.statement: A network is interference-free if beta_{j,T}=0 for all j in F and nonempty T subset [n] (sign-flipped modes at a used frequency cancel in the logit table)
item.what_to_check: Check related notions in Morwani/Gromov/Nanda (cos(a-b) terms) and any 'clean' circuit definitions

chk.evidence:
I read the full texts, pulling the PDFs and grepping them for cancel/interference/phase/a-b terms.

(1) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568), App. F.2. The max-margin witness uses 8 neurons per frequency: pairs of neurons with phases (0,0,0) and (0,pi,pi), and so on, so that the sum is exactly sum_zeta cos_zeta(a+b-c). They write: "for each input (a,b), f takes the same value on all incorrect labels c', satisfying C.1." Their network is therefore interference-free, but they never isolate that property. Condition C.1 is stronger than ours. Their sparse-parity construction (Thm 8, App. G) uses 2^{k-1} sign-pattern neurons, and "every term other than Pi x_{S_i} cancels out in the sum". This is the Boolean analogue.

(2) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025 (arXiv 2402.09469), App. E. They build an explicit k-input network with 2^k * 2^{k-1} neurons per frequency, using sign-pattern polarisation. It computes exactly sum cos(sum a_i - c) and satisfies Condition 3.8. So an interference-free construction exists for every k, at 2^{2k-1} neurons per frequency against our nu. It is a construction only; there is no class and no cost lemma.

(3) Gromov, arXiv 2301.02679. Eq. 11 lists the sign-flipped waves cos(n-m-q) etc. Eq. 12 is the phase constraint phi1+phi2=phi3, which gives "constructive interference". The paper says "we need to ensure that all other waves ... interfere destructively", and Eq. 15 is the "destructive interference condition", satisfied only approximately by random phases. This is the closest conceptual precedent and even uses the same word.

(4) Doshi, He, Das, Gromov, "Grokking Modular Polynomials" (ICLR 2024 BGPT workshop, arXiv 2406.03495). The multi-operand version of Gromov: "all other terms will vanish due to random phase approximation".

(5) He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849. Def. 4.1(iii) is an exact phase-moment cancellation: sum_{m in N_k} exp(i*iota*phi_m)=0 for iota in {2,4}. It kills the "residual noise" terms of Eq. 4.1. In Prop. 4.2 spurious peaks at 2x and 2y survive, so their condition is not interference-free in our sense. It is nonetheless a close cousin of our Eq. (JF).

(6) Zhong, Liu, Tegmark, Andreas, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2306.17844). Clock logits are cos(w(a+b-c)). Pizza logits are |cos(w(a-b)/2)| cos(w(a+b-c)). The a-b factor is label-independent same-frequency interference, so informally Clock is interference-free and Pizza is not.

Conclusion: exact or approximate cancellation of the sign-flipped copies across neurons is a known construction device. Not found in any of these papers: interference-freeness as a named class over which the margin is maximised, the sign rule, the finite system (JF), and the nu-neuron cost. item.statement: For product and power neurons, beta_{ij,T} = beta_{ij} prod_{t in T} xi_{itj} with unit xi
item.what_to_check: Elementary; confirm not stated elsewhere in the same form

chk.evidence:
Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r10-sign-rule/CHECK.md.

(1) The lemma is textbook Hermitian symmetry of the DFT of real weights: hat u(-j) = conj(hat u(j)) = xi * hat u(j), with |xi| = 1.

(2) He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849 (2026), Sec. 4 (fetched from arxiv.org/html/2602.16849).
- Eq. 4.1 splits one quadratic neuron with phase phi_m into three parts: the signal cos(omega(x+y-j)); cos(omega j + 2 phi_m); and cos(omega(x+y+j) + 4 phi_m). The last is a sign-flipped copy with a unit phase factor.
- Def. 4.1(iii) requires, for each frequency k and iota in {2,4}, that exp(i iota phi_m) summed over the neurons of frequency k is 0. That is cancellation of these copies across neurons, the 2-input quadratic analogue of our eq:JF.

(3) Morwani et al. ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568 HTML) uses hat u(j) hat v(j) hat w(-j) with conjugate symmetry and states the phase condition theta_u + theta_v = theta_w (Thm 7). It gives no per-operand sign-flip factor.

(4) Li et al. AISTATS 2025 (arXiv 2402.09469 HTML): the neurons are one-sparse cosines (Lemma 4.2), and the paper has no sign-flip or conjugate lemma.

(5) Gromov 2023 (arXiv 2301.02679): the abstract does not cover this.

Web search on "modular addition Fourier conjugate phases cancel spurious terms cos(a-b-c) sum over neurons roots of unity" returned only He et al.

Conclusion: the general n-operand form was not found anywhere, i.e. one unit factor per operand, multiplied over the flipped set T, for both product and power neurons. That form is a trivial generalisation of Hermitian symmetry, and its quadratic special case, including cross-neuron cancellation, is in He et al.

recommended_citations.why: This supports the sentence after lem:sign saying that a single neuron is never interference-free and that sign-flipped copies must cancel across neurons. Eq. 4.1 shows one quadratic neuron producing the flipped-mode term cos(omega(x+y+j)+4phi_m), and Def. 4.1(iii) requires phase sums over neurons to vanish. The title, the arXiv id and the surnames He, Wang, Chen, Yang were confirmed on the fetched HTML page. The first names were not checked on the page, so confirmed is false; verify them before use.

item.statement: Under the interference-free system (JF), sum_l |beta_l|^r >= nu^{1-r} |beta|^r for r in (0,1]; for r<1 equality iff exactly nu terms of modulus |beta|/nu with pairwise orthogonal chain vectors
item.what_to_check: Key lemma; search tensor/Waring rank of products of cosines, multilinear cancellation, majorization via Bernstein functions, polyphase code cancellation

chk.evidence:
Reframing (the paper does not say this): on one frequency block, (JF) asks for an exact real rank-1 (separated) decomposition of cos(theta_1+...+theta_n-theta_0), which is the tensor Re(z_1...z_n conj z_0) in (R^2)^{⊗nu}. Over C this tensor has rank 2. The count part of the lemma (at least nu neurons) is therefore a real-rank lower bound, and the nu-block is a known trig identity.

(1) Beylkin & Mohlenkamp, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 26(6):2133-2159, 2005. I read the PDF and confirmed the metadata on Crossref.
- §2.1.1 "Sine of a sum", Lemma 2.4 (eq. 2.9): sin(sum x_j) = sum_j sin(x_j) prod_{k≠j} sin(x_k+alpha_k-alpha_j)/sin(alpha_k-alpha_j). That is d real separable terms, against 2^{d-1} from the angle-addition formulas.
- Def. 2.2 defines an l2 coefficient condition number, kappa = (sum s_l^2)^{1/2}/||F||.
- §3 observes that "choosing alpha_j equally spaced in the identity leads to kappa ≈ 7". This is a numerical remark with no proof and uses an l2 cost, not l_r.

(2) Mohlenkamp & Monzón, Math. Intelligencer 27(2):65-69, 2005. I read the preprint PDF and confirmed the metadata on Crossref.
- Thm 2 is the n-variable identity.
- On minimality they write: "to find a minimal rank representation ... is still an open problem. We believe that our Theorems 2 and 5 are an example of such minimal representations." So the lower bound is NOT proved there.

(3) Comon & Ottaviani, Linear Multilinear Algebra 60(6):657-667, 2012 (arXiv 0909.4865; abstract fetched, Crossref-confirmed).
- The abstract states "a real binary form of degree d with d real roots has rank d". This gives real Waring rank d for Re((x+iy)^d), which is the symmetric (power-neuron) analogue of the count. It carries no weights.
- Related: Blekherman arXiv 1205.3257 (typical ranks), and Huang-Tang-Ye-Zhu arXiv 2601.03560 (harmonic binary forms have Waring rank equal to their degree).

(4) The transfer from Thorin-Bernstein functions to x^r is known (Rajan-Tepedelenlioglu 2015; Schilling-Song-Vondracek). See the sibling item r13. The ML phase-cancellation precedents (He et al. Def 4.1(iii), Gromov, Morwani App F.2, Li App E) are covered in items r9 and r10.

What I did not find:
- A proof that the non-symmetric real tensor rank of Re(z_1...z_d) equals d. Mohlenkamp and Monzón leave it as a belief. Our Prop esym gives it, since e_nu(x) ≥ 1.
- Any weighted l_r (r<1) lower bound on the coefficients of such decompositions, or an equality characterisation (equal weights, orthogonal chain vectors, rotated roots of unity).

Searches run:
- sine-of-sum separation rank lower bound
- real rank of Re(z_1...z_d) and of 2x...x2 tensors
- real rank of binary forms with all real roots
- Reznick sums of powers with equally spaced angles
- polyphase / roots-of-unity cancellation with l_p weights
- det(I+tA) with Bernstein-function majorization

One caveat: I did not read Hackbusch's tensor book or Wang-Seigal 2023 in full. Check them before claiming the rank-d lower bound as new.

item.location: appendix lem:chain, prop:esym, prop:gen, Remark 'other penalties'
item.statement: Chain lemma (H=sum beta_l m_l m_l^* upper-triangular with diagonal beta), e_k(x) >= binom(nu,k), prod(1+x_l t) >= (1+t)^nu; the cost lemma extends to any Bernstein-type penalty psi(x)=cx+int log(1+xt) mu(dt)
item.what_to_check: Check whether the elementary-symmetric/generating inequality transfer to power sums is a known majorization or Bernstein-function result

chk.evidence: The transfer from the generating inequality to power sums and other penalties is a known general principle. Rajan & Tepedelenlioglu (IEEE TIT 61(4):1619-1628, 2015; arXiv 1302.5383) define the "ergodic capacity order" (Def. 1): X <=_c Y iff E log(1+rho X) <= E log(1+rho Y) for all rho >= 0. Their Property S1 states "X <=_c Y <=> E[g(X)] <= E[g(Y)] for all g in TBF", where TBF is the Thorin-Bernstein class g(x) = a + bx + int log(1+x/s) mu(ds) (their eq. 6). The proof of Property M1 (App. A, eqs. 28-31) matches ours step for step: take rho -> 0 for the linear term, then integrate log(1+t rho x) against a positive measure. Applied to the empirical measure of x (zero padding is allowed because a=0), it gives Remark "other penalties" verbatim, and Lemma cost at 0<r<1 is the case g = x^r. The class psi = cx + int log(1+xt) mu(dt) is exactly the Thorin-Bernstein functions vanishing at 0, which is Schilling-Song-Vondracek, Bernstein Functions, de Gruyter Studies in Math 37, Ch. 8 (1st-ed. TOC fetched; Ch. 8 starts p. 73). Lemma bernstein (the integral formula for x^r) is a standard Beta-integral representation. item.what_to_check: Main theorem; compare Morwani (b=nu), Li et al. 2025, Gromov analytic solution; any work pricing sparsity by nu-b

chk.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r20-cyclic-theorem/CHECK.md.

**The theorem itself: not found anywhere.** No paper gives the max-margin value for b<nu. No paper reduces the margin to a budget programme or derives a frequency count from one. No paper proves that exactly nu neurons per frequency is necessary at a norm optimum. No paper prices sparsity by the gap nu-b.

**The construction that attains it (prop:block): known.** It appears in Marchetti, Kunin, Myers, Acosta, Miolane, "Sequential Group Composition: A Window into the Mechanics of Deep Learning", arXiv 2602.03655. The arXiv comment field reads "Accepted at ICML 2026". The construction is App. B, Lemma B.8 Case 1:
- N >= (k+1) n_rho^{k+1} sigma-pi-sigma (product) neurons solve the per-irrep cost minimisation.
- Inputs are multiplied by e^{pi i j/(k+1)} and the output by e^{-pi i j k/(k+1)}/(k+1), for j=1..k+1. For real irreps they take real parts.
- Cross terms are then scaled by (1/(k+1)) sum_j e^{-2 pi i j (k-|A|)/(k+1)} (their eq. 71). This vanishes "since A is a proper subset of {1..k}, 0<k-|A|<=k, and thus k-|A| != 0 (mod k+1)".

For cyclic groups (n_rho=1) this is exactly our nu-block: nu=k+1 neurons, input phases pi l/nu, output phase n alpha_l. They use it only as a sufficient construction for square-loss minimisation under AGF dynamics. They make no claim that it is norm-optimal or necessary, and give no count. Their Lemma B.6 and Remark B.7 (Waring decomposition, 2^{k-1} powers needed, citing Carlini et al. 2011) explain why power neurons need exponential width (Li et al. need m >= 2^{2k-2}(p-1)) while product neurons need only nu.

**Other related work:**
- **Tian, NeurIPS 2025** (arXiv 2410.01779 v4, PDF read). Quadratic nets, L2 loss, weight decay.
  - Corollary 2: global solutions in which "each frequency [is] affiliated with 6 hidden nodes (order-6)", built from 3rd/4th roots of unity (Table 1).
  - Corollaries 4 and 5: order-4 and mixed order-4/6 solutions.
  - Theorem 5 ("Occam's Razer"): "lower-order solutions are preferred if trained with L2 regularization".
  - All frequencies are used. There is no margin and no norm optimum.
- **Gromov 2023** (arXiv 2301.02679, PDF read):
  - Uses all frequencies, with random phases under the constraint phi1+phi2=phi3 (Eq. 12).
  - Cancellation is only approximate at large N (Eq. 15).
  - Nothing is claimed about norm or margin optimality.
- **Morwani et al. ICLR 2024** (fetched): Thm 7 is the b=nu=3 dense endpoint.
- **Li et al. AISTATS 2025** (fetched): Thm 4.1 is the L_{2,k+1} endpoint for power neurons; every frequency is used.
- **Checked and not relevant:** Huang & Li 2511.23443. Among the citations of Li et al. on Semantic Scholar, only Marchetti et al. is relevant.

item.statement: nu product neurons with phases alpha_l = pi l/nu produce table nu lambda^nu 2^{-n} cos(2 pi j(sum a - c)/p), norm nu lambda^2 p/2 each; one block per support frequency attains the class value
item.what_to_check: Compare constructions in Morwani, Gromov 2023, Li et al. 2025, Nanda; trig/roots-of-unity cancellation

chk.evidence:
The trigonometric identity behind the nu-block is classical. Mohlenkamp and Monzón, "Trigonometric identities and sums of separable functions", Math. Intelligencer 27(2):65-69 (2005), DOI 10.1007/BF02985795 (metadata confirmed via Crossref; preprint read at ohiouniversityfaculty.com/mohlenka/research/sine.pdf). Their Thm 2 gives sin(sum_{j=1}^n x_j) = sum_j sin(x_j) prod_{k!=j} sin(x_k+alpha_k-alpha_j)/sin(alpha_k-alpha_j) for any distinct alpha, together with a shifted version with free a_j (sum a_j = 0). They state that sin of a sum "is exactly separated with separation rank n", compared with 2^{n-1} terms from the standard trig expansion. Their Fig. 1 (right) uses equally spaced alpha = 0, pi/3, 2pi/3. Minimality is only conjectured ("We believe..."). I checked numerically that the choice alpha_k = pi k/nu, a_k = -alpha_k, together with prod_{k=1}^{nu-1} sin(pi k/nu) = nu/2^{nu-1}, gives exactly our identity sum_{l=0}^{nu-1} (-1)^l prod_{k=1}^{nu} cos(x_k + pi l/nu) = nu 2^{1-nu} cos(sum x_k). This matches for nu = 2..7, and our block is that identity with x_nu = -theta_c.

None of the ML constructions uses a nu-neuron roots-of-unity block:
- Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, App. F.2 (PDF read): 8 neurons per frequency. They expand cos(a+b-c) into 4 trig terms and implement each with a neuron pair, with phases (0,0,0)/(0,pi,pi), (pi/2,-pi/2,0)/(pi/2,pi/2,pi) and so on. They credit Gromov's scheme.
- Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025, Lemma E.1 Part 3 and Lemma E.2/E.3: 2^{2k-1} neurons per frequency pair, built by sign-vector polarisation of 2^k trig terms. No roots-of-unity phases.
- Gromov 2023 (arXiv 2301.02679), Eqs. 6-16: random uniform phases with phi1+phi2=phi3. Spurious terms cancel only approximately (the random phase approximation). Doshi, He, Das, Gromov 2024 (arXiv 2406.03495), Eq. 2 is the same random-phase scheme for S-term sums.
- He, Wang, Chen, Yang (arXiv 2602.16849), Def 4.1(iii): phase-moment cancellation for iota in {2,4} within each frequency group (roots of unity satisfy it). Their setting is quadratic sum-activation nets, where noise peaks at 2x and 2y survive (Prop 4.2). There is no minimal block and no norm optimality.

The roots-of-unity filter itself is the textbook series-multisection identity.

What remains ours: the product-network norm accounting (nu lambda^2 p/2), the amplitude weighting lambda_j^nu = 2^n y*_j/nu, and the result that one block per support frequency attains Gamma_s. Cost-optimality of nu neurons is the separate lem:cost; the minimal-rank question is only conjectured in Mohlenkamp and Monzón.

Searches run: PDFs of Morwani, Li, Gromov, Doshi and He et al. grepped for their constructions and phases; web search for Mohlenkamp and Monzón; web search for the tensor rank of sin(x1+...+xd) (no minimality proof found). Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r21-nu-block/CHECK.md

item.statement: For s>1 maximizers are Gamma_s(p) times vertices of polyhedron P_p minimizing sum v^{1/s}; minimizing vertex set piecewise constant on finitely many s-intervals; support and amplitude ratios piecewise constant
item.what_to_check: Relies on classical concave minimisation and exponential-sum zero counts; novelty only in application

chk.evidence:
Both proof ingredients are classical, and step (i) is almost a direct specialisation of a known theorem. I found no prior work that applies them to Gamma_s(p) or states that the shape is piecewise constant in the exponent s.

(i) Minimisers of sum v^{1/s} over P_p are vertices, and every minimiser is a vertex.
- Hirsch & Hoffman, CPAM 14(3):355-369, 1961: a concave function on a polyhedron attains its minimum at an extreme point. Metadata confirmed via Crossref, DOI 10.1002/cpa.3160140313. The Wiley page returned 403, so I did not read the body.
- Ge, Jiang & Ye, Math. Program. 129(2):285-299, 2011 (DOI 10.1007/s10107-011-0470-2, confirmed via Crossref). I read the preprint at web.stanford.edu/~yyye/lpmin_v14.pdf. Problem (1) is: minimise sum x_j^p subject to Ax=b, x>=0, with 0<p<1. Preprint Theorem 3 reads: "The set of all basic feasible solutions of (1) or (2) is exactly the set of local minimizers." Its proof that a non-vertex cannot be a minimiser uses the same strict-concavity-along-a-segment argument as ours. Our P_p = {v>=0 : Cv>=1} reduces to their standard form once slack variables are added. Their Thm 1 also shows that lp minimisation over a polyhedron is strongly NP-hard.

(ii) Finitely many switches, via a Rolle-induction bound on the real zeros of an exponential sum.
- This is Laguerre's extension of Descartes' rule of signs to generalised polynomials (Polya-Szego, Part V).
- Expository source: Jameson, Math. Gazette 90(518):223-234, 2006, DOI 10.1017/S0025557200179628. Metadata confirmed via Crossref and Cambridge Core. The body is paywalled, so only the title and abstract (which cover generalised polynomials) are confirmed.

Searches for the combined statement found nothing: "lp quasi-norm minimization polyhedron piecewise constant in p", "concave minimization polytope parametric exponent optimal vertex changes finitely many times", and the parametric-LP literature. Parametric-LP work covers only linear parametric costs. The ML sweep papers (Morwani, Li et al., Kam et al., McCracken) contain nothing on how the shape depends on s.

Proof check: (i) and (ii) are correct.
- Minor wording issue: at a switch value of s, the minimising set is the union of the two neighbouring sets. The statement should allow one-point intervals, or say "outside finitely many values of s".
- Optional sharpening: the zero count can be bounded by the number of sign changes of c_k.

item.statement: A maximizer with K features has K tight offsets with linearly independent coverage rows on the support; y is the unique solution; 2K candidates are simultaneously hardest wrong answers
item.what_to_check: Relation to LP basic solutions and Chebyshev equioscillation

chk.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r23-bottleneck/CHECK.md.

The proof in appendix.tex (app:shape) has three steps:
(a) a maximizer is Gamma_s times a vertex of P_p, because a concave, monotone phi is minimised over a line-free polyhedron;
(b) at a vertex the active constraints have full rank, so K coverage rows are independent on the support;
(c) y_S is the unique solution of the square system.

Steps (a) and (b) are textbook: concave minimisation at extreme points (Rockafellar, Convex Analysis, Sec. 32) and the vertex characterisation of LP basic feasible solutions.

Closest prior art is Shapley and Snow, "Basic Solutions of Discrete Games" (Contributions to the Theory of Games Vol. I, AM-24, Princeton UP, pp. 27-36). Crossref lists it as 1951, DOI 10.1515/9781400881727-004; it is often cited as 1950. At s=1 the programme is the matrix game with payoff cov(j,delta), and Shapley-Snow characterise extreme optimal strategies through a square sub-game G'. Restated as Thm 2.3.1 in Attia and Oliu-Barton, arXiv 1810.08798: "A couple (x,y) is a basic solution of G iff there exists a square sub-game G' satisfying ... G' y' = val(G) 1". Prop 2.3.4(iii) there gives Ker(G' - vU') = <y'>, which is uniqueness. Our proposition is the s>1 analogue: the concave budget keeps the optimum at a vertex of the same polyhedron.

Chebyshev equioscillation is only an analogy. Alternation needs the Haar condition, and the Kolmogorov / Rivlin-Shapiro characterisation gives at most n+1 extremal points (survey: Goldsztejn, arXiv 2310.01851). Our coverage system is not Haar, the problem is a budgeted max-min, and our count is a lower bound from vertex rank.

On the ML side, Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, Lemma 6, says "all points in the support of q* are on the margin for any maximum margin solution". That is the dense analogue of tight wrong labels.

I found no paper stating that there are at least K tight wrong-answer offsets for K features in modular addition, or that the amplitude ratios are fixed by an equalising system. Search queries covered Shapley-Snow basic solutions, concave minimisation at vertices, Chebyshev/Haar characterisation, the max-min cosine-sum LP, and modular addition max-margin with tight wrong labels and vertices.

item.statement: m - 2y_j <= m_{-j} <= (1-w_j)^s m/(1-eps); removing feature j costs at least 1-(1-w_j)^s in [w_j, s w_j] of the margin
item.what_to_check: Compare feature-ablation results in mech interp (Nanda, Chughtai); no known theoretical analogue expected

chk.evidence:
I found no theoretical result that bounds the margin or loss from removing one feature by that feature's share of the regularization budget. The prior work is empirical only.

1. Nanda et al., ICLR 2023 (arXiv 2301.05217; I checked the PDF text).
   - Sec. 4.4 "Correctness checks: ablations": "ablating any key frequency causes a significant increase in loss. ... In contrast, ablating other frequencies does not hurt the model at all."
   - Fig. 6 shows the loss after ablating each frequency k=1..56.
   - The intro says: "ablating key frequencies used by the model reduces performance to chance, while ablating the other 95% of frequencies slightly improves performance."
   - Sec. 5 defines restricted and excluded loss.
   - None of this is a quantitative law.

2. Chughtai, Chan, Nanda, ICML 2023, PMLR 202:6243-6267 (confirmed on the PMLR page). They confirm the GCR algorithm "using ablations". This is empirical, with no bound.

3. McCracken et al., arXiv 2505.18266v1.
   - App. G.8 "Noise and ablation studies", Fig. 38, removes neurons from frequency clusters and reports loss and accuracy. This is empirical.
   - Their Thm 4.7/Cor 4.8 relate the margin to the number of frequencies, not to removing one frequency.

4. Morwani et al. (arXiv 2311.07568, HTML read): no theorem about the margin effect of removing a frequency or neuron group.

5. Adjacent fields (SVM feature removal, sparse max-margin): I found nothing about a share-to-fractional-loss bound under a concave l_{1/s} budget. The result follows in one line from degree-s homogeneity (rescale the reduced vector back to unit budget) plus |coverage| <= 2. It is elementary, but I found no prior statement of it.

Queries run:
- "theoretical bound margin loss ablating a single Fourier frequency modular addition network"
- "Nanda progress measures grokking ablating key frequencies loss restricted excluded loss"
- "Chughtai toy model of universality ablation irreducible representations key representations loss"
- "ablation single frequency grokked network loss increase proportional to its norm share weight decay theory"
- "provable bound effect of removing one feature on max-margin classifier sparse Fourier features lower bound loss fraction of margin"

item.statement: Any network with K = o(log p) nonzero amplitudes attains a vanishing fraction of gamma*_b(p), interference allowed
item.what_to_check: Relation to lower bounds on size of epsilon-biased sets / expander generating sets in Z_p

chk.evidence:
Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r26-few-features/CHECK.md.

Reduction. The coverage is F_y(delta) = sum_j y_j (1 - cos(2 pi j delta/p)). With equal weights on a set S, min over delta != 0 of F is K minus half the largest non-trivial eigenvalue of Cay(Z_p, S u -S); the eigenvalues of that graph are character sums (Alon-Roichman Sec. 3). So the equal-share form of cor:few is the statement that an abelian Cayley graph with o(log p) generators has a vanishing normalised one-sided spectral gap.

(1) Alon & Roichman, "Random Cayley graphs and expanders", RSA 5(2) 1994. I fetched the PDF at web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf.
- Prop 3: "For every fixed delta>0 there is a constant c=c(delta)>0 such that the following holds; If A is an Abelian group of order n, and X(A,S) is a delta-expander, then |S| >= c log2 n." The proof is a diameter/volume count.
- The abstract says of the log bound: "For Abelian groups this is essentially tight".
- The paper already cites this work, but only for the random lower bound (appendix l.196).

(2) Friedman, Murty & Tillich, "Spectral estimates for Abelian Cayley graphs", JCTB 96(1):111-121, 2006, DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2005.06.012.
- Main result: for fixed d, a d-regular Cayley graph on an abelian group of order n has second eigenvalue >= d - O(d n^{-4/d}), with an absolute constant.
- How confirmed: the ScienceDirect listing is pii S0095895605000948, and the DOI resolves to that pii. The article page itself gave a 403. I fetched Cioaba, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 342 (2006) 635-638, which cites it as ref [6] with this bibliographic data and quotes "second largest eigenvalue of a k-regular Abelian Cayley graph with n vertices is at least k - O(k n^{-4/k})".
- With d = 2K and equal shares y = K^{-s}, this gives m <= C K^{1-s} e^{-2x}. So m / Gamma_s <= C x^{s-1} e^{-2x} -> 0, which is exactly cor:few for equal shares, with a better exponent.
- The one-line reason is folklore Dirichlet simultaneous approximation: some delta != 0 has ||j delta/p|| <= p^{-1/K} for all j in S.

(3) Two-sided epsilon-biased-set lower bounds, e.g. Alon, "Perturbed identity matrices have high rank", CPC 18 (2009). I only saw this in search results and did not fetch the paper. It is less relevant: two-sided and mainly Z_2^n.

What appears new:
- The weighted version under the concave l_{1/s} budget (sum y^{1/s} <= 1, support <= K), compared against Gamma_s ~ (ln p)^{1-s} and hence against gamma* over all networks, interference included.
- The naive Dirichlet bound gives only m <= 2 pi^2 e^{-2x} ||y||_1 <= 2 pi^2 e^{-2x}. That vanishes relative to (ln p)^{1-s} only for K = O(log p / log log p).
- The paper's positive-Fourier / Bessel-I_0 averaging (eq:posfourier, eq:psisum) extends this to all K = o(log p).
- I found no weighted or quasi-norm-budget analogue in the expander, Bohr-set or ML literature. Queries run: FMT title; "Cayley graphs of abelian groups not expanders need log n generators Klawe lower bound"; a weighted cosine-sum / simultaneous-Dirichlet query (no relevant hits); Alon epsilon-biased lower bound.
- The Bessel moment-generating trick is standard in flavour, but I found no exact source.

Verdict: the unweighted / equal-share specialisation is classical (Alon-Roichman Prop 3 qualitatively; Friedman-Murty-Tillich quantitatively). The weighted l_{1/s} result for every K = o(log p), and its application to network margins, are novel as far as found.

recommended_citations.why: Already in refs.bib. Cite also at cor:few: Prop 3 proves any Abelian Cayley graph that is a delta-expander needs |S| >= c(delta) log2 n generators, which is the qualitative equal-share form of 'o(log p) features cannot cover every offset'.

For cor:few. Proves lambda_2 >= d - O(d n^{-4/d}) for d-regular abelian Cayley graphs. With d=2K on Z_p this bounds the equal-share coverage by O(K p^{-2/K}), which is the quantitative equal-share special case of cor:few. Metadata confirmed via the DOI redirect to the pii and via Cioaba 2006's reference list; the article page itself returned 403, so it is marked unconfirmed.

chk.recommended_change: After Corollary cor:few (cyclic.tex l.130), or at the start of its proof in appendix.tex l.250, add: "For equal amplitudes this is classical: Cayley graphs of abelian groups need Omega(log n) generators to expand \citep[Prop.~3]{alon1994random}. Quantitatively, a 2K-regular Cayley graph on Z_p has second eigenvalue 2K - O(K p^{-2/K}) \citep{friedman2006spectral}, which gives the corollary for equal shares. Add the friedman2006spectral bib entry.

item.what_to_check: Internal numerics; relate to McCracken dense/sparse transition

chk.evidence:
NUMERICS REPRODUCED
I wrote an independent vertex-enumeration script: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r27-dense-window/dense_thresh.py.
- It enumerates every vertex of P_p = {v>=0 : sum_j v_j(1-cos(2 pi j delta/p)) >= 1}.
- It then bisects for the largest s at which a full-support vertex minimises sum v^{1/s}.
- Results: 1.5475, 1.3454, 1.2850, 1.2166, 1.1938, 1.1597 at p = 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. All six match the paper.
- The only full-support vertex is the uniform one, v = 2/p.
- The p=13 value matches the 6->4 switch at s=1.285 stated in the shapes paragraph.

ANALYTIC BOUND
The bound s-1 <= ln4/ln((p-1)/(2 ceil(8 ln p))) is correct, but it is vacuous for p <= 71.
- Its values: 49.2 at p=73, 3.58 at p=113, 0.63 at p=1009, 0.33 at p=10^4, 0.165 at p=10^6.
- It says nothing at any p where the exact values were computed.
- It forces sparsity at weight decay with nu=3 (s=3/2) only for p > ~2000.
- It uses the proof-internal share floor 4^{-1/(s-1)}/ceil(8 ln p). The theorem states 4^{-1/(s-1)}/(9 ln p), which gives 18 ln p in place of 2 ceil(8 ln p). This is a small mismatch.
- (s-1) ln p at the exact thresholds falls from 1.07 to 0.50. This is consistent with the O(1/log p) upper bound, but neither tightness nor monotonicity is proven.

LITERATURE
- McCracken et al., arXiv 2505.18266 (fetched https://arxiv.org/html/2505.18266). One-hot 1-layer MLPs learn floor(n/2) frequencies. "adding either depth, or a trainable embedding matrix ... causes the network to transition from learning floor(n/2) types of neurons to much fewer types". They also write "we don't know why it occurs". Cor 4.8 is sufficiency only: "Learning O(log n) distinct frequencies gives a logit margin Omega(log n)".
  - Their transition is along an architecture axis; ours is along the norm-exponent axis. So this is related context, not prior art for the window.
- Morwani Thm 7 and Li Thm 4.1 cover only the s=1 dense endpoint.
- Kam et al. 2609.17926 find a dense optimum under a convex l2 budget, with no threshold.
- Jacobs-Montufar 2605.19458 Thm 4.9 relates homogeneity to sparse vs dense in mirror flow. It has no p-dependent window.
- lp (q<1) minimisation theory (Ge-Jiang-Ye 2011) gives vertex optimality, but no full-support window.

SEARCHES
- "modular addition number of frequencies dense to sparse transition weight decay exponent log p max margin"
- "lp quasi-norm minimization q<1 nonnegative cosine coverage constraints sparse solution threshold q close to 1 dense"
- I also checked 2606.17399 and 2608.04451; neither is relevant.

chk.evidence:
No prior work computes the maximiser of the L_{1/s}-budget coverage max-min at specific p. None reports switch points in s either. Morwani ICLR24 Thm 7 and Li AISTATS25 Thm 4.1 give dense optima (b = nu). McCracken 2505.18266 Cor 4.8 is a sufficiency bound for random frequencies, with no optimum count.

Empirical counts, all verified from the PDFs:
- Nanda et al. (arXiv 2301.05217), Sec 4.1 / Fig 3. A 1-layer transformer at p=113 uses "five key frequencies ... k in {14,35,41,42,52}". W_E has 6 non-negligible frequencies.
- Chughtai et al. (ICML 2023, PMLR 202:6243-6267), App. Table 6. Transformers on C113 have 3, 4, 4, 3 key frequencies across seeds 1-4.
- Chughtai et al., App. Table 5. MLPs with embeddings on C113 have 13, 11, 15, 10. C118, D59 and D61 have about 9-15 reps.
- Zhong et al. (2306.17844), p=59. Model A's top 3 circles (k=17, 3, 44) give 91.4% accuracy. The full count is not tabulated.
- McCracken et al. 2505.18266, Sec 4.3. Nets with embeddings learn "handfuls of frequencies (3-7)". A log fit of count vs n appears in Fig 3, and Fig 4 covers moduli 59-66. One-hot 1-layer MLPs use floor(n/2).

Our p=113 values (7/4/4) sit inside the empirical 3-15 range. But those models are transformers or ReLU MLPs, not L_{2,b} product/power nets, so the numbers are context and not a validation. Chughtai's MLP counts of 10-15 exceed our nu=3 value of 7.

item.statement: Irrep analogue: ceiling priced by decomposition cost of the matrix-multiplication tensor (schoolbook at even degree, d^nu neurons); one irrep on S5, Galois pair on A5; structured interference beats ceiling on D3, S4, Z12
item.what_to_check: Compare Chughtai, Morwani group theorem, Stander et al. 2024; matrix multiplication tensor rank (Strassen, Blaser); no proofs in appendix yet

chk.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r31-groups/CHECK.md. The claim was checked against heracles/s5theory/S5_THEORY.md §4-5 and §9, because groups.tex is only a skeleton.

What is known (all fetched this session):

(1) Derksen, FoCM 16:779-811 (2016), arXiv 1308.3860.
- Thm 1.9: the schoolbook decomposition sum e_ij(x)e_jk(x)e_ki of M_{p,q,r} is a diagonal SVD, with all pqr singular values equal to 1.
- Cor 1.10: ||M_{p,q,r}||_* = pqr.
- He remarks that Strassen's decomposition has length 2sqrt2+12 > 8: "minimization of the rank, and minimization of the nuclear norm do not always coincide".
- Thm 1.11: the group-algebra tensor T_G has singular values sqrt(n/d_i), each with multiplicity d_i^3. So ||T_G||_* = sqrt|G| sum d_i^{2.5}, which is exactly the d^{2.5} in Morwani Thm 9.
- Consequences: our K1 at r=1 (kappa=1) is Derksen Cor 1.10, and our "Strassen costs 10 > schoolbook 8" is the quasi-norm analogue of his remark.

(2) Christandl & Zuiddam, Comput. Complexity 28:27-56 (2019), arXiv 1606.04085.
- Eqs. 7-8: the max-cut flattening gives n^{f(G)} <= R(T_n(G)). "For bipartite graphs, each inequality in (8) is an equality."
- Even cycles are bipartite, so the rank of tr(A1...Ak) is d^k for even k. Our rank corollary (tr(ABCD) has rank d^4) is known, and the proof of K2 uses the same cut argument.

(3) Fan, Ding, Yang, Zhang, Udell, TMLR 01/2023, arXiv 2012.03436.
- Def 3 defines the tensor Schatten-p quasi-norm.
- Thm 1: ||X||_{S_{q/d}}^{q/d} = inf (1/d) sum_i sum_j ||x_i^(j)||^q.
- Our price N_r(T) is exactly ||T||_{S_r}^r with r = q/nu.

(4) Cheng et al., arXiv 2506.22134, Thm 1: the variational S_p quasi-norm upper-bounds ||T_(D)||_{S_p}^p for every unfolding. This is our flattening bound, Lemma F applied to a flattening. Hu, LAA 478:188-199 (2015), proves the p=1 case; that entry was confirmed through the Crossref API only.

(5) Shutman-Louidor-Tessler, arXiv 2509.06931. Prop 5.2: the single-irrep projection has rank <= m_d, 3m_{d/2} or 8m_{d/2}, where m_d is the tensor rank of dxd matrix multiplication. The net "effectively implements efficient matrix multiplication in the sense of Strassen". Their setting is plain GD with no weight decay, and the price is width (rank), not a norm.

(6) Marchetti-Kunin-Myers-Acosta-Miolane, ICML 2026, arXiv 2602.03655. Lemma B.8: (k+1) n_rho^{k+1} sigma-pi-sigma (product) neurons suffice for one irrep. The construction is the schoolbook, with s_w = E_{a0a1} and S = E_{a_h a_{h+1}}, i.e. d^nu terms. It is an existence construction only.

(7) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024, Thm 9: at L_{2,3} with quadratic nets, gamma* = 2/(3sqrt(3|G|)) / sum d^{2.5}, and every non-trivial irrep is used (S_k, k<=5). This is our dense endpoint at b=nu.

(8) Chughtai-Chan-Nanda, ICML 2023. On S5 (50 seeds), "the 1d sign and 4d standard representations are most commonly learned... 6d is never learned", and the number of reps varies. They write: "standard sign offers better performance for fixed weight norm... models are trading off weight against performance... which is least complex, is unclear". This is the question our price answers. It is also a tension: they observed variable counts, not one irrep.

(9) Stander-Yu-Fan-Biderman, ICML 2024: S5/S6 nets use coset circuits. Our §9.3(a) coset-relaxation mechanism, by which interference beats the ceiling on D3/S4/Z12, is the margin-side counterpart. Wu-Jaburi-Drori-Gross (ICLR 2025) unify the irrep and coset accounts.

(10) Levine, arXiv 2609.15289, MAIS-O5 poses exactly "which irreps are learned ... as a function of width and decay strength".

What was not found:
- A computation of the Schatten-r (r<1) quasi-norm of <d,...,d> or of cycle tensors (our K2). It is, however, a short combination of (2) with (3)/(4) and McCarthy/Rotfel'd.
- The main claim: the L_{2,b}, b<nu, ceiling fixes the count at one faithful irrep (+ sign) on S5 and the Galois pair on A5, and structured interference exceeds the ceiling on D3/S4/Z12. This is novel as far as found.

Searches run: nuclear norm of matmul tensor Derksen; Morwani group d^{2.5}; Chughtai S5 sign/standard; tensor rank of iterated matmul/trace flattening; tensor Schatten-p quasi-norm matmul; Hu nuclear norm flattenings; Schatten-p flattening lower bound CP; weight decay group irrep cost schoolbook Strassen; nuclear norm of the cyclic trace tensor; max-margin group composition irreps weight decay 2025-2026. I also grepped full texts of Kam 2609.17926, He 2606.02993, Marchetti 2602.03655 and Levine 2609.15289; none prices irreps by a norm.

recommended_citations.why: Cor 1.10: ||<p,q,r>||_* = pqr, and the schoolbook is a diagonal SVD (Thm 1.9). This is our r=1 price (kappa=1, schoolbook optimal) and supports the remark that Strassen loses under the norm. Thm 1.11: ||T_G||_* = sqrt|G| sum d^{2.5}, which explains Morwani Thm 9's d^{2.5}. Cite at 'schoolbook algorithm'.
Eqs. (7)-(8): max-cut flattening, with equality for bipartite graphs. The even-cycle tensor tr(A1...Ak) has rank d^k. This is the cut argument behind our even-nu theorem (K2) and its rank corollary.
Thm 1: L_q penalties on CP factors equal the tensor Schatten-(q/d) quasi-norm. Our irrep price N_r = ||T_rho||_{S_r}^r with r = q/nu is this quantity. Cite where the price is defined.

Thm 1: the variational Schatten-p quasi-norm upper-bounds the Schatten-p quasi-norm of every unfolding. This is our flattening inequality N_r(T) >= sum sigma_k(flat T)^r. Optional; the journal venue is unconfirmed, so cite as arXiv.

Prop 5.2: the per-irrep rank is at most the tensor rank m_d of matrix multiplication (Strassen). This is the no-norm, width-priced version of our 'irrep price = cost of writing the matmul tensor as a sum of products'.

Lemma B.8: (k+1) n_rho^{k+1} product (sigma-pi-sigma) neurons implement one irrep via the schoolbook E_{a_h a_{h+1}} construction. This gives prior existence of our d^nu-neuron construction; our addition is its optimality under weight decay.
Thm 9: the L_{2,3} max margin for groups is 2/(3sqrt(3|G|))/sum d^{2.5}, and every non-trivial irrep is used. This is our dense b=nu endpoint, contrasted with one irrep at b<nu.

S5 nets mostly learn sign + 4d standard, and the count varies. The paper explicitly leaves open which rep is preferred under the weight-norm trade-off. This is the empirical data and the question our price answers.
S5/S6 nets use subgroup and coset circuits. This is the empirical counterpart of our coset-structured interference, which exceeds the symmetric ceiling on D3/S4/Z12.
Unifies the irrep (Chughtai) and coset (Stander) accounts. Cite alongside Stander at the interference sentence.

In groups.tex:

(a) After "written as a sum of products", add: "Without a norm, this is the tensor-rank bound of Shutman et al. (2025, Prop. 5.2). Under weight decay the relevant quantity is the tensor Schatten-(b/nu) quasi-norm (Fan et al., 2023, Thm 1)."

(b) After "the schoolbook algorithm", add: "At b = nu this is Derksen's (2016, Cor. 1.10) ||<d,d,d>||_* = d^3. The same computation for the group-algebra tensor (Thm 1.11) produces the sum d^{2.5} in Morwani et al. (Thm 9). At even nu, optimality follows from the bipartite-cut flattening (Christandl & Zuiddam, 2019) together with the Schatten flattening inequality. The d^nu-neuron construction itself appears in Marchetti et al. (2026, Lemma B.8). What we add is its optimality under the norm and the count that follows. Unlike rank, the norm prefers the schoolbook to Strassen (Derksen's remark; our numerics at nu = 3)."

(c) Change "one representation on S_5" to "one faithful representation (with a sign patch) on S_5". Add: "consistent with the sign+standard circuits of Chughtai et al. (2023), and answering their open question of which representation the weight-norm trade-off prefers". Also note the contrast with Morwani Thm 9, where every irrep is used at b = nu.

(d) After the D_3/S_4/Z_12 sentence, add: "the excess comes from coset-structured interference, the margin-side counterpart of the coset circuits of Stander et al. (2024); see also Wu et al. (2025)."

(e) Present the even-nu schoolbook theorem as a lemma assembled from known pieces, not as a headline. Do not claim the rank corollary (tr(ABCD) has rank d^4) as new.

item.statement: Weight decay on ReLU one-hidden-layer network (nu=2) is the b=nu endpoint; universal bound's maximizer is flat
item.what_to_check: Morwani ReLU treatment, Gromov, McCracken ReLU dense observations

chk.evidence:
Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r32-relu-endpoint/CHECK.md.

The empirical side is known. The formal ReLU budget bound (C_2 <= p^{-n}/2, from the 1-Lipschitz variance bound) was not found anywhere.

(1) Morwani et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv 2311.07568 (full PDF read):
- Sec 2 defines the homogeneity constant nu, and Thm 2's neuron-combining step needs b = nu. ReLU with plain L2 is therefore nu = b = 2 by their own definitions, a trivial specialisation.
- All their theory uses x^2 / x^k activations. Conclusion: "Our proof holds for the case of x2 activations ... and L2,nu norm ... Empirical findings suggest that the results may be transferable to other architectures and norms."
- ReLU appears only in experiments. App. C, Fig 7(a): "Final distribution of the neurons corresponding to a particular frequency in (a) ReLU network trained with L2 regularization ... the final distribution across frequencies is close to uniform."
- Fig 4(b): ReLU + L2 neurons are "nearly 1-sparse in frequency space but not quite."

(2) Gromov, arXiv 2301.02679 (full PDF read):
- The analytic solution uses the whole frequency set k = 0..(p-1)/2 with random phases, built for quadratic activation.
- "The weights (6)-(7) also work for other activation functions, including ReLU ... We do not have an analytic proof of this fact."
- There is no regularisation, norm or margin.

(3) McCracken et al., arXiv 2505.18266, Sec 4.4 (HTML): "Previous work shows floor(n/2) types of neurons are found, each specializing to a sinusoid with one frequency with 1 hidden layer" (citing Gromov and Morwani). Depth or trainable embeddings cut this to far fewer frequencies. Empirical only.

(4) He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849 (HTML):
- ReLU experiments, x^2 theory.
- Observation 3 (Sec 3.1): "every frequency k is represented among the neurons" (empirical). Def 4.1: full diversification.
- No ReLU margin theorem.

(5) Memana, arXiv 2608.04451: ReLU single-neuron dynamics counterexample. Not overlapping.

Searches run:
- "ReLU network modular addition max margin all frequencies weight decay theorem one hidden layer"
- "\"modular addition\" ReLU \"maximum margin\" ... dense uniform theory 2025 2026"
- "two-layer ReLU network modular addition weight decay provably Fourier features all frequencies theorem"

No paper bounds the per-neuron budget of a ReLU neuron, or connects L2 + ReLU to the flat maximiser of a frequency-budget programme. The paper's own caveat (the bound is not attained, and there is no theorem about the network) is appropriate. Var(sigma(X)) <= Var(X) is standard and needs no citation.

recommended_citations.why: App. C Fig. 7(a): ReLU+L2 networks spread neurons close to uniformly over all frequencies (empirical precedent for the flat b=nu endpoint); Fig. 4(b): ReLU neurons nearly but not exactly single-frequency (supports not claiming the sign lemma for ReLU). Already in refs.bib.
All-frequency analytic solution that also works with ReLU (App. B, 'We do not have an analytic proof'); no norm/margin. Dense precedent for the ReLU sentence. Already in refs.bib.

Observation 3 (Sec 3.1): trained ReLU two-layer nets represent every frequency; Def 4.1 full diversification. Empirical density for ReLU; no margin theorem. Add to refs.bib if not already present under another key.

chk.recommended_change: appendix.tex:283, ReLU paragraph. After "weight decay on this degree-2 network \emph{is} the $b=\nu$ endpoint.", insert: "This matches what is observed: ReLU networks trained with $L_2$ regularization spread their neurons nearly uniformly over all frequencies \citep[App.~C, Fig.~7a]{morwani2024feature}; see also \citet{gromov2023grokking} and \citet[Obs.~3]{he2026mechanism}. Their neurons are close to, but not exactly, single-frequency \citep[Fig.~4b]{morwani2024feature}." Keep the existing caveat sentence. Do not claim novelty for "ReLU+L2 is the b=nu case": it follows directly from Morwani's homogeneity setup. What is new is only the budget constant C_2 <= p^{-n}/2 and the fact that it feeds into Thm universal.

item.what_to_check: Internal; 'certified aiming depth' undefined and proofs absent; check nothing external settles it

chk.evidence:
Searches run on 2026-09-25:
(1) global maximum margin modular addition network sparse Fourier features conjecture interference proof;
(2) "modular addition" max-margin "local maximum" not global multilinear network Fourier sparse optimum 2026 arXiv;
(3) max-min trigonometric polynomial nonnegative coefficients l_q budget maximize minimum sum beta_k(1-cos k s) optimal support;
(4) MAIS open problem maximum margin modular addition global optimum weight decay Levine 2026.

No paper found proves or refutes the claim that the interference-free (sparse) value is the global max of the L_{2,b} margin for b < nu. None exhibits an interfering local max, and none gives a group counterexample.

The one partial overlap is the endpoint b = nu of the paper's "window". There the global optimum over all networks, interference included, is already known:
- Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568, fetched), Thm 7: the L_{2,3} maximum for the quadratic net, certified by a dual (Lemma 2/6), which uses all frequencies.
- Li et al., AISTATS 2025, PMLR 258:523-531 (fetched), Thm 4.1: the same for power neurons at L_{2,k+1}.
The paper's own appendix (l.279) already says the Morwani net attains the bound at n=2, b=3. The window result for product nets, nu-4/(3(p-1)) <= b <= nu, therefore reads as extending the Morwani/Li certificate method a distance O(1/p) below b = nu. The endpoint should be credited to them.

Other results checked:
- arXiv 2608.04451 (Memana, Aug 2026) is a counterexample to MAIS-O60 about single-neuron ReLU dynamics. It is irrelevant here.
- Harmonic-analysis hits are Littlewood/Fejer cosine-polynomial extremal results, and none settles the programme.

Internal problems (not literature):
- "certified aiming depth" is undefined. The source flags this itself with a TODO at sections/appendix.tex l.294.
- The "Known" claims (p=3, the window, b>=5/2 at p=5, the 0.3476 class result, the 0.837 local max, the group counterexamples) have no proofs or pointers in the appendix.

item.what_to_check: Mostly internal; check known remarks on L_{2,b} norms beyond homogeneity (Morwani, Savarese et al.)

chk.evidence:
Remarks checked one by one. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/r37-appendix-remarks/CHECK.md.

(1) The equal-share bound Gamma_s >= max_K K^{-s} M_K, and the averaging bound M_K <= pK/(p-1), follow directly from the programme. They are internal. M_K = K(1 - Fourier bias of S) links to small-bias sets, which Alon-Roichman already covers in app. B.

(2) Only interval patterns are needed in (JF). Internal.

(3) The factor counts operand factors, not degree. Internal.

(4) Power-net interference-free population facts (6 neurons, 0.408; none exists with tied embeddings). Internal computations. Li et al. AISTATS 2025 Thm 4.1 covers only b = nu.

(5) b > nu gives a margin unbounded in width. Split a neuron into H copies scaled by H^{-1/nu}: the output is unchanged and sum ||.||^b ~ H^{1-b/nu} -> 0. This is the classical width-splitting argument for group norms in Neyshabur, Tomioka, Srebro, COLT 2015 (PMLR 40:1376-1401; read in full from arXiv 1503.00036v2).
- Sec. 3.1, after Thm 1: "the dependence on the width H disappears ... as long as q <= p* (i.e. 1/p+1/q >= 1)".
- Sec. 3.2, Thm 3 proof: "replacing the top unit with H copies of it ... we have reduced the norm by factor H^{1/q-1/p*}".
- Sec. 3.2 also says: "we can shatter an arbitrarily large number of points with arbitrarily low gamma by using enough hidden units".
Their setting (ReLU, mu_{p,q}) differs from ours, but the mechanism is the same, so our remark is a trivial specialisation.

(6) b < 2: superadditivity fails by |F|^{1-b/2}. Elementary.

Morwani et al. (arxiv.org/html/2311.07568):
- Sec. 3.2: "we will primarily focus on maximum margin with respect to L_{2,nu} norm".
- App. E.1: "the analysis ... can be used to compute optimal norms for b != nu as well -- however, for any such b we would not get the same flexibility to build a theta*".
They make no remark about b > nu being unbounded or about b < 2.

Savarese-Evron-Soudry-Srebro COLT 2019 (PMLR 99:2667-2690) is about the representation cost of weight decay on infinite-width ReLU networks. It is relevant only to the ReLU paragraph, not to these remarks.

Sources read: the Morwani HTML, the Neyshabur PDF, and the PMLR pages for Neyshabur and Savarese.

recommended_citations.why: Supports 'For b>nu the normalized margin is unbounded as the width grows'. Sec. 3.2 / Thm 3: duplicating units H times reduces the mu_{p,q} group norm by H^{1/q-1/p*} with the output unchanged, so width-independence holds only when 1/p+1/q>=1. It is the same splitting mechanism.

Optional. It is the standard reference for the representation cost of weight decay (via rescaling balance) on 2-layer ReLU networks. Relevant to the ReLU-neuron paragraph (b=nu=2), not needed for the remarks themselves.

chk.recommended_change: In app:conjecture, paragraph "b outside [2,nu]", change the first sentence to: "For b>nu the normalized margin is unbounded as the width grows: replacing a neuron by H copies scaled by H^{-1/nu} leaves f unchanged and multiplies its contribution to ||theta||_{2,b}^b by H^{1-b/nu} (the width-splitting argument of \citet{neyshabur2015norm}, Sec. 3.2)." No other changes are needed. Optionally, in the Equal shares paragraph, note that M_K = K - max_{delta!=0} sum_{j in S} cos(2 pi j delta/p), i.e. K times one minus the Fourier bias of S.

item.statement: AM-GM over nu weight factors makes amplitude A cost A^{b/nu}: weight decay on degree-nu products acts as an l_{b/nu} quasi-norm on amplitudes
item.what_to_check: HIGH risk: well known in representation-cost / implicit-bias literature (Gunasekar 2018 linear convnets, Woodworth 2020 diagonal nets, Dai-Karzand-Srebro 2021, Tibshirani 2021, Jacobs-Montufar); must cite

chk.evidence:
The AM-GM step is standard, and the paper gives no citation for it at approach.tex:45 (the sentence ending "(AM--GM), so amplitude A costs a multiple of A^{b/nu}=A^{1/s}"). Sources, all fetched this session:

(1) Tibshirani 2021, "Equivalences Between Sparse Models and Neural Networks" (working notes, stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/papers/sparsitynn.pdf).
- Sec 2.1 states min_{ab=c}(a^2+b^2)=2|c| and adds that "this is just saying that the arithmetic mean-geometric mean (AM-GM) inequality ... is tight when a = b."
- The k-layer case states min_{prod a_l=c} sum a_l^2 = k|c|^{2/k}, so a k-layer diagonal network with weight decay equals an l_p penalty with p=2/k<1, which is "nonconvex" (eqs. 8-9).
- This is our step verbatim at b=2.

(2) Hoff 2017, CSDA 115:186-198 (arXiv 1611.00040; DOI 10.1016/j.csda.2017.06.007). Abstract: "a subclass of L_q penalties with q<=1 can be expressed as sums of L_2 penalties" via a Hadamard reparametrisation.

(3) Gunasekar, Lee, Soudry, Srebro, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv 1806.00468). Thm 2a: GD on depth-L linear convolutional networks converges in direction to a first-order stationary point of min ||beta_hat||_{2/L} s.t. y_n<beta,x_n> >= 1, where beta_hat is the Fourier transform. This is the closest analogue to our setting: max-margin, an l_{2/L} quasi-norm on Fourier coefficients, and sparsity in frequency. It is an implicit-bias result rather than explicit wd.

(4) Dai, Karzand, Srebro, NeurIPS 2021 (proceedings page fetched). Studies the representation cost that l2 on parameters induces, including l_p norms.

(5) Kolb, Weber, Bischl, Rugamer, ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2502.02496). Thm 1: L2 on D Hadamard factors has the same global and local minima as L_{2/D} on the collapsed weights. They credit Hoff 2017, Grandvalet 1998 and Tibshirani 2021.

Only related, not cited for this step:
- Woodworth et al. 2020 (arXiv 2002.09277): implicit bias from init scale.
- Grandvalet 1998 ICANN: found by search only, bib unconfirmed.

What is ours:
- The L_{2,b} generalisation (exponent b/nu). This is a trivial one-line extension of the same step.
- Pricing Fourier amplitudes of multilinear/power neurons through the single-neuron constant C_b, plus the subadditivity sum that makes it hold for all networks.
- Coupling the l_{1/s} budget to the worst-offset coverage programme. K* and the log p law come from this coupling, not from the quasi-norm.

Searches run: Tibshirani equivalences sparse models neural networks; Hoff Hadamard product parametrization CSDA; Grandvalet least absolute shrinkage quadratic penalization; plus direct arXiv/proceedings fetches for 1611.00040, 2502.02496, 1806.00468 (the PDF text was grepped for Thm 2a), 2002.09277, 1412.6614, and NeurIPS 2021/2018 pages.

item.statement: det(I+tH)=(1+t)^nu via triangularity, Sylvester/principal-minor expansion, Hadamard bound on Gram determinants, then Bernstein integral x^r = (r sin pi r/pi) int log(1+xt) t^{-1-r} dt to pass to power sums
item.what_to_check: Cite Horn-Johnson for Sylvester/Hadamard; check majorization literature (Bhatia; Marshall-Olkin) for the generating-function-to-power-sum transfer

chk.evidence:
Every step of the technique in app:cost is standard. The inequality it proves, sum_l|beta_l|^r >= nu^{1-r}|beta|^r for 0<r<=1, also has a two-line classical proof.

(a) Sylvester's determinant identity, the principal-minor expansion of det(I+tX), and Hadamard's inequality for Gram/PSD matrices are textbook results in Horn & Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed. I confirmed the book on cambridge.org. I did not verify section numbers.

(b) The integral x^r = (r sin(pi r)/pi) ∫ log(1+xt) t^{-1-r} dt is the Stieltjes/complete-Bernstein representation of x^r. The operator-monotone chapter of Bhatia gives x^r = (sin r pi/pi) ∫ x/(x+lambda) lambda^{r-1} dlambda, and integrating by parts gives the log form. I did not verify Bhatia's section or equation numbers. I could not fetch the de Gruyter page for the Schilling-Song-Vondracek monograph.

(c) The step from the generating function to power sums (prod(1+x_l t) >= (1+t)^nu for all t implies sum x^r >= nu) has no named majorization-literature precedent that I found. It is not ordinary weak majorization, but it is elementary.

(d) Main finding: the lemma follows from two classical theorems.
- Weyl's majorant theorem: Weyl, PNAS 35:408-411, 1949, fetched via PMC; also Bhatia Thm II.3.6 per secondary sources. It says sum phi(|lambda_i|) <= sum phi(sigma_i) when phi(e^s) is convex. H is upper triangular with unit diagonal, so all its eigenvalues are 1, and with phi = x^r this gives nu <= sum sigma_i(H)^r.
- The Rotfel'd/Thompson inequality: R.C. Thompson, Pacific J. Math 66(1):285-290, 1976. I fetched the PDF. Its eq. (1) reads: "f(γ1)+...+f(γn) <= f(α1)+...+f(αn)+f(β1)+...+f(βn) when f is an increasing concave function of a nonnegative real variable, with f(0)=0", where α, β, γ are the singular values of A, B, A+B. Apply it to the rank-one summands d_l u_l u_l^* with f = x^r. This gives sum sigma_i(H)^r <= sum_l |d_l|^r.
- Together these give sum|d_l|^r >= nu, which is the lemma.

The paper's own route is still valuable because it gives the equality case cleanly. Searches run: Thompson 1976 title; Rotfel'd concave singular values; Weyl majorant Bhatia II.3.6; Weyl 1949 PNAS; Bernstein integral representation of x^r; Schilling-Song-Vondracek. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t3-determinant-gram/CHECK.md.

item.statement: Phases forming a rotated copy of nu-th roots of unity cancel every sign-flipped product-to-sum copy
item.what_to_check: Gromov 2023 analytic solution, Li et al. 2025 constructions, polyphase codes / DFT cancellation

chk.evidence:
Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t4-roots-of-unity-phases/CHECK.md.

(1) Mohlenkamp & Monzon, "Trigonometric identities and sums of separable functions", Math. Intelligencer 27(2):65-69, 2005.
- Metadata confirmed via Crossref. Full text read from the Ohio University preprint.
- Theorem 2: sin(sum_{j=1}^n x_j) = sum_j sin(x_j) prod_{k!=j} sin(x_k+alpha_k-alpha_j)/sin(alpha_k-alpha_j), for any distinct alpha. So the sine of a sum of n variables has separation rank (tensor rank) n instead of 2^{n-1}.
- Fig. 1 (right) uses alpha=0, pi/3, 2pi/3 "The amplitude has been equidistributed". These are exactly our nu=3 phases.
- Their Remarks say the result extends to cos.
- I checked numerically that their identity with equally spaced alpha_j=pi j/nu holds, and that our nu-block identity sum_l prod_t cos(theta_t+alpha_l) cos(theta_c+n alpha_l) = nu 2^{-n} cos(sum theta - theta_c) holds, for nu=2..5.
- Our block is the equally spaced cosine case of this rank-nu decomposition.

(2) Gromov 2023 (arXiv 2301.02679), Eqs. (6)-(16).
- Phase constraint (12) is phi1+phi2=phi3.
- The unwanted product-to-sum terms are suppressed only approximately, using i.i.d. uniform random phases (Eq. 15: sum_k cos(2pi k s/p+phi_k) << N): "each frequency appears several times with different random phases ultimately leading to a better wave interference."

(3) Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, App. F.2.
- Uses 8 neurons per frequency with phase triples (0,0,0), (0,pi,pi), (pi/2,-pi/2,0), (pi/2,pi/2,pi), (-pi/2,0,-pi/2), (-pi/2,pi,pi/2), (0,-pi/2,-pi/2), (0,pi/2,pi/2).
- Each of the 4 cos/sin terms of cos(a+b-c) comes from a sign pair. Cancellation is exact, but it relies on sign and quarter-turn phases.
- App. C (parity) has the sign-vector version: "every term other than Pi x_{S_i} cancels out in the sum".

(4) Li, Liang, Shi, Song, Zhou, AISTATS 2025, App. E.3 (Lemma E.3).
- Uses 2^{2k-1} neurons per frequency: the 2^k cos/sin terms of Eq. 25, each built by 2^{k-1} neurons.
- This is the +-1 polarization identity 2^k k! prod d_i = sum_{c in {+-1}^k} (-1)^{(k-sum c)/2}(sum c_j d_j)^k, i.e. the Z_2 version of the roots-of-unity idea.

(5) He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849, Def. 4.1(iii).
- Requires sum_{m in N_k} exp(i iota phi_m)=0 for iota in {2,4}. Equally spaced phases satisfy this phase-moment cancellation.
- The setting is quadratic nets, and the 2x and 2y noise peaks are left uncancelled (Prop 4.2).

- I found no ML paper that uses the rank-nu separated form.

item.statement: Concave nondecreasing function over a line-free polyhedron is minimized at a vertex; strict concavity forces all minimizers to be vertices
item.what_to_check: Classical (Rockafellar Convex Analysis Sec 32; Horst-Tuy); cite

chk.evidence:
This is a classical textbook fact. The proof in appendix.tex:151 is correct and self-contained.

What I could confirm:
- **Rockafellar, Convex Analysis (Princeton UP 1970).** Metadata confirmed from the Princeton UP page and Crossref (DOI 10.1515/9781400873173). A search snippet names Sec. 32 "The Maximum of a Convex Function", pp. 342-346. I could not fetch the theorem text: JSTOR, Google Books and De Gruyter were all blocked. From memory, Thm 32.3 is the version for closed convex sets containing no lines and Cor. 32.3.x the polyhedral case, but the number is unverified. Cite the section, not a theorem number.
- **Horst & Tuy, Global Optimization: Deterministic Approaches (Springer 1996).** Crossref-confirmed, DOI 10.1007/978-3-662-03199-5. It is the standard concave-minimization reference. Theorem number not confirmed.
- **Benson, "Concave Minimization: Theory, Applications and Algorithms".** Handbook of Global Optimization, 1995, pp. 43-148. Crossref-confirmed, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4615-2025-2_3. It is a survey of this property.
- **vom Dahl & Loehne, arXiv 1905.11228.** I fetched the full text. The proof of their Thm 1 uses exactly our argument. They write the polyhedron as Q + 0^+ (polytope plus recession cone) and state "Concavity of f implies that f attains its minimum at a vertex (x0,r0) of Q". Monotonicity along recession directions (their eq. 5) then finishes it. So the technique is standard.

Proof check:
- Every recession direction of P, which lies in R_{>=0}^F, is nonnegative, so the nondecreasing phi handles that part.
- The strictness step is valid: t^r with 0<r<1 is strictly concave, and at least one coordinate varies along any nondegenerate segment.
- The strictness half is folklore and needs no citation.

Searches run: Rockafellar Thm 32.3 contains-no-lines (several variants), Horst-Tuy concave minimization vertex, Bauer maximum principle (Wikipedia; compact case only), Benson Handbook chapter, Crossref lookups.

item.statement: A real exponential sum with N distinct exponents has at most N-1 real zeros (Rolle induction)
item.what_to_check: Classical (Polya-Szego Part V; generalized Descartes rule of signs); cite

chk.evidence:
The claim, in the appendix (app:shape (ii), sections/appendix.tex around line 156): a real exponential sum sum_k c_k e^{lambda_k u} with N distinct exponents, not all c_k zero, has at most N-1 real zeros. The paper proves it by Rolle induction.

This is classical. It is the generalized Descartes rule of signs (Laguerre): substitute t = e^u, and the number of zeros is at most the number of sign changes in (c_k), which is at most N-1. Equivalently, the functions e^{lambda_k u} form a Chebyshev (Descartes) system.

Sources I checked:
- arXiv 1709.06891, App. 3.1 (fetched). It titles the result "Elementary proof of the Pólya-Szegő estimate" and gives the same Rolle induction "following [37, page 10]", where [37] is Karlin-Studden, Tchebycheff Systems (1966). Its general form: sum_i P_i(x) exp(mu_i x) has at most sum_i (1+deg P_i) - 1 real roots.
- Erdélyi, arXiv 1602.02315 (fetched). It says "Descartes' Rule of Signs is stated and proved on page 102 of [3]", where [3] = Borwein-Erdélyi, Polynomials and Polynomial Inequalities (1995). It also points to Section 3.2 of [1] for Descartes systems.
- Crossref confirmed the metadata for:
  - Pólya-Szegő, Problems and Theorems in Analysis II (DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-61905-2)
  - Borwein-Erdélyi, GTM 1995 (DOI 10.1007/978-1-4612-0793-1)
  - Jameson, Math. Gazette 90(518):223-234 (2006), "Counting zeros of generalised polynomials: Descartes' rule of signs and Laguerre's extensions" (DOI 10.1017/S0025557200179628)
- The Part Five title "The Location of Zeros" and its Ch. 1 "Rolle's Theorem and Descartes' Rule of Signs" come from a search-result summary. I could not open the book, so the problem number that is commonly quoted (V.75) is not verified.

Searches run:
- "exponential sum at most n-1 real zeros Polya Szego Part V ... generalized Descartes rule of signs Laguerre"
- "Pólya Szegő Problems and Theorems in Analysis II Springer 1976 Part Five"
- "Problem 75 Pólya Szegő exponential polynomial real zeros Part V"

Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t6-exp-sum-zeros/CHECK.md

The exact problem number (often quoted as V.75) was not verified, so cite by Part/Chapter.

A point of a polyhedron in R^n is a vertex (extreme point) exactly when it is a basic feasible solution, meaning n of its active constraints are linearly independent. Source: Bertsimas & Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Linear Optimization (1997), Def. 2.9 (p. 50) and Theorem 2.3 (vertex = extreme point = BFS).

How this was confirmed:
- Wikipedia "Basic solution (linear programming)" was fetched. It gives the definition ("of all the constraints that are active at that vector, at least n of them must be linearly independent") and cites B&T 1997, Athena Scientific, p. 50, ISBN 978-1-886529-19-9.
- arXiv 2302.12364 was fetched and its text extracted. It states "basic feasible solutions are precisely extreme points (vertices) of the feasible set (Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, 1997, Theorem 2.3)". Its bib entry is "Athena Scientific, 1st edition, 1997. ISBN 1886529191".

Our argument is the standard basis-matrix argument (B&T Sec 2.3):
- The active bounds v_j=0 for j outside S are unit vectors supported outside S.
- So the active coverage rows, restricted to S, must have rank K, and the resulting K×K system is invertible.
The step is correct and nothing in the technique is new.

Chebyshev alternation analogue: the programme is a discrete max-min problem. A basic optimal solution of the LP form of discrete Chebyshev approximation is pinned by a reference set of n+1 active points, which becomes alternation under the Haar condition. We get K tight offsets rather than K+1 because the normalisation constraint is absorbed into the scaling. I did not fetch a canonical approximation-theory source (e.g. Cheney 1966), so it is unconfirmed and has no bib entry.

What is ours is the interpretation of the tight offsets as simultaneous hardest wrong answers in the constructed network.

- "Bertsimas Tsitsiklis Theorem 2.3 vertex extreme point basic feasible solution"
- "basic feasible solution linearly independent active constraints Theorem 2.3"
- "discrete Chebyshev minimax LP n+1 extremal points Haar"

item.statement: Random multiset of ceil(8 ln p) frequencies plus Hoeffding and a union bound gives every offset coverage >= L/2
item.what_to_check: Cited to Alon-Roichman and Hoeffding; also small-bias sets (Naor-Naor 1993; Alon-Goldreich-Hastad-Peralta 1992)

chk.evidence:
The technique is standard. The paper already attributes it correctly ("cyclic case of the random Cayley graph argument of Alon-Roichman", appendix.tex l.196). The arithmetic is correct. Hoeffding with range 2 gives exp(-L t^2/2), and the needed deviation is t = 1/2 + 1/(p-1) >= 1/2, so the bound is <= e^{-L/8} <= 1/p. The union bound over p-1 offsets gives (p-1)/p < 1.

(1) Alon & Roichman, RSA 5(2):271-284, 1994. Metadata confirmed via Crossref 10.1002/rsa.3240050203; I read the PDF at https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf.
- Thm 1: "For every 1>delta>0 there is a c(delta)>0 such that ... Let G be a group of order n and let S be a set of c(delta) log2 n random elements of G. Then E(|mu1*[X(G,S)]|) < 1-delta."
- Sec 3.1, Thm 2 (Abelian groups): a multiset S of (1+eps) log2 n random elements, chosen with repetitions, gives |mu1*| <= 1-delta almost surely.
- The proof bounds each nontrivial character separately (Pr(chi(sigma+sigma^-1) >= 1.8) <= 1/2) and then takes a union bound over characters.
- The eigenvalues of X(Z_p, ±J) are 2 sum_l cos(2 pi J_l delta/p). Our lemma is exactly this for Z_p, with a one-sided threshold of 1/2, explicit constant 8, and a Hoeffding step. The random-multiset model is also the same.

(2) Small-bias sets (explicit constructions over Z_2^n; they supply the eps-biased-set vocabulary):
- Naor & Naor, SICOMP 22(4):838-856, 1993 (Crossref 10.1137/0222053).
- Alon, Goldreich, Hastad, Peralta, RSA 3(3):289-304, 1992 (Crossref 10.1002/rsa.3240030308).
- Azar, Motwani & Naor, Combinatorica 18(2):151-171, 1998 (10.1007/pl00009813), covers small-bias spaces over Z_d. I confirmed its metadata only, not the statement.

(3) Direct ML precedent: McCracken et al., arXiv 2505.18266 (fetched abs and HTML).
- Thm 4.7 (verbatim as rendered): "Suppose that an integer m and reals 0<rho,delta<1 satisfy the inequality m>2 log_e n - 2 log_e(2-2rho) log_e(pi/delta) - 1. Then, with probability at least rho, for all k != i+j mod n, we have h(i+j)-h(k) > delta m." Here h is a sum of cosines at uniformly random frequencies.
- Cor 4.8: "Learning O(log n) distinct frequencies gives a logit margin Omega(log n)".
- This is the same random-cosine argument in the modular-addition setting, with an unnormalised margin and no optimality claim.

Searches run:
- WebSearch for the Alon-Roichman random Cayley graphs PDF.
- Crossref lookups of the Alon-Roichman, Naor-Naor, AGHP and Azar-Motwani-Naor DOIs.
- arXiv abs and HTML pages for 2505.18266.

item.statement: (1/p) sum_delta exp(-t F_y(delta)) >= prod_j e^{-t y_j} I_0(t y_j) because e^{z cos} has nonnegative Bessel Fourier coefficients; resonances only add nonnegative terms
item.what_to_check: HIGH risk: Chowla cosine problem and minimum-of-cosine-sum lower bounds (Bourgain 1986, Ruzsa 2004, Sanders), Uchiyama; exponential-moment tricks in additive combinatorics

chk.evidence:
Main finding: the mechanism behind eq:posfourier is a known closed-walk (trace) comparison for abelian Cayley graphs; what is new here is the weighted, budget-normalised version and its log p consequence. Full notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t9-positive-fourier/CHECK.md.

How to read the inequality: take unit weights on K frequencies. Then F_y(delta) = K - lambda_chi/2, where lambda_chi is the eigenvalue of Cay(Z_p, {+-j}) at character delta.
- The left side is e^{-tK} times the exponential generating function of closed walks, i.e. the continuous-time return probability on that Cayley graph.
- The right side, prod e^{-t} I_0(t), is the same return probability on the free cover Z^K.
- "Resonances only add non-negative terms" means that extra relations mod p only add closed walks.

(1) Cioaba, "Closed walks and eigenvalues of Abelian Cayley graphs", C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Ser. I 342 (2006) 635-638 (PDF fetched from numdam).
- Sec. 2 puts closed r-walks in bijection with r-tuples whose product is 1.
- It counts only the "trivial" 2r-tuples, where each x_i is paired with x_i^{-1} and each involution appears an even number of times. This gives Phi_{2r}(X) >= n W_{2r}(X) (eq. 2, Lemma 2.1).
- This is the moment/combinatorial form of our inequality: the trivial pairings are our constant-term product, and summing over r with t^{2r}/(2r)! gives prod I_0.
- Cioaba uses it to prove Thm 1.2, a Serre-type result: C|G| eigenvalues are >= k - eps.

(2) Friedman, Murty, Tillich, "Spectral estimates for Abelian Cayley graphs", JCTB 96 (2006) 111-121 (author PDF fetched from Tillich's page).
- Abstract: a d-regular Abelian Cayley graph on n vertices has lambda_2 >= d - O(d n^{-4/d}), and this is tight for prime n.
- Sec. 2 proves it by sphere packing/pigeonhole (Thm 2, Cor 3).
- Sec. 3 uses a covering argument: a Dirichlet eigenfunction on the universal cover Z^r is pushed forward to G.
- Sec. 1 names the "large trace" approach [Ci05] as another route.
- They call "Abelian Cayley graphs cannot be good expanders" a folklore result, credited to Alon-Roichman [AR94, Sec. 3].
- Our upper bound on m(y) is the weighted, l_{1/s}-budget analogue of this spectral-gap bound: m(y) is the normalised weighted gap.

(3) Alon-Roichman, "Random Cayley graphs and expanders" (author PDF fetched). Sec. 3 says the log n generator count is "essentially tight" for abelian groups (Prop. 2, stated for Z_2^m only). The paper already cites this for its lower-bound half.

What we have not found anywhere:
- the weighted version with a concave l_{1/s} budget;
- the scalar bound psi(z) <= a_s ln(1+z^r);
- the conclusions m(y) <= C (ln p)^{1-s} and eq:Kbound, and K* = Theta(log p).
The published results are for fixed degree with unit weights.

Checked and not overlapping:
- The Chowla cosine problem (Bourgain 1986, Ruzsa 2004, Sanders, Bedert arXiv 2509.05260) is about how negative min_x sum cos(a x) must be. Our bound controls the other side: some delta != 0 makes sum y_j cos close to sum y_j, i.e. simultaneous approximation / Bohr-set non-emptiness. The direction and method differ.
- Wang-Ye, arXiv 2503.06908 (positive definite functions on finite abelian groups; I read only the abstract) is adjacent, not overlapping.
- The Bessel generating function e^{z cos theta} = sum I_n(z) e^{in theta} is textbook; I did not fetch a source for it.

Searches run:
- abelian Cayley spectral gap, log n generators
- Bessel nonnegative Fourier coefficients and cosine-sum minimum
- Alon-Roichman abelian tightness, Klawe
- Friedman-Murty-Tillich
- heat-kernel return probability with I_0 on the covering Z^k
- Chowla / Bourgain / Ruzsa / Sanders

item.statement: psi(z)=z-ln I_0(z) <= a_s ln(1+z^r), using a Laplace-type lower bound I_0(z) >= e^{z-1/2}/(pi sqrt z)
item.what_to_check: Standard Bessel asymptotics (DLMF 10.30/10.40); cite

chk.evidence: Paper (appendix.tex lines 198-214) uses three things. (1) The integral representation I_0(z) = (1/pi) int_0^pi e^{z cos th} dth, which is DLMF 10.32.1 (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.32, section 10.32(i)). (2) The Fourier coefficients of e^{z cos th} are I_k(z) >= 0. This is the Jacobi-Anger expansion DLMF 10.35.2, "e^{z cos th} = I_0(z) + 2 sum_{k>=1} I_k(z) cos(k th)" (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.35), and non-negativity follows from the power series in 10.25.2. (3) An elementary Laplace-type lower bound, I_0(z) >= e^{z-1/2}/(pi sqrt z) for z >= 1. You get it by cutting the integral off at th <= z^{-1/2} and using cos th >= 1 - th^2/2. I checked the derivation and it is correct. Numerically, I_0/bound = 2.41 at z=1 and tends to about 2.07 as z grows, so the constant is weaker than the leading asymptotic e^z/sqrt(2 pi z) from DLMF 10.40.1 (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.40). That does not matter here, because only psi(z) <= (1/2) ln z + O(1) is needed. The bound would fail for small z (e.g. z=0.01), but the paper applies it only for z >= 1 and handles z <= 1 through I_0 >= 1, so the argument is valid for all z >= 0. Sharper inequalities (Baricz; Soni-type monotonicity) exist in the literature and turned up in a WebSearch, but I did not fetch them in full, so I do not cite them. This is a standard textbook fact. Nothing novel is claimed, and none is needed. Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t10-bessel-bound/CHECK.md. Searches: DLMF 10.32/10.35/10.40 pages; "inequality modified Bessel I_0(x) > e^x/sqrt(2 pi x) lower bound Baricz".

recommended_citations.why: Supports line 198. Eq. 10.32.1 gives I_0(z) = (1/pi) int_0^pi e^{z cos th} dth, and Eq. 10.35.2 (Jacobi-Anger) gives e^{z cos th} = I_0 + 2 sum I_k cos k th, so the Fourier coefficients are I_k(z) >= 0. Eq. 10.40.1 gives the sharp large-z constant 1/sqrt(2 pi z) for an optional remark at line 214. I confirmed the equation contents on the fetched pages. The editor list and release version are the standard DLMF citation; I did not re-verify them on the fetched pages.

chk.recommended_change: Line 198: change to "... $I_0(z)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi e^{z\cos\vartheta}d\vartheta$ \citep[Eq.~10.32.1]{dlmf} ... the Fourier coefficients of $\vartheta\mapsto e^{z\cos\vartheta}$ are the modified Bessel values $I_k(z)\ge0$ (Jacobi--Anger expansion, \citealp[Eq.~10.35.2]{dlmf})." Line 214 (optional): after the lower bound, add "(the sharp constant is $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, \citealp[Eq.~10.40.1]{dlmf}; only the order $\frac12\ln z$ matters here)." No correctness fix is needed.
