item.statement: Flat maximizer unique via Fourier inversion of constant coverage
item.what_to_check: Compare Morwani's dense proof

chk.evidence:
Source read: Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao, Kakade, "Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks", arXiv 2311.07568v2. The arXiv abs page says "Accepted as Spotlight at ICLR 2024". I fetched the full HTML and extracted the math from its alttext.

(1) Our averaging step (average the coverage over delta != 0 to get Gamma_1 <= p/(p-1)) is their uniform class-weighting certificate. Sec 4 proof outline: "We will use the uniform class weighting: tau(x,y)[y'] = 1/(p-1) for all c' != a+b". This is combined with Lemma 5 (class-weighted margin) and Lemma 6 (the max-min certificate). The second part of Lemma 6 says: "all points in the support of q* are on the margin for any maximum margin solution."

(2) Our equality/uniqueness step is App. F.3, "Proof that all frequencies are used". Lemma 6 makes the margin equal across classes, so they write f(a,b,c) = F(a,b) + lambda * 1_{a+b=c}. The 3-D DFT of the indicator term is "lambda p^2 if j=k=-l". They conclude: "Hence, when j=k=-l != 0, we must have f^(j,k,l) > 0 ... there is at least one neuron for each frequency."

Our proof uses the same argument: constant margin/coverage, Fourier inversion of an indicator, every frequency nonzero. Their Theorem 7 claims only (1) single-frequency neurons and (2) every frequency used by at least one neuron. It does not state equal amplitudes, although their decomposition already gives the same value lambda p^2 at every diagonal frequency.

What is new in ours:
- uniqueness of the whole flat amplitude vector y_j = 2/(p-1) in the reduced programme Gamma_1;
- this holds for any network at b = nu, via Thm universal;
- a one-variable inversion in place of a 3-D DFT.

The averaging-then-constant-correlation pattern also resembles Welch/simplex bounds (folklore). I found no citation that fits better than Morwani. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t12-dense-uniqueness/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.why: Supports the averaging and uniqueness steps in app:dense. Lemmas 5-6 with uniform class weighting tau=1/(p-1) are the averaging bound. App. F.3 proves every frequency is present, using the constant margin and a Fourier transform of lambda*1_{a+b=c}. That is the same inversion argument; ours sharpens 'present' to 'equal amplitude'. The entry already exists in refs.bib; it only needs citing at the proof.

chk.recommended_change: Add this sentence to the proof in the appendix subsection app:dense: "The averaging step is the uniform class-weighting certificate of \citet{morwani2024feature} (Lemmas 5--6), and the Fourier-inversion step parallels their App. F.3, which shows every frequency is present in any max-margin network; in the reduced programme the same inversion gives the stronger conclusion that the amplitudes are equal and the maximizer is unique." Do not describe the uniqueness technique as new. The new parts are equal amplitudes and the fact that the result holds for all networks at b = nu.

item.statement: Cauchy-Schwarz + Parseval + 1-Lipschitz variance bound give the ReLU single-neuron budget
item.what_to_check: Compare Morwani/Gromov ReLU arguments

chk.evidence:
The Fourier + Cauchy-Schwarz single-neuron template comes from Morwani et al. ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568v2; I read the full PDF).
- App. F.1, "Proofs for cyclic groups (Theorem 7)", bounds a quadratic neuron in three steps: "By Plancherel's theorem, the norm constraint is equivalent to ...", then Cauchy-Schwarz (and AM-GM), giving sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)).
- The same section says "E_c[w(c)] = 0, because shifting the mean of w does not affect the margin".
- Morwani treats ReLU only empirically (Fig 1a, Fig 4, the L2-regularised ReLU runs). There is no ReLU bound.

Gromov 2023 (arXiv 2301.02679; I grepped the full PDF) analyses quadratic activation. It says only "The weights (6)-(7) also work for other activation functions, including ReLU", which is an empirical claim with no bound.

Other papers checked:
- Li et al. AISTATS 2025 (2402.09469): power activations only.
- Memana 2026 (arXiv 2608.04451, single ReLU neuron): a dynamics counterexample to MAIS-O60, with no margin or budget bound.
- McCracken et al. 2505.18266: random-frequency constructions, with no single-neuron norm budget.

The step Var(f(X)) <= L^2 Var(X) for L-Lipschitz f is a textbook fact, proved in one line with an independent copy of X. It needs no citation.

I found no paper that bounds the ReLU single-neuron Fourier budget for modular-addition margins. So the ReLU extension (the 1-Lipschitz variance step on top of diagonal Parseval) is new as far as I found, but the template is Morwani's.

A possible technical issue: the text sums over j in F_p, but Var(h) does not control the j = 0 term h^(0) ~ E[h]. This should be justified, either by w^(0) = 0 (the mean of w is margin-irrelevant, as in Morwani F.1) or by summing over j != 0.

Searches run:
- "ReLU network modular addition maximum margin upper bound Fourier single neuron proof"
- "1-Lipschitz function variance contraction Var(f(X)) <= Var(X) lemma"

Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/t13-relu-budget/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.bibtex: (already in refs.bib as morwani2024feature)
recommended_citations.why: App. F.1 (proof of Thm 7) is where the Plancherel + Cauchy-Schwarz single-neuron Fourier budget originates, for quadratic neurons. It also shows that the mean of w does not affect the margin, which justifies dropping the j=0 term. Cite it in the ReLU paragraph as the template being extended.

recommended_citations.bibtex: (already in refs.bib as gromov2023grokking)
recommended_citations.why: Optional. Its quadratic analytic solution reportedly also works for ReLU, but only empirically, with no bound. It supports the statement that no prior ReLU margin bound exists.

chk.recommended_change:
In appendix.tex, ReLU paragraph (l.283):
1. Change "Cauchy--Schwarz over j, Parseval for the diagonal coefficients, and Var(h)<=Var(sum_t u_t)" to "The Plancherel/Cauchy--Schwarz single-neuron argument of \citet[App.~F.1]{morwani2024feature}, extended to ReLU by the 1-Lipschitz variance bound Var(sigma(X))<=Var(X) (take an independent copy X': Var f(X)=\tfrac12\E(f(X)-f(X'))^2)".
2. Justify the j=0 term. Either sum over j in F_p\{0}, or add "w.l.o.g. \hat w(0)=0, since shifting the mean of w does not change the margin". The reason is that Var(h) does not bound \hat h(0,...,0).

item.statement: Explaining the number of features in a network has been a long-desired result in mechanistic interpretability
item.what_to_check: Needs citation (Olah 2020, Elhage 2022 superposition, Sharkey et al. open problems) or softening

chk.evidence:
refs.bib currently has no Olah, Elhage or Sharkey entry, so the sentence has no citation. I checked it with grep.

(1) Elhage et al. 2022, Toy Models of Superposition (Transformer Circuits Thread, page fetched):
- The Open Questions section asks: "How many features should we expect to be stored in superposition? ... results from compressed sensing should be able to give us useful upper-bounds, but it would be nice to have a clearer understanding – and perhaps tighter bounds!"
- The main text says: "one question is just how many features the model learns to represent" (measured by ||W||_F^2).
- The SAE replication section says: "we ultimately want to count the features used by real neural networks, where the number of features is unknown."

(2) Sharkey et al. 2025, Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability (arXiv 2501.16496, fetched HTML), Sec. 2.1 on reverse-engineering/decomposition. It says conceptual work "may ... provide bounds on the number of features we should expect models to be capable of learning (Hänni et al., 2024; Adler & Shavit, 2024; Bushnaq & Mendel, 2024)".

(3) Olah et al. 2020, Zoom In (Distill, doi 10.23915/distill.00024.001), Claim 1: "Features are the fundamental unit of neural networks." This supports only that features are central.

Assessment: the question is explicitly posed as open, so the sentence is supported in substance. "Long-desired result" overstates things, though. The question has been posed since about 2022, and in mech interp "number of features" means superposition capacity or SAE feature counts, not Fourier frequencies or irreps. Search method: fetched the arXiv/Distill/transformer-circuits pages and grepped the full texts for "how many features" and "number of features". Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/f1-long-desired/CHECK.md

recommended_citations.why: Supports abstract sentence 1. Its Open Questions section asks 'How many features should we expect to be stored in superposition?' and calls for tighter bounds. It also states 'we ultimately want to count the features used by real neural networks'.

Sec. 2.1 lists as an open problem the need to 'provide bounds on the number of features we should expect models to be capable of learning'. This directly supports calling the question open in the field.
Optional. Claim 1, 'Features are the fundamental unit of neural networks', supports the idea that features are central. It does not ask about how many there are.

(Olah et al. 2020 is optional and supports only the notion of a feature.) Drop "long-desired result". In the intro, add one clause linking superposition-style feature counts to this paper's features (Fourier frequencies/irreps), so the framing does not suggest mech interp asked for exactly this.

item.location: abstract 'networks trained with ordinary weight decay consistently show a sparse selection'; intro 'Trained networks do not look like this'
item.statement: Networks trained with ordinary weight decay consistently use a sparse set of features
item.what_to_check: 'consistently' may overclaim; McCracken reports dense circuits in some settings; cite Nanda, Chughtai, Zhong et al. Clock and Pizza, Stander et al.

chk.evidence:
Supporting evidence, all fetched this session:
- Nanda et al., ICLR 2023 (arXiv 2301.05217). Sec 3 uses AdamW with weight decay lambda=1. Sec 4.1: "only 5 appear to be used significantly (k in {14,35,41,42,52})", and W_E "only has significant nonnegligible norm at 6 frequencies". Sec 4.4: ablating everything except the key frequencies improves performance.
- Chughtai, Chan, Nanda, ICML 2023, PMLR 202:6243-6267. App C uses AdamW with weight decay lambda=1. Sec 5.1: the logits are explained by "a very sparse set of directions ... 'standard' and 'sign' representations". Sec 6: "different numbers of representations are learned" across seeds.
- Zhong et al., Clock and Pizza, NeurIPS 2023. App F.1 uses AdamW with weight decay 2. Sec 3.3: "first six principal components (three circles)" give 91.4% accuracy. Models use a few circles, but the paper gives no count law.
- Stander et al., ICML 2024, PMLR 235:46441-46467. S5/S6 MLPs decompose the task through subgroups and cosets.

Contradicting evidence:
- McCracken et al., arXiv 2505.18266. Sec 4.4 / Fig 4: "Previous work shows floor(n/2) types of neurons are found, each specializing to a sinusoid with one frequency with 1 hidden layer ... adding either depth, or a trainable embedding matrix ... causes the network to transition from learning floor(n/2) types of neurons to much fewer types". Also: "The presence of the trainable embeddings is why the models trained in [prior work] ... learn handfuls of frequencies (3-7) instead of floor(n/2)". App E.4 Table 5: the one-hot 1-hidden-layer MLP (1024 neurons) was trained with L2 regularization 1e-5. That is a weight-decayed network that is dense.
- Gromov (arXiv 2301.02679): the quadratic 2-layer MLP uses the full set of frequencies. Its main setup has no explicit regularisation.
- The paper's own theory and experiments (nu=2 dense window, dense ReLU 2-operand MLP) also contradict "consistently".

So "consistently sparse" is false as stated. Sparsity holds for transformers, embedding or deeper MLPs, and group MLPs, but not for one-hot one-hidden-layer MLPs.

Secondary issue: the intro says the dense-to-sparse move happens "as the degree of the network changes" and cites McCracken. McCracken attributes it to depth or a trainable embedding. Both raise the homogeneity degree, so the reading can be defended, but the text must say so explicitly.

Searches: fetched arXiv HTML for 2505.18266 (grepped App E for the L2 coefficients), 2301.05217, 2302.03025, 2306.17844 and 2301.02679, plus the PMLR pages for chughtai23a and stander24a. Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/f2-weight-decay-sparse/CHECK.md

recommended_citations.why: Supports the sparse claim: the AdamW (wd=1) transformer uses 5 key frequencies (Sec 4.1), and ablating everything else improves performance (Sec 4.4). The title and authors were confirmed on arXiv. The ICLR 2023 venue comes from the sweep notes, not from a page fetched here.
Supports the few-irreps claim: with AdamW (wd=1), a very sparse set of directions (standard and sign irreps) explains the logits (Sec 5.1). The number learned varies across seeds (Sec 6).
Supports the few-frequencies claim: AdamW (wd=2) models use a few circles, and three circles give 91.4% accuracy (Sec 3.3).
Supports the group-composition half: S5/S6 MLPs converge on circuits built from subgroups and cosets.

Qualifies and contradicts 'consistently'. One-hot 1-hidden-layer MLPs trained with L2 1e-5 (App E.4 Table 5) learn floor(n/2) frequencies, i.e. dense. **The paper:** "Uncovering a Universal Abstract Algorithm for Modular Addition in Neural Networks" by Gavin McCracken, Gabriela Moisescu-Pareja, Vincent Letourneau, Doina Precup and Jonathan Love, NeurIPS 2025. The refs.bib entry has a nonexistent title and first author ("Andrew McCracken") and must be replaced.

**What McCracken varies and observes:**
- Sec 4.4 / Fig 4 ("Average number of frequencies found in MLPs over moduli 59-66"): "Previous work shows floor(n/2) types of neurons are found ... with 1 hidden layer. We show that adding either depth, or a trainable embedding matrix for inputs, causes the network to transition from learning floor(n/2) types of neurons to much fewer types in Fig. 4."
- App E.4 / Table 5: one-hot ReLU MLPs with 1-4 hidden layers, plus an embedding MLP with 1 hidden layer. Width 1024, lr 7.5e-4, 90% train split, and L2 regularization 1e-5 in every row. Regularization is held fixed.
- All networks are ReLU. The activation or polynomial degree is never varied; quadratic nets are cited only as Gromov's prior theory.
- App G.9.1: "More overparameterized means less frequencies". G.9.2: "Adding depth also means less frequencies are learned".
- Sec 5.1: "While we are the first to point out how to cause a phase transition from O(n) to O(log(n)) learned frequencies (Fig. 4), we don't know why it occurs."

**Degree half: defensible as our reinterpretation.** McCracken's knobs are depth and a trainable embedding. Both raise the homogeneity degree of a ReLU network:
- one-hot, 1 hidden layer: nu=2=b, the dense endpoint (our appendix.tex:283 says this);
- with an embedding or an extra layer: nu>=3 > b=2, the sparse regime.
The sparse count they observe, O(log n), matches our K*=Theta(log p).

**Regularization half: no external support.** McCracken fixes L2 at 1e-5. Morwani et al. 2311.07568 (fetched HTML) do not show a regularization-driven change in frequency count either. **"Explains" overreaches for ReLU.** Our theorems cover product and power neurons. For ReLU the appendix proves only the b=nu upper bound, and says density of the max-margin ReLU network is "a statement about the bound's maximizer, not a theorem about the network". The deep and embedding ReLU nets McCracken studies are covered by no theorem of ours.

item.statement: Morwani find best individual neurons then combine; combining is free exactly at L_{2,nu}; for b<nu output amplitude is cheaper when concentrated so features have a price
item.what_to_check: Verify Morwani's proof structure; check whether Morwani or others already remark on b<nu

chk.evidence:
Source: Morwani et al. (arXiv 2311.07568, ICLR 2024), fetched as arXiv HTML.
- Sec 3.3 blueprint: (1) take a uniform q, (2) find the optimal single neurons with Lemma 5 "Single neuron optimization", (3) combine them with Lemma 5 "Combining neurons".
- Lemma 3 (binary; Lemma 5 is the multi-class version), verbatim: "If b=ν (the homogeneity constant of the network) and ω1*,...,ωm*∈Ωq*, then for any neuron scaling factors Σλi^ν=1, λi≥0 we have that θ={λiωi*} belongs to Θq*." Combining is free exactly at b=ν.
- Sec 3.2: "we will primarily focus on maximum margin with respect to L_{2,ν} norm".
- App. E.1 remark, verbatim: "the analysis can be used to compute optimal norms for b≠ν however, for any such b we would not get the same flexibility to build a θ* satisfying Equation [1]".
- Sec 7: "Our proof holds for ... x² activations ... and L_{2,ν} norm".
- Fig 4b: an L2-trained ReLU net is "nearly 1-sparse" per neuron. That is neuron-level, not a frequency count.

What this means for the claim:
- The paper's description of Morwani's proof structure is accurate.
- Morwani do notice that b≠ν breaks the combining step, but they say nothing about the direction of the effect: that concentrated amplitude is cheaper, that sparsity follows, or that each feature has a price. That part is new here.
- The generic mechanism is known. L2 on a product of D factors equals a concave l_{2/D} quasi-norm cost: Hoff 2017 (CSDA; arXiv 1611.00040) and Kolb et al. ICLR 2025 (2502.02496, abstract: L2 on D factors is equivalent to l_{2/D} sparse regularisation). Dai-Karzand-Srebro NeurIPS 2021 covers the representation-cost framework.
- The sweep found no one applying this to margin or Fourier features. Kam et al. 2609.17926 use a convex l2 amplitude budget and get a dense allocation.

Searches and fetches: arXiv HTML of 2311.07568 (3 targeted reads), 1611.00040 abstract, 2502.02496 abstract, and the NeurIPS 2021 proceedings page for Dai-Karzand-Srebro.

McCracken, Moisescu-Pareja, Letourneau, Precup, Love, arXiv 2505.18266v1 (fetched https://arxiv.org/html/2505.18266v1):

The claim is at approach.tex line 3. It cites Wei et al. 2019 Thm 4.1 for "regularized global minimizers tend to max margin" and states that GD is out of scope. refs.bib has lyu2020gradient, but grep shows it is never cited.

Lyu & Li, ICLR 2020 (arXiv 1906.05890). I read the PDF text.
- Thm 4.1 (Cor. of A.7): under gradient flow, a smoothed normalized margin is non-decreasing.
- Thm 4.4 (Cor. of A.8/E.3): for gradient flow, or GD under (S1),(A2)-(A4),(S5), "any limit point of theta(t)/||theta(t)||_2 is along the direction of a KKT point of (P): min 1/2||theta||^2 s.t. q_n(theta)>=1".
- App. G extends this to multi-class cross-entropy with the logit-difference margin.
- Sec. 4.3 says directly: "it is easy to construct examples that gradient descent does not lead to a normalized margin that is globally optimal. Thus, proving the convergence to KKT points is perhaps the best we can hope for".
- Caveat: this is the plain L2 norm (b=2 only). For b != 2, GD targets KKT points of the L2 problem, not of the L_{2,b} problem.

Ji & Telgarsky, NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv 2006.06657). I read the PDF. Thm 3.1: under Assumptions 2.1 and 2.3 (homogeneous, definable network), for exp/logistic loss, W_t/||W_t|| converges. The result covers binary classification and gradient flow only.

item.location: abstract; intro para 1; intro informal theorem bullet 1
item.statement: Morwani proved that at L_{2,nu} with nu = homogeneity all features (all frequencies / irreps) are used for modular addition and group composition; for quadratic networks every max L_{2,3}-margin net uses Fourier features, one frequency per neuron; our bound at b=nu recovers their max margin exactly
item.what_to_check: Quote Morwani's main theorems (modular addition, sparse parity, group) with numbers; 'one frequency per neuron' wording

chk.evidence:
Sources I fetched: the arXiv 2311.07568 abstract page, which confirms the title, the five authors and "Accepted as Spotlight at ICLR 2024"; the full LaTeX source (e-print); and the arXiv HTML v2 page, which I used for theorem numbers. The refs.bib entry is correct.

What Morwani et al. actually state:
- **Neuron (Sec 2):** the neuron is (u_a+v_b)^2 w. This is a quadratic neuron, so nu=3.
- **Thm 1:** restates Wei et al. 2019 Thm 4.1 about global minimisers: gamma_lambda -> gamma* as lambda -> 0.
- **Thm 7 (modular addition):** "with m >= 4(p-1) neurons. The maximum L_{2,3}-margin ... is gamma* = sqrt(2/27)·1/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). Any network achieving this margin satisfies: (1) for each neuron ... there exists a scaling constant lambda and a frequency zeta" so that u, v, w are cosines at zeta with theta_u+theta_v=theta_w; "(2) For every frequency zeta in {1..(p-1)/2}, at least one neuron in the network uses this frequency."
- **Thm 8 (sparse parity):** uses x^k neurons with L_{2,k+1} and m >= 2^{k-1}, and gives gamma* = k! sqrt(2(k+1)^{-(k+1)}). Every neuron's support is exactly S. This is not an "all features" result.
- **Thm 9 (groups):** quadratic neurons, L_{2,3}, groups with REAL irreps. It needs m >= 2·sum d^3 and the character condition sum_{n>=2} d^{1.5} chi_{R_n}(C) < 0 for every non-trivial conjugacy class. Then gamma* = 2/(3 sqrt(3|G|) sum d^{2.5}). Each neuron is spanned by one non-trivial irrep, and every non-trivial irrep is used.
- **Informal theorem (intro):** "For m >= 4(p-1), any global minimizer ... For every neuron, there exists a frequency such that the input and output weight vectors only use that frequency. There exists at least one neuron of each frequency."
- **Sec 3, "Combining neurons":** works only at b=nu. This supports our intro paragraph 3.
- **Discussion:** "Our proof holds for the case of x^2 activations (x^k activations, in the k-sparse parity case) and L_{2,nu} norm, where nu is the homogeneity constant."

How the paper's claims compare:
- **Intro paragraph 1:** "every max L_{2,3}-margin net uses Fourier features, one frequency per neuron, every frequency" is supported by Thm 7. The theorem needs width m >= 4(p-1).
- **Our b=nu bound recovers their margin:** 2B_p p/(p-1) = 4(6p)^{-3/2} p/(p-1) = sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). I checked this numerically (4/6^1.5 = 0.27217 = sqrt(2/27)). Supported for Thm 7.
- **Overreach in the abstract / paper.tex paragraph 1:** "in networks where L_{2,nu} matches homogeneity nu, all features would be used for modular addition or group composition" goes beyond what Morwani proves. Their proof is for nu=3 only. The general-nu modular-addition result is Li et al. AISTATS 2025 Thm 4.1. Their group result also carries the conditions above (real irreps, character sum, width).
- **"Networks approach max margin"** is Morwani Thm 1 / Wei Thm 4.1. It holds for global minimisers, not for trained networks. This is minor.

Searches: none were needed. I read the primary source directly. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/c1-morwani-dense-baseline/CHECK.md.

item.location: intro para 1 'with vanishing regularization, networks approach the maximum margin solution'
item.statement: With vanishing regularization networks approach the max-margin solution, which can be characterized analytically
item.what_to_check: Wei et al. 2019 Theorem 4.1 statement

chk.evidence:
Checked Wei, Lee, Liu, Ma, "Regularization Matters: Generalization and Optimization of Neural Nets v.s. their Induced Kernel", NeurIPS 2019. I fetched the arXiv 1810.05369 PDF and confirmed the NeurIPS proceedings page.

**Wei et al., Section 4 setting.** f is a-positive-homogeneous and continuous in Theta. The norm can be any general norm. The objective is binary logistic loss + lambda||Theta||^r with r>0 fixed (eq. 4.1).

**Wei et al., Theorem 4.1 (verbatim).** "Assume the training data is separable by a network f(.;Theta*) in F with an optimal normalized margin gamma*>0. Then, the normalized margin of the global optimum of the weakly-regularized objective (equation 4.1) converges to gamma* as the regularization goes to zero ... gamma_lambda -> gamma* as lambda -> 0."

**Wei et al., multi-class version.** Theorem 4.1 is binary only. The multi-class cross-entropy statement is Theorem C.1 in App. C, with margin f_y - max_{j!=y} f_j: "Assume gamma*>0 in the multi-class setting with cross entropy loss. Then as lambda -> 0, gamma_lambda -> gamma*."

**Hypotheses hold in our setting.** L_{2,b} with 2<=b<=nu is a true norm. Here r=b. The polynomial neurons are continuous and nu-homogeneous, and the width is fixed. The result covers global minimizers only, and approach.tex already says so.

**Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2311.07568, PDF fetched).** Section 2 restates "Theorem 1 (Wei et al. (2019a), Theorem 4.1). For any norm, a fixed r>0 and any homogeneous function f with homogeneity constant nu>0, if gamma*>0, then lim gamma_lambda = gamma*." It continues: "This provides the motivation behind studying maximum margin classifiers as a proxy for understanding the global minimizers of L_lambda." Its abstract says "the principle of margin maximization alone can be used to fully specify the features learned by the network." So the "one principle" framing in our sentence is correctly attributed.

**Minor points.**
- The precise multi-class result is Thm C.1, not Thm 4.1. Morwani cites 4.1 too, so this is not an error.
- "Networks approach" informally means that global minimizers of the regularized loss approach gamma* in normalized margin.

**Bib entries.** Both refs.bib entries match the fetched pages.

item.statement: Global minimizers of cross-entropy plus lambda ||theta||_{2,b}^b attain normalized margin tending to gamma*_b as lambda -> 0
item.what_to_check: Verify Theorem 4.1 hypotheses: homogeneous networks, multiclass CE, arbitrary norm (does it cover L_{2,b} with b != nu?), exact statement

chk.evidence:
Read the full text of Wei, Lee, Liu, Ma (arXiv 1810.05369 PDF). Confirmed the venue at proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/8744cf92c88433f8cb04a02e6db69a0d-Abstract.html (NeurIPS 32, 2019).

Sec. 4 setup: f(.;Theta) is a-positive-homogeneous in Theta and continuous. The regulariser uses "some general norm ||.||", with L_lambda = logistic loss + lambda||Theta||^r for fixed r>0 (eq. 4.1). gamma_lambda is the margin of Theta_lambda/||Theta_lambda||, and gamma* = max_{||Theta||<=1} of the min margin.

Theorem 4.1 covers binary logistic loss only: "Assume the training data is separable ... gamma*>0. Then the normalized margin of the global optimum of the weakly-regularized objective (equation 4.1) converges to gamma* as the regularization goes to zero." The text adds: "Though the result in this section is stated for binary classification, it extends to the multi-class setting with cross-entropy loss ... Section C."

Theorem C.1 (App. C) uses softmax CE + lambda||Theta||^r (eq. C.1) and the margin f_y - max_{j!=y} f_j: "Assume gamma*>0 in the multi-class setting with cross entropy loss. Then as lambda -> 0, gamma_lambda -> gamma*." Theorem 4.1 is proved by reduction to C.1.

How the hypotheses match our setting:
- Our net is nu-positive-homogeneous and polynomial, so a = nu and continuity holds.
- ||theta||_{2,b} with 2<=b<=nu (prelim.tex) is a genuine norm, an l_b norm of l_2 norms with b>=1. Wei's general-norm hypothesis therefore covers b != nu.
- The regulariser exponent is r = b.
- The normalized margin h/||theta||^nu and the unit-ball gamma* match Wei's definitions.
- Separability holds because gamma*_b > 0.
- The paper's "global minimizers" and "nothing about GD" agree with Wei's scope.

The only mismatch: modular addition is a multi-class problem, so the correct pointer is Theorem C.1, not 4.1, which is binary. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/c3-wei-thm41/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.why: Supports the approach.tex sentence. Theorem C.1 (the multi-class analogue of Thm 4.1) proves that for any positively homogeneous continuous f, any norm, and any r>0, the global minimizers of cross-entropy + lambda||Theta||^r have normalized margin tending to the max margin gamma*>0 as lambda->0. With a=nu, r=b and ||.||=L_{2,b} (a norm since b>=2), this gives exactly the paper's claim.

Alternatively, cite just [Theorem~C.1]. Add volume={32} to the bib entry.

item.location: intro para 2 'a few irreducible representations'; abstract 'consistent with the empirical results seen in Chughtai'
item.statement: Networks trained on group composition use a few irreps; our optima consistent with Chughtai

chk.evidence:
Checked the PMLR page https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/chughtai23a.html. It confirms Chughtai, Chan, Nanda, ICML 2023, PMLR 202:6243-6267. I also extracted the full text from the arXiv PDF of 2302.03025.

**Setup (App. C).** The networks are one-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs with left/right embeddings, plus a 1-layer transformer. Training uses AdamW with wd lambda=1. They are not product/power neurons and not max-margin. The groups tested are C113, C118, D59, D61, S5, S6 and A5. **S4 is never tested.**

**Table 5 (MLP, 4 seeds each):**
- S5: {sign, standard} twice, {sign, standard, 5d-b}, {sign, standard-sign, standard, 5d-a}.
- A5: {standard, 3d-a, 3d-b} twice, {3d-a, 5d-a, standard}, {5d-a, 3d-a, standard, 3d-b}. The 4d standard irrep appears in every A5 MLP seed.
- C113: 10-15 key frequencies.

**Table 6 (transformer):**
- S5: {sign, standard-sign} twice, {sign, standard} twice.
- A5: {3d-a, 3d-b} twice, {5d-a, 3d-b, 3d-a}, {standard}.

**Fig 7 (S5 MLP, 50 seeds):** "Most commonly we have two key representations (typically sign and standard), but sometimes we learn more."

**Sec 6:**
- "Number of representations learned varies" across seeds.
- "Transformers consistently learn fewer representations than MLPs."
- Networks preferred standard over standard-sign "when in fact standard sign offers better performance for fixed weight norm."

**What this means for each sentence:**
- Intro, "a few irreducible representations": supported for S5, S6 and A5 (1-5 irreps). It overstates for their cyclic and dihedral MLPs, which use 9-15.
- Abstract, "optima consistent with Chughtai": holds for S5, where our one faithful irrep plus the sign patch matches the modal {sign, standard}. For A5, the predicted Galois 3d pair matches only 2 of the 4 transformer seeds. Every MLP seed also uses the 4d standard irrep.
- S4 (named in groups.tex): Chughtai has no data for it.
- groups.tex says "as observed" without saying who observed it.

item.location: abstract; intro para 2 'count moves from dense to sparse as the degree changes'
item.statement: Empirically the number of features moves from dense to sparse as network degree changes
item.what_to_check: Verify McCracken arXiv 2505.18266 findings and full author list (bib has 'and others')

chk.evidence:
I fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18266 and the HTML version on 2026-09-25.

**The bib entry is wrong.** At this ID the paper is "Uncovering a Universal Abstract Algorithm for Modular Addition in Neural Networks" by Gavin McCracken, Gabriela Moisescu-Pareja, Vincent Letourneau, Doina Precup and Jonathan Love. It is arXiv v1, 23 May 2025, the only version, with no venue. The refs.bib title "Emergence of sparse and dense circuits in modular arithmetic networks" and the author "McCracken, Andrew and others" do not exist at that ID.

**What the paper supports.** Sec 4.4 / Fig 4 (caption: "Average number of frequencies found in MLPs over moduli 59-66") says: "Previous work shows floor(n/2) types of neurons are found, each specializing to a sinusoid with one frequency with 1 hidden layer. We show that adding either depth, or a trainable embedding matrix for inputs, causes the network to transition from learning floor(n/2) types of neurons to much fewer types." The setup is ReLU MLPs trained with Adam and a fixed weight decay. So the dense-to-sparse transition itself is supported.

**What it does not support:**
- The trigger McCracken name is depth or a trainable embedding, not "degree". They never mention homogeneity or polynomial degree. For bias-free ReLU nets, each of those changes raises the homogeneity degree from 2 to 3, so "degree" is our reinterpretation. The fetched page did not say whether the nets use biases.
- They never vary weight decay or the regularizer. The abstract's "homogeneity degree or regularization" must not read as if McCracken observed a transition driven by regularization.

**Related results in the same paper:**
- Thm 4.7 / Cor 4.8: O(log n) frequencies give an unnormalised logit margin of Omega(log n). This shows sufficiency only.
- Sec 5.1: "We don't know why it occurs."

Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/c6-mccracken-transition/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.why: Supports the intro and abstract sentence that the count moves from dense to sparse. Sec 4.4 / Fig 4 show 1-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs learn floor(n/2) frequencies, and adding depth or a trainable embedding drops this to far fewer, about log n. Thm 4.7 / Cor 4.8 (O(log n) frequencies suffice for an Omega(log n) unnormalised margin) should also be cited at the lower bound of our log-scaling theorem.

1. Replace the refs.bib entry mccracken2025 with the corrected bibtex (correct title, and all five authors starting with Gavin McCracken).

chk.evidence:
Fetched the arXiv 2311.07568 PDF from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.07568 and extracted it with pdftotext. Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao, Kakade, ICLR 2024.

1. **The L_{2,ν} norm.** Sec. 2 defines ||θ||_{a,b} = (Σ_i ||ω_i||_a^b)^{1/b}, and homogeneity as φ(λω,x) = λ^ν φ(ω,x). Sec. 3.2 says "we will primarily focus on maximum margin with respect to L2,ν norm in this work". This matches "b=ν is Morwani's norm".

3. **The margins.** Sec. 3 defines:
   - g(θ,x,y) = f(θ,x)[y] − max_{y'≠y} f(θ,x)[y'];
   - h(θ) = min_{(x,y)∈D} g;
   - γ* = max_{θ∈Θ} h(θ) with Θ = {||θ|| ≤ 1};

Both papers treat Fourier frequencies as the learned units, but neither defines a feature as a frequency with nonzero logit amplitude. "As in" is therefore too strong.

**Nanda et al., ICLR 2023** (arXiv 2301.05217; PDF fetched, header says "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023").
- Sec. 4.1: "W_E is sparse in the Fourier basis -- it only has significant nonnegligible norm at 6 frequencies. Of these frequencies, only 5 appear to be used significantly in later parts of the model (k in {14,35,41,42,52}). We dub these the key frequencies of the model."

- The paper never calls frequencies "features". The only occurrence of the word is "some feature of the loss landscape".
- Its criterion is empirical and thresholded, and it excludes a frequency that has nonzero embedding norm. So it is not "exactly nonzero means feature". It does match the idea of an amplitude measured at the logit level (in W_L).

**Morwani et al., ICLR 2024** (arXiv 2311.07568v2; PDF and HTML fetched).
- Abstract: "analytically characterize the features learned ... the trained networks utilize Fourier features to perform modular addition".
- Informal theorem and Thm 7: "For every neuron, there exists a frequency such that the Fourier spectra of the input and output weight vectors are supported only on that frequency" and "at least one neuron in the network uses this frequency".
- Here a feature is the Fourier structure of the weights, and "uses a frequency" is defined per neuron by spectral support. That is close in spirit to A_j>0, but it is a different definition.

item.location: approach.tex 'as in Morwani, a single-neuron optimization'
item.statement: Pricing amplitudes in norm reduces to a single-neuron optimization
item.what_to_check: Their single-neuron lemma

chk.evidence:
I read Morwani et al., ICLR 2024 Spotlight, arXiv 2311.07568 v2, in full from the arXiv PDF and checked the venue on the abs page.

Sec 3.1, Lemma 3 (binary; proof in App E.1) and Sec 3.2, Lemma 5 (multi-class, class-weighted; App E.2) each have a 'Single neuron optimization' bullet. It says that for a fixed distribution q, any theta in argmax_{||theta||_{a,b}<=1} E_q[g(theta)] 'has directional support only on' Omega*_q = argmax_{||omega||_a<=1} E_q[psi(omega)]. The justification is that 'the expected margin of the network decomposes into the sum of expected margin of individual neurons', so E_q g = sum_i ||omega_i||^nu E_q psi(omega_i/||omega_i||) <= gamma max_{||w||_b<=1} ||w||_nu^nu. Combining neurons needs b = nu, and the Remark in App E.1 says other b values do not give the flexibility needed to satisfy Eq. 1. These lemmas serve the certificate-pair method (Lemma 2 / Lemma 6). Thm 7 applies it by maximising sum_j u^(j) v^(j) w^(-j) over one unit neuron.

What is shared: a network sum is reduced by homogeneity to a single unit-norm neuron problem.

What differs:
- Morwani's per-neuron objective is a linear expected margin under a dual q, used for a primal-dual certificate at b = nu.
- The paper's C_b = max_{||omega||<=1} sum_j |beta_j(omega)|^{b/nu} is a concave l_{b/nu} budget. It feeds a subadditivity upper bound for all 2 <= b <= nu and uses no dual distribution.

So 'as in Morwani' fits the decomposition idea but not their lemma as stated. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/c11-morwani-single-neuron/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.why: Lemmas 3 and 5 ('Single neuron optimization') support the reduction of a network-level objective to a unit-norm single-neuron maximisation via per-neuron additivity and homogeneity. Keep the citation, but point to those lemmas and say the objective differs.

Here the per-neuron quantity is an $\ell_{b/\nu}$ budget of its Fourier coefficients rather than an expected margin under a dual distribution."

item.location: approach.tex cor:dense; appendix app:dense and app:models power neuron
item.statement: 2B_p p/(p-1) = sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) is exactly Morwani's max L_{2,3} margin; their network attains the bound so C_3 = 2B_p
item.what_to_check: Verify constant in Morwani's modular-addition theorem

chk.evidence:
I fetched https://arxiv.org/html/2311.07568 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07568. The paper is "Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks" by Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao and Kakade; the arXiv comment says "Spotlight at ICLR 2024".

What the paper says: Theorem 7 (cyclic groups) covers a prime p>2, width m >= 4(p-1), quadratic activations, and the neuron phi({u,v,w},a,b)=(u_a+v_b)^2 w. It states: "the maximum L_{2,3}-margin is gamma* = sqrt(2/27)*1/(p^{1/2}(p-1))". At the maximum, each neuron is a single-frequency cosine and every frequency zeta in {1..(p-1)/2} is used by some neuron.

How it matches our paper:
- Our power neuron at n=2 is exactly their neuron.
- b=nu=3 is their L_{2,3} norm.
- Our margin definitions g, h and gamma*_b match theirs.

Arithmetic: 2B_p p/(p-1) = 4(6p)^{-3/2} p/(p-1) = (2/(3 sqrt6))/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) = sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)). I checked this numerically at p=3, 5 and 113; the two sides agree to machine precision.

Attainment: their theorem gives the global maximum, and their construction attains it. Our bound is an upper bound at every width. Since the two are equal, C_3 = 2B_p follows. One caveat is that their theorem assumes width m >= 4(p-1).

The intro sentence ("every frequency is used, one frequency per neuron") also matches Theorem 7.

recommended_citations.why: Theorem 7 gives the maximum L_{2,3} margin sqrt(2/27)/(p^{1/2}(p-1)) for quadratic networks (u_a+v_b)^2 w of width >= 4(p-1) on modular addition. It supports cor:dense, app:dense and the claim C_3 = 2B_p. The existing bib entry is correct.

item.location: appendix app:scaling 'cyclic case of the random Cayley graph argument'
item.statement: Random O(log p) frequency set lower bound is the cyclic case of Alon-Roichman
item.what_to_check: Alon-Roichman theorem statement and bib details (RSA 5(2):271-284, 1994)

chk.evidence:
The citation is at sections/appendix.tex line 196, closing the lower-bound proof in app:scaling. That proof draws L = ceil(8 ln p) frequencies at random and uses Hoeffding plus a union bound over offsets to show that the average of cos(2 pi J delta/p) is at most 1/2 for every delta != 0.

Bibliographic details:
- Crossref (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/rsa.3240050203) confirms the bib entry exactly: "Random Cayley graphs and expanders", Noga Alon and Yuval Roichman, Random Structures & Algorithms 5(2):271-284, 1994.
- Semantic Scholar (DOI:10.1002/rsa.3240050203, DBLP journals/rsa/AlonR94) agrees.

What the paper says, from the Crossref abstract: for every 0 < delta < 1 there is a c(delta) such that, for any group of order n, a random set of c(delta) log n elements gives a Cayley graph whose expected second-largest normalised adjacency eigenvalue is at most 1 - delta. The abstract adds that the result is "essentially optimal for Abelian groups".

I could not get the full text. The Wiley page returned 403 and the author-site PDFs returned 404, so I have no theorem number.

Why the attribution holds:
- For G = Z_p, the eigenvalues of Cay(Z_p, {±J_l}) are exactly (1/L) sum_l cos(2 pi J_l delta/p) for delta != 0.
- So our step is the Alon-Roichman statement on a cyclic group, with 1 - delta = 1/2 and c = 8.
- For abelian groups, the Alon-Roichman proof is the same Chernoff bound over characters plus a union bound.
- Both bounds are one-sided (on the second-largest eigenvalue), so the direction matches.

Searches: I ran no WebSearch (the session's budget was exhausted). I fetched Crossref, the Semantic Scholar API and the Wiley DOI page (403).

recommended_citations.why: Supports app:scaling line 196. A random set of c(delta) log n group elements gives second eigenvalue <= 1-delta. On Z_p the eigenvalues are the cosine averages our Hoeffding argument bounds by 1/2, so our lower bound is the cyclic instance. The abstract also says the result is essentially optimal for abelian groups.

Optionally, add doi={10.1002/rsa.3240050203} to the bib entry and sharpen the sentence to: "This is the cyclic case of the random Cayley graph theorem of \citet{alon1994random}: the averages $\frac1L\sum_\ell\cos(2\pi J_\ell\delta/p)$ are the nontrivial eigenvalues of $\mathrm{Cay}(\sZ_p,\{\pm J_\ell\})$, and $O(\log p)$ random generators push them all below $1/2$. item.statement: Weight decay on products of nu factors induces an l_{2/nu}-type quasi-norm sparsity penalty
item.what_to_check: Find and cite representation-cost papers (Gunasekar 2018, Woodworth 2020, Dai et al. 2021, Tibshirani 2021, Jacobs-Montufar)

chk.evidence:
The sentence in question is approach.tex line 45: "The exponent comes from homogeneity ... AM--GM, so amplitude A costs a multiple of A^{b/nu}". It currently has no citation.

Closest match is Tibshirani, "Equivalences Between Sparse Models and Neural Networks" (note dated 15 Apr 2021). I read the full PDF text at https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/papers/sparsitynn.pdf.
- Sec 2.2 (Multi-layer case), eqs (8)->(9): min_{prod a_l=c} sum a_l^2 = k|c|^{2/k}, with the minimum at |a_l|=|c|^{1/k}. The note says "we can interpret this as saying that the AM-GM inequality ... is tight when a_1=...=a_k".
- So a k-layer net with weight decay equals l_p-penalised regression with p=2/k<1, which is "nonconvex" and gives sparse solutions, "even more so for greater depth".
- Sec 3.2 gives the group-lasso l_{2/k} version.
- This is exactly our statement for b=2. Ours is the one-line generalisation to an L_{2,b} cost, which gives A^{b/nu}.

Other sources, each confirmed on a fetched page:
- Hoff, arXiv 1611.00040. Abstract: "a subclass of L_q penalties with q<=1 can be expressed as sums of L_2 penalties".
- Dai, Karzand, Srebro, NeurIPS 2021 (proceedings page). The representation cost that l2 on parameters induces, including which l_p and group norms arise.
- Gunasekar, Lee, Soudry, Srebro, NeurIPS 2018 (papers.nips.cc). Gradient descent on depth-L linear conv nets converges to a predictor related to the "l_{2/L} bridge penalty in the frequency domain". This is a Fourier-sparsity parallel, but it is implicit bias, not weight decay.
- Kolb et al., ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2502.02496). L2 on factors is equivalent to nonconvex sparse regularisation.
- Ongie-Parhi, arXiv 2606.14954. Weight-decay cost of deep ReLU nets is a quasi-norm with a nonconvex ball for L>2.

Rejected as off-point:
- Woodworth et al. 2020 (arXiv 2002.09277): kernel vs rich regimes and init scale; no weight-decay quasi-norm identity.
- Jacobs-Montufar: better placed in related work.

Limits: WebSearch budget was exhausted and Semantic Scholar returned 429. Tibshirani's venue is not shown in the PDF, so cite it as a technical note. Notes are in /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/u1-representation-cost/CHECK.md.

recommended_citations.why: Supports the AM-GM exponent sentence. Sec 2.2, eqs (8)-(9): min over prod a_l=c of sum a_l^2 = k|c|^{2/k}, which is AM-GM tight at equal factors, so a k-factor ridge penalty becomes an l_{2/k} quasi-norm that induces sparsity. Sec 3.2 gives the group version. This is our statement at b=2. The venue is not shown in the PDF, so cite it as a technical note.

The abstract says a subclass of L_q penalties (q<=1) can be written as sums of L_2 penalties under a multiplicative (Hadamard) reparametrisation. This is the scalar version of our AM-GM step. The journal ref CSDA 115:186-198 (2017) comes from the sweep and was not shown on the fetched arXiv page.

The general framework: the representation cost in predictor space induced by l2 regularisation on parameters, including which l_p and group norms arise from a parameterisation. Our A^{b/nu} price is a representation cost in this sense.

Optional 'cf.' citation. Gradient descent on depth-L linear conv nets converges to a predictor related to the l_{2/L} bridge penalty in the frequency domain. This is the closest earlier instance of a 2/depth exponent producing sparsity over Fourier frequencies, but it is implicit bias, not explicit weight decay.

Depth-D weight factorisation with L2 on the factors is provably equivalent to nonconvex sparse regularisation. This is the modern ML statement of the same mechanism. The ICLR 2025 venue is from the arXiv page.

item.statement: Minima of cosine sums over Z_p / sets with small Fourier bias need Theta(log p) elements
item.what_to_check: Chowla cosine problem, epsilon-biased sets, Alon 2009 lower bounds; sidelobe design

chk.evidence:
Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/u6-cosine-sum-minima/CHECK.md.

Setup: with equal weights on K frequencies, m(y) = min_{delta!=0} sum_j y_j(1-cos(2 pi j delta/p)) equals K minus half the second eigenvalue of Cay(Z_p, {±j}). So the classical background is "abelian Cayley graphs need Omega(log n) generators to expand, and O(log n) random ones suffice."

Sources I fetched and read this session:

(1) Alon & Roichman, RSA 5(2):271-284, 1994. Metadata from Crossref; text from the author PDF web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/exp1.pdf.
- Abstract: "For Abelian groups this is essentially tight."
- Sec. 3, Proposition 3, verbatim: "For every fixed delta>0 there is a constant c=c(delta)>0 such that the following holds; If A is an Abelian group of order n, and X(A,S) is a delta-expander, then |S| >= c log_2 n."
- Prop. 7' gives a closed-walk lower bound on |mu_1| for arbitrary S. This is the same device as eq:posfourier.
- This entry is already in the bib (alon1994random), but the paper cites it only for the random lower bound. It is not cited for the Omega(log) necessity.

(2) Friedman, Murty & Tillich, JCTB 96(1):111-121, 2006. Metadata from Crossref; text from the author PDF at rocq.inria.fr.
- Abstract, verbatim: "a d-regular Cayley graph on an Abelian group of order n has second eigenvalue bounded below by d - O(dn^{-4/d}) ... for a large odd prime, n, the O(dn^{-4/d}) cannot be improved."
- Sec. 2, Thm 2 is the sphere-packing proof. Sec. 4, Thm 7 covers random Cayley graphs on Z/nZ with n prime.
- This is the quantitative unweighted form of our upper bound.

(3) Alon, "Perturbed identity matrices have high rank", CPC 18(1-2):3-15, 2009. Metadata from the Cambridge page; text from the author PDF identity1.pdf.
- Thm 7.1: an eps-biased family of n ±1 variables needs a sample space of size Omega(n/(eps^2 log(1/eps))).
- It is two-sided and stated only for Z_2^n, so it is adjacent at best.

Checked and rejected:
- Chowla cosine problem (Bedert arXiv 2509.05260, JMTZ arXiv 2509.03490, Shankar arXiv 2609.05338; from the sweep). It bounds how negative min sum cos must be, which is the opposite tail from ours. Neither result implies the other.
- Sidelobe and coding literature (AIKPS 1990 thin sets). Two-sided explicit constructions only; optional.
- Dirichlet / Bohr-set bound (Tao-Vu Lemma 4.20). Not fetched, so I give no bib entry.

What none of these covers: they are all unweighted, fixed-degree statements. I found no weighted concave-l_{1/s}-budget analogue. That analogue is the two-sided Theta((log p)^{1-s}), the Theta(log p) support with a share floor, and the o(log p) vanishing fraction. My web-search budget was exhausted, so this relies on the fetched PDFs and the sibling items t9, r25 and r26.

recommended_citations.why: Already in bib. Cite it in the thm:scaling discussion for the necessity half: Prop. 3 says an abelian Cayley graph that is a delta-expander needs |S| >= c(delta) log2 n. Thm 2 covers sufficiency for random sets. Together they are the unweighted Theta(log p) statement.

The quantitative unweighted version of the upper bound on m(y): lambda_2 >= d - O(d n^{-4/d}) for d-regular abelian Cayley graphs, tight for prime n. With equal shares this gives m = O(K p^{-2/K}), so K must be Omega(log p).

Optional 'cf.' citation. Thm 7.1 is the two-sided small-bias lower bound: an eps-biased family of n variables needs a sample space of size Omega(n/(eps^2 log 1/eps)), i.e. eps-biased sets in Z_2^n have size Omega(log|G|). It is stated for Z_2^n only and is two-sided, so it is weaker than what the paper needs.

chk.recommended_change:
In cyclic.tex, after the paragraph following thm:scaling (or after cor:few), add:

"With equal shares, $m(y)$ is $K$ minus half the second eigenvalue of $\mathrm{Cay}(\sZ_p,\{\pm j\})$. So the unweighted case of Theorem~\ref{thm:scaling} is the classical fact that Cayley graphs of abelian groups need $\Omega(\log n)$ generators to expand, while $O(\log n)$ random ones suffice \citep[Thm.~2, Prop.~3]{alon1994random}. Quantitatively, $\lambda_2\ge d-O(dn^{-4/d})$, which is tight for prime $n$ \citep{friedman2006spectral}. Our contribution is the weighted version under the concave budget $\sum_j y_j^{1/s}\le1$, where pigeonhole alone gives only $K=O(\log p/\log\log p)$. Unlike Chowla's cosine problem, which asks how negative a cosine sum must become, this concerns how close to its peak it must return."

Also add the friedman2006spectral bib entry. Do not cite the Chowla papers as support.

item.statement: Products of cosines produce label-independent cos(a-b) copies in trained networks
item.what_to_check: Nanda 2023, Gromov 2023, Morwani discuss these terms

chk.evidence:
The paragraph in cyclic.tex cites nothing. Three sources support it; Nanda does not.

1. Gromov 2023, arXiv 2301.02679, Sec. 3.1. I read the PDF text directly.
   - Eq. (10): the squared activation expands to include "+ cos(2pi k(n-m)/p + phi1 - phi2)".
   - Eq. (11): the second-layer preactivation includes cos(2pi k(n-m-q)/p + ...) and cos(2pi k(n-m+q)/p + ...). These are exactly the paper's beta_{j,T} copies.
   - Eq. (12): phi1 + phi2 = phi3 gives constructive interference.
   - Eqs. (14)-(15): "we need to ensure that all other waves (i.e. all terms, but the third term in (11)) interfere destructively". Random phases achieve this, since sum_k cos(2pi k s/p + phi_k) << N.
   - The cancellation is approximate. Our condition is exact (Def. if), and our per-neuron sign rule is new.

2. Morwani et al. ICLR 2024, arXiv 2311.07568 (HTML read).
   - App. F.3: a neuron's DFT is nonzero only if j = 0, k = 0, or "j,k,l = ±zeta". That set includes the mixed-sign, label-independent modes.
   - A max-margin f has f_hat supported only on j = k = -l (plus l = 0).
   - App. F.2 builds 8 neurons per frequency with paired phases, so the sum is exactly cos(a+b-c) and the rest cancels. This is an implicit interference-free construction; they never name the a-b term.

3. He, Wang, Chen, Yang, arXiv 2602.16849 (Feb 2026), Sec. 4.
   - Eq. (4.1): a quadratic neuron outputs the signal times cos(omega(x-y)/2)^2, plus "residual noise".
   - Def. 4.1 (full diversification, phase sums exp(i·iota·sum phi_m) = 0) and Prop. 4.2: the diversified neurons collectively cancel that noise.

4. Nanda et al. 2023 (PDF text grepped): discusses constructive and destructive interference of the logit cosines only. There is no a-b product-to-sum term, so do not cite it here.
